en: The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of the Golden-Colored Boy, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao San Dafu,
Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Grand Master of Light and Dharma, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa.
I, the subject Jing and others, having received the imperial decree, have translated as follows:

We have heard that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa has already attained the perfect and eternal state; the Venerable Ānanda possesses great majestic virtue and profound wisdom, being no different from the Venerable Śāriputra. With a compassionate heart like that of the Buddha, he universally gathers all beings, and throughout kingdoms, cities, villages, and regions, wherever they may be, he employs supreme skillful means to discipline and transform all sentient beings.

Then, at a later time, for the sake of extensively teaching and transforming hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings, he proclaimed the True Dharma and rained down the nectar of immortality, pouring it into their hearts and crowns; throughout the entire Āmra Grove of the City of Vaiśālī, he brought about benefit and happiness for all.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a merchant leader named Sūryodgata who resided within the city. He was exceedingly wealthy in treasures and jewels, with a vast and flourishing retinue; his extensive and great accumulation of wealth was no different from that of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King.

Because of his great prosperity, he had married into a noble family, and they lived together in play, recreation, and enjoyment. However, after a long time, no offspring were born; the elder’s relatives harbored deep longing and became filled with extreme distress.

At that time, there was a certain son of heaven among the Trāyastriṃśa gods who possessed merit, majesty, and virtue. As his celestial retribution was nearing its end, the five signs of decay appeared; nevertheless, because he desired to behold the Buddha’s appearance in the world and all matters concerning his parinirvāṇa and adornments, he sought to take rebirth in succession within the human realm.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, observing that the devaputra was about to pass away and desiring to behold the Buddha’s majestic adornments and other such matters, wished to take rebirth in succession among human beings.
Having understood this, he then said to that deva:
"If you desire to be born among humans, you should know this: in the city of Rājagṛha there is a merchant leader named Sūryodgata, and his wife is fit for you to deposit your consciousness."
The devaputra replied,
"I have heard in the past that this merchant leader has no pure faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Śakra spoke again:
“O Benevolent One!
Now you should act as I have instructed; I am able to cause that merchant leader Sūryodgata to give rise to profound pure faith in the Buddha-dharma.
The devaputra replied:
“As the Lord of Devas has spoken, so shall it be; we accept your instruction.
If that merchant leader and his wife take refuge in the Triple Gem for as long as they live, I shall comply with your command and enter their womb.”

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, vanished from among the gods and appeared in mid-air within the house of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha in the great city of Rājagṛha. Abiding there with the physical form and majestic power of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, he caused a subtle, wondrous light to radiate all around the house, illuminating it completely.

At that time, the merchant leader Sūryaprabha, having seen this subtle and wondrous radiance, was struck with profound wonder. Raising his joyful eyes, he gazed intently in all four directions; upon careful observation, he beheld the sublime form of Śakra, Lord of the Devas. He immediately prostrated himself at the deity’s feet and addressed him, saying:
"Lord of Devas!..."
Today I have attained a most excellent benefit, for you, O Holy Lord of Devas, have descended to this humble abode;
what instructions do you intend to give, and what auspicious and supreme matters shall be accomplished?
The Lord of Devas replied:
“O Merchant Chief!

Knowing that you have no son, if you desire to have offspring, you and your wife should from this day forward, until the end of your lives, give rise to a pure heart and take refuge in the Triple Gem; thus shall a noble son be born.”
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader Sūrya felt his mind become serene; leaping for joy, he spoke thus:
"O Lord of Devas!
"Following your venerable instructions, from this day forward until the end of our lives, we, together with our wives, shall all give rise to a pure mind and take refuge in the Triple Gem."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having inspired pure faith in the merchant Sūryaprabha and his wife and led them to take refuge in the Triple Gem, immediately vanished from the city of Rājagṛha and returned to his celestial palace among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. Standing before that devaputra, he proclaimed in full detail each of the aforementioned events and circumstances for him.
Subsequently, that deva, having passed away from his celestial existence in that heaven, was conceived in the womb of the wife of the merchant leader Divākara in the city of Rājagṛha.

When the Noble Son entered the womb, these wondrous signs appeared: the wife of the merchant lord naturally possessed the most sublime physical marks and majestic radiance, and a pleasing fragrant breeze frequently came to blow upon her.
At that time, within the noble families of the city, women of virtue were all born with wisdom, and they possessed five further extraordinary characteristics.
What are these five?
First, they are able to know what others love and delight in.
Second, being able to know those who do not find pleasure [in the teaching];
third, knowing the proper time;
fourth, being able to discern the subtle details within that time.
Fifth, he is able to know the matter of entering the womb.

Regarding the matter of entering the womb: it means that at the time of entry, he knows whether the one to be born will be male or female; if it is male, he dwells within the womb on the right side, and if it is female, he dwells within the womb on the left side.
At that time, his wife felt great joy in her heart and said to her husband:

"You should know this: as I observe the noble child I now carry, the stages of the fetal development are gradually increasing and maturing; it dwells on my right side, and it is certain that he will later be born as a male."
Upon hearing this, her husband was filled with even greater joy.
At that time, the merchant’s wife felt her body become light; she extended her right arm and spoke these words:
“For a long time I have yearned for an offspring and wished to behold my son’s face. Now that I carry this child, whether it be born or yet unborn, I ought to perform meritorious deeds.”
He immediately summoned his steward and said:
"Gather precious wealth and practice generosity according to your means, so that my lineage may endure for a long time in prosperity.
For what reason?..."

In my previous lives, whether it was little or much, I practiced giving and performed meritorious deeds; consequently, in this present life, the reputation for generosity does not fall away, and it continues to follow me from birth to birth without being lost.
At that time, the wife of the merchant leader’s womb gradually developed; perceiving the signs in advance, she stayed in a secure place on a high terrace and carefully nurtured herself.

When it is cold, they provide excellent nourishment in accordance with the cold; when it is hot, they provide excellent nourishment in accordance with the heat. Through the administration of medicines and the regulation of diet, the flavors of bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland are all kept free from excess; the six tastes are harmonized and balanced, remaining devoid of any faults.

Furthermore, their bodies were adorned with necklaces and ornaments like those of celestial maidens; they constantly sported in the Joyful Garden (*Nandana-vana*), where their seats and couches adjusted their height according to their ease. When walking upon the ground, it was never hard or rough, nor did they ever hear unpleasant sounds.

Subsequently, as the stages within the womb reached full maturity—whether after eight months or nine months—a boy was born. His physical appearance was exceptionally beautiful and pleasing to behold; he was upright and handsome, with fully developed limbs. His body possessed a golden radiance that shone brilliantly, and all his faculties were complete, delighting the eyes and gladdening the heart.
The assembly beheld him together: a golden-yellow robe spontaneously covered his body, a breeze fragrant with sandalwood perfumed his person, and from his mouth issued the fragrance of blue lotuses.

When the boy was born, a rain of various exquisite garments fell once more within the elder’s house; all the garments that rained down were of golden hue, and *kaniṅka* flowers fell in profusion. Thus did such rare and auspicious signs manifest, vast and perfectly fulfilled.
At that time, the merchant-suzerain Sūrya, together with his wife and all his kinsmen, having witnessed this event, were all filled with wonder and amazement.
The merchant-suzerain then emerged from his house and stood by the gateway; looking out from without, his joy increased all the more. Having seen these signs, he thought to himself:
"The birth of this boy is truly a source of great increase; my heart is filled with the most supreme and ultimate delight."
He returned to his house, and later, upon seeing this youth—whose physical appearance was exceptionally beautiful, upright, and magnificent—he leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
"How wonderful! How marvelous!"
I have now attained a sublime benefit!
How joyful!
My heart's desire is fully accomplished.
"A son of merit and majesty has been born today; therefore, my heart is filled with great joy.

Having spoken these verses, out of his joy, he further brought forth exquisite garments from his home and bestowed them universally upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the orphaned, the destitute, his kinsmen, and his relatives, thereby performing meritorious deeds.

At that time, twenty-one days had already passed since the boy’s birth, and after extensive preparations for various meritorious rites had been completed, his kinsmen deliberated together on what name should be given to him. A relative said:
"This boy’s body possesses a golden hue and a brilliant, radiant light; therefore, we, his kinsmen, shall now give this boy the name 'Golden One' (Suvarṇa)."
Once the assembly had reached a consensus, the boy was thus named Suvarṇavarṇa.
At that time, the merchant leader selected eight women for the boy Suvarṇavarṇa to serve as his mothers:
two to nourish him;
The second is for washing;
the second is for suckling;
and the second is for play and amusement.

By this means, he is swiftly nurtured and brought to maturity, like a pure lotus emerging from the mud; he shall then gradually be instructed in the arts and skills of a youth, whether writing, arithmetic, or various occupations:
first, the arrangement of writing, arithmetic, and seals;
second, the arrangement of all necessary implements.
Third, the distribution of clothing;
fourth, the arrangement of horses;
fifth, the provision of carriages.
Sixth, they distributed precious jewels;
seventh, they distributed young boys;
eighth, they distributed young girls.
Once these eight types [of arts] had been extensively arranged for him, he was made to observe them all in order to test his inclinations.

Subsequently, the youth’s artistic skills were perfected; his speech became clear and sharp; his faith was pure, and his resolve was noble and virtuous. He was capable of benefiting both himself and others, possessing great majesty and virtue; he skillfully cultivated compassionate conduct and achieved a desire for the Dharma; he cherished sentient beings with wisdom that was lucid and penetrating; he was well-versed in literary treatises; thus, the youth’s accomplishments were fully complete.
At that time, the merchant leader thought to himself:
"This youth possesses the full perfection of clothing, wealth, and treasures through the power of his merit and majesty; yet I do not know what the cause of this merit and majesty may be."
"Is it not because of the supreme power of my taking refuge in the Triple Gem that this son was born and obtained such excellent merit?
Thereafter, the merchant leader developed pure faith in the Buddha's Dharma and performed various Buddhist rites according to the proper time and requirements.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a merchant leader named Vimala. Having traveled across the great ocean, he returned safely with his profits fully realized. He prepared a pure and abundant meal offering for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and his retinue of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus; having completed this, he further bestowed three robes upon each individual bhikṣu as an act of charity.
Thereupon, the fame of the merchant leader Vimala’s pure faith pervaded the world, and all praised him, saying:

"Now this merchant leader is a skillful guide for merchants; having crossed the great ocean, his fruits and benefits were not in vain, as he is able to perform vast and sublime deeds within the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader Sūryodgata wished to emulate them and formed this thought:

"If I, like them, traverse the great ocean and return without difficulty, I vow that I shall gather all the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, even those dwelling throughout this Jambudvīpa, into a single assembly by means of the Buddha’s instructions."

I shall provide all of them with the finest food and drink until they are fully supplied, and furthermore, I shall bestow upon each and every bhikṣu a set of the three excellent robes for their constant use.
Having formed this thought, he related all that had occurred to his wife. His wife immediately replied, "Husband!
If you possess the power and means, whatever you wish for will surely be accomplished."

At that time, the merchant leader Sūrya, having sounded the bell three times throughout the city of Rājagṛha to issue a universal warning, set out upon the great ocean with his retinue of five hundred merchants; having successfully crossed over, they were established securely in that region.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already entered parinirvāṇa; subsequently, it was heard that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had also entered parinirvāṇa.
Later, while at the Bamboo Grove Monastery, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa heard a bhikṣu reciting the verse on impermanence:
“Whether by day or by night, Whether walking or standing still,”
Like the swift current of a great river, which never ceases for even a single thought-moment,
life diminishes with every passing night;
like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be in this?
This physical form decays and withers; when sickness gathers, it is destroyed.
Like a sheep being slaughtered, once life departs, death is not far off.
This body does not endure for long; it is composed of the six great elements, such as earth and the rest.
It is like dwelling in a desolate wilderness, Without gates or locks.
What joy is there in this body?
Filled with a torrent of filth and impurity, Entangled by the suffering of illness, One is constantly terrified by old age and death.
"This foul and impure body, when afflicted by disease, immediately falls apart;
when one attains supreme tranquility, that is the highest bliss.

At that time, having heard this verse, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa conceived a profound sense of weary detachment toward saṃsāra and rejoiced in nirvāṇa, praising it extensively. He then immediately paid homage to the bhikṣu and asked:
"I have heard the verses recited by the Noble One; what do you say they mean?
The bhikṣu replied, "You should know now that these are the words of the Buddha."
Having heard this, the youth conceived even deeper pure faith in the Buddha’s Dharma and, with sincere earnestness, desired to go forth.
Bowing most reverently before the bhikṣu once more, he prostrated himself and addressed him, saying:
“Noble One!
"I now desire to leave the household life for the sake of purity; I only pray that the Noble One, out of compassion, will take me in so that I may go forth.
The bhikṣu replied, "Do your parents permit you to go forth?"
The youth replied,
"I have not yet received his command.
The bhikṣu said:
"You should now go and inform your parents; if they grant their permission, you may then leave the household life.
The youth replied, "I shall do as your reverence instructs."

At that time, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa felt profound weariness toward birth and death and was struck with great fear; his mind was set on the joy of renunciation. He immediately returned to his own home, went to his mother’s presence, prostrated at her feet, and addressed her, saying: "May my mother know this:
I now desire to leave the household life for the sake of purity and to practice the True Dharma within the Buddha's teachings. I pray only that you will grant me your permission."
Having heard these words, the mother was struck with terror and alarm; she clasped her knees and lamented piteously, saying to her son:
"You are my only child, whom I love and cherish. I have followed your every wish in a hundred ways; why do you now abandon me to go forth into the religious life?"
The son said to his mother:

"Mother, you should now know that all those things we hold dear are certain to be separated from us; I pray that you will now permit me to leave the household life to practice the sublime Dharma and Vinaya."
Having heard these words, the mother’s heart was filled with even greater distress; her throat choked with emotion and tears falling, she spoke again to her son:
"My son, you should know now: do not repeat such words before me three times more, lest hot blood flow from your own mouth."
His mother immediately reflected to herself:
"If it is thus impossible to ultimately restrain his inclinations, I should employ skillful means to resolve his mind."
He then spoke again, saying:
"Young man!

Your father possesses pure faith and has extensively undertaken great deeds for the sake of the Buddha-dharma; he has already set out upon the great ocean and will return before long. You should now wait for your father’s return, for once he returns, he will surely give you his command to allow you to go forth."
At that time, the youth, out of filial devotion to his mother, thought to himself:
"If I were to address my request to her again, it would surely cause my mother extreme distress; I should instead obey her command and wait for my father to return home."
Thereupon, the youth silently accepted the instruction.

At that time, because the youth Suvarṇavarṇa was so adorned with such exquisite and magnificent physical marks, wherever he traveled through the four crossroads, the crowds gazed upon him, never tiring of the sight.
At that time, the boy’s mother again thought to herself:

"My son is handsome and his physical features are exceptionally beautiful; he is beloved by all. Yet, my son has developed a deep sense of revulsion toward worldly dharmas, and for this reason, my mind is constantly filled with doubt as to why this son would suddenly abandon me to go forth into homelessness."
"I should now follow and protect him; once my son has departed, suffering will surely arise.
*The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of the Golden Boy*, Fascicle One.
*The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of the Golden Boy*, Fascicle Two.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Radiant Dharma, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing and others, by imperial decree.

At that time, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa constantly associated with wise śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, following them to listen to and receive their excellent teachings on the Dharma of the path to liberation; furthermore, he personally transcribed the scriptures and engaged in other noble undertakings.

At that time, outside the city of Rājagṛha, the merchant leader Sūryodgata possessed a great park, lush with flowers and fruits and adorned with clear, flowing streams; the youth Suvarṇavarṇa went there daily for recreation, sometimes staying there to recite the sūtras.
At that time, there was a courtesan in the city of Rājagṛha named Kāśisundarī, who was young, beautiful, and admired by all.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru had a minister named Virūḍhaka, whom the king held in extreme favor and entrusted with many duties; he had long been deeply attached to that courtesan and invited her daily to his garden to amuse himself with her.

Thereafter, at one time, that maiden Kāśisundarī, adorned with exquisite ornaments, departed from the city of Rājagṛha for the Caitraratha Garden. Just as she reached the road, she saw the youth Suvarṇavarṇa also departing from outside Rājagṛha for the Sūryaprabha Garden. His physical appearance was exceptionally beautiful, upright, and dignified; his body possessed a golden radiance that blazed brilliantly, and a golden-yellow robe naturally covered his form. He was pleasing to the eye and gratifying to the mind, and all beheld him with admiration.
Having seen her, she then thought:
"How marvelous!
Her physical form and features are so exceptionally sublime."
"How marvelous!
His majestic radiance is incomparably brilliant.
Having thought this, he immediately gazed at him to his heart's content, and further reflected:

"If there is a woman in the world endowed with merit, she should obtain such a son as her husband; for a woman of little merit, it would be difficult to find such a man for her pleasure and amusement."
But as for me now, what shall I do?
Do I wish to pray for a favorable connection, and will there be no hindrance?
For what reason?
Now this youth is uniquely and exquisitely beautiful among all men; although I have conceived a profound affection for him, by what means might I achieve a union with him?
He immediately hurried before the youth and gazed at him with focused attention, reflecting to himself:

"This youth’s physical nature is upright and serene, endowed with great majestic virtue; he has turned his back on worldly desires, defilements, and improper conditions, and is proceeding toward the true, correct path of Nirvana. Although I cherish and admire him, he does not accept me;
I must not suffer such humiliation here. I shall no longer remain in the Park of the Fierce and Impetuous, but should follow him to wherever he dwells."
Having spoken thus, he immediately followed behind the youth in secret.
At that time, the youth, having become aware of this matter, quickly went on ahead and entered the park, ordering the gatekeeper to close the gate.
At that time, the maiden Kāśisundarī spoke from behind the door, saying:
"Young man!
What is the reason for closing the garden gate?"
"I have come here specifically for your sake; yet you now stubbornly refuse to allow me to behold you, which is not appropriate.
The youth remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the woman reflected again:
"This youth will come to one of two outcomes:
first, he may never be defiled by worldly desires at all;"
Second, he may be possessed by a malevolent spirit.

In every instance, whether through my physical appearance or my speech, one will be unable to draw near him. Although I now desire to approach him with intimacy, he observes me and keeps his doors closed; no matter what skillful means or expedients I employ, he will ultimately bar my way.

I shall now ensure that he does not perceive me; instead, I will wait until tomorrow morning to enter the garden first, remaining hidden and staying there through the night. This youth will surely arrive later, at which point I will approach him and draw near in secret.
Having formed this thought, the woman immediately turned back and entered the city;
on that day, she was unable to go to the Park of Fierce Valor.

At that time, Virūḍhaka spent the entire day enjoying himself in his own garden; as the sun was about to set and she had still not arrived, he waited for her in vain for a long while before returning to the city. He then dispatched a messenger to the house of the courtesan Kāśisundarī, saying to the woman:
"For what reason did you not come to the garden today?"
At that time, the woman, employing a clever stratagem, replied to the messenger:
"You may inform the minister on my behalf:
'Today I am afflicted by a wind-disorder; my head and eyes are dizzy and painful. Because of this matter, I am unable to go to the park.'"
Before the messenger had even finished receiving these words and could yet turn back to report them, a relative living nearby had already secretly informed him:
"The princess was not at all ill that day; she simply went to the Golden Youth’s Garden to sightsee, and for that reason did not come to the minister’s park."
At that time, having heard these words, the fierce and cruel minister was suddenly overcome with indignation and reflected deeply:
"If this girl Kāśisundarī has had an illicit liaison with that youth Suvarṇavarṇa, this will truly bring me harm and disadvantage."
Thus, his mind was bound by the fetter of wrath; indeed, what the world calls the "enmity-bond" of women is the foremost of all.
At that time, the minister’s heart was scorched by the fire of anger, and he passed the night in extreme distress.
When morning arrived, he summoned an attendant and said to him:
"You should take up a sword and follow behind me as we leave Rājagṛha for the Āditya Garden; I have a minor matter to attend to that must be quickly accomplished."
The attendant replied,
“As Your Honor commands. Then,
taking up his sword, the attendant followed the fierce and violent minister out of Rājagṛha and entered the garden of the merchant-sūtra master Sūryodgata.

At that time, the courtesan Kāśisundarī, having adorned herself in various ways, also went out from the city of Rājagṛha and entered the garden of the merchant leader Sūryodgata, following closely behind him.
At that time, the woman suddenly saw the minister Virūḍhaka in her garden; upon seeing him, she was struck with terror and found no place to flee, thinking to herself:
"Today this minister will surely do me great harm and commit a most wicked and unrighteous act."

At that time, when the minister saw the woman, the fire of his wrath blazed up, consuming his mind and heart. With knitted brows and a furrowed forehead, his countenance contorted with rage, he rushed forward at once and seized the woman by her hair.

Her tresses became disheveled as she fell face-down upon the ground; in a harsh voice, he said to her: "You have come here now with a secret pact with that Golden-Clad Youth. You falsely told me that you were afflicted by a wind-disorder, using clever stratagems to deceive and seduce me. Since the facts are thus, how can you escape the bonds of enmity? It is certain that you shall find it difficult to remain alive this very moment."
At that time, having heard these words, the courtesan Kāśisundarī was overcome with anguish and summoned her own suffering, giving rise to great terror:
"Shall I now have no life remaining?"
Deeply moved by grief, she wept and wailed aloud; rising from the ground, she approached the minister, prostrated at his feet, and spoke with gentle words, making her plea most earnestly:

"O Benevolent One, take pity on me and do not take my life. A woman’s body is prone to many faults; from this day forward, I shall never commit them again. For as long as I live, I vow to serve you as your slave. I pray that you, out of compassion, will restrain your anger and grant me the remainder of my life so that I may continue to exist."

At that time, although the minister heard these words of such bitter lamentation, his heart was so hardened by malice that he would not accept them at all; the fire of his anger flared up even more intensely, and he said to his attendant:
"You should now quickly brandish a sharp sword and sever his head, casting it upon the ground."
At that time, having heard these wicked and fierce words from the evil man, the attendant was seized with great terror and thought to himself: "Alas!
This foolish man is utterly devoid of compassion;
though he has long shared deep karmic ties with this woman, why does he now seek to take her life for such a minor offense?"
Alas! That I now seek my livelihood from this person is truly as terrifying as snake venom; why do I seek reliance upon such a base individual?
I have encountered hardships and perils in various places; could it not be that the time of my death has now arrived?

Or perhaps I should now speak out clearly and declare this, for if I speak openly, he might be able to cease such sinful karma; having recognized this as an improper dharma, he may then reproach his own mind.
Furthermore, seeing this woman terrified, distressed, and weeping in sorrow, he formed this thought and immediately joined his palms, stepping forward to address the minister Vīrabhadra:

"I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will cease your grief; do not cause me to perform such unwholesome deeds, do not make me a man of slaughter, and do not let me now act with such fierce intent as to commit the karma of killing."

"Our Lord is compassionate; may he grant us protection! Furthermore, this woman is of dignified and graceful bearing, a sight that delights all who behold her. Having resided for a long time within the city of Rājagṛha, she is admired by many people who come from all directions."
Furthermore, this woman is beloved and cherished by all people; how can my lord, who is wise and discerning, give rise to anger toward one who is so universally loved?

I pray that such evil conditions may now cease, so that we may avoid the most grievous karma of killing in two lifetimes; do not remain so stubbornly attached as to bring about our destruction, lest I commit this evil deed and consume myself with fire.

Furthermore, this woman, whose physical appearance was in the prime of youth and whom all loved with compassion, is now overcome by grief before you, O Benevolent One, and entreats you with earnest and gentle words.

Upon hearing those words, my heart was greatly struck with terror; and hearing that you, O virtuous one, spoke such fierce and cruel words desiring to take his life, my fear increased all the more. Even among the wicked people of the borderlands, there is no courage to harm another's life, so how much less could a virtuous person like you possess the audacity to do so?

"If even all species of animals, upon seeing others in peril or distress, still give rise to a heart of compassion, how much more so should those of human lineage refrain from thoughts of killing and harming?
At that time, the attendant spoke a verse, saying:
"The words you have uttered are irrational; I do not wish to hear them spoken."
"How much more so when it concerns what I am truly practicing; I pray that you now cease this most wicked karma.

When the minister Vīraka heard these words, because of his stubborn anger he clung to them firmly and would not let go. His mind became deranged and lost its original clarity; his wrath increased further as he manifested various evil signs, and in a harsh voice he said: "Alas!..."
"Man! You also harbor deep affection for this woman; with a mind intent on protecting her, you have defied my instructions by obstructing me everywhere, not wishing for her to be killed."
"If you now obey my command and kill him, it will be well;
if you do not kill him, your own life shall likewise not endure at this moment.
At that time, the attendant, beholding such a stubborn and malevolent obsession and the imminent threat, reflected to himself:
"Alas! I have now followed him into this perilous and evil calamity; if I do not comply with his command and bring about his death, he will certainly take my life in retaliation."
Why is this? This woman has always cherished me with deep affection; if she still intends to harm me so persistently, how much more so would she not seek my death?
If I were to obey her command and brandish my blade against this virtuous and noble body of hers, how then could I be called a man?
"I would rather sacrifice my own life in every circumstance than ever intentionally harm that woman.
Subsequently, the attendant devised another stratagem, reflecting to himself:
"I should now take up my sword and flee; whether for myself or for others, this will surely preserve our lives."
Having thought this, he immediately took up his sword and fled, hurrying his steps as he sought to exit the park.
At that moment, the minister Vīrabhadra also pursued him from behind, reaching the side of the gate.
At that time, the courtesan Kāśisundarī was so physically emaciated and exhausted that her remaining life was but a brief moment; she wished to flee, yet her strength was insufficient.
Having thought this, she immediately exerted herself to rise and quickly ran forward until she reached a wall. The wall was so high that she could not scale it.

Just as the minister returned to that place, the woman immediately fled and hid within the Aṭimuktaka flower grove; the minister did not see her at first, but after pacing about and surveying the area, he saw the woman hidden in the grove beside a high wall.

At that time, beneath the wall, there was previously a black snake dwelling in its hole; consequently, it emerged from the hole and bit the woman’s right foot, causing her injury. Upon seeing this, the minister also fled in haste.
At that time, the woman thought to herself:
"This must be the minister coming to take my life.
At that moment, she focused her mind entirely on the fear of death; not long thereafter, she realized she had been bitten by a snake in that place.

At that time, the minister returned to the grove to observe the woman; his anger intensified greatly and his heart was devoid of compassion. He immediately stepped forward and dragged the woman’s body, trampling her hair-knot until she was even more exhausted and distressed.
"Alas! This woman has suffered such cruel injury; her strength is utterly exhausted and she lies unconscious upon the ground.
At that time, the minister looked closely once more and, seeing the woman prostrate on the earth, thought to himself:
"Now that this woman's life has come to an end, I ought to return.
However, fearing that others might observe his movements, he immediately leaped over the wall with his entire body and entered the city.
At that time, the various patrol officers and police of Rājagṛha, while on their rounds, arrived at the garden of the merchant-suzerain Sūryodgata.
Having arrived, they saw the youth Suvarṇavarṇa leaving Rājagṛha and entering his own garden, and they even saw the courtesan Kāśisundarī lying prostrate upon the ground.
Having seen this, they immediately felt profound pity and compassion; the ministers then collectively examined the situation closely:
"Who is this wicked person, devoid of a heart of mercy and compassion, who does not fear the retribution for sinful karma in future lives?"
Deeply bound by enmity, they take his life. Alas!
Human beings harbor such cruel and venomous intent; lacking compassion for a woman’s body, they bring her harm.
At that time, the officials searched throughout the garden, scrutinizing it with great care, yet they observed no other signs. They further reflected:
"This woman’s deportment has always been dignified and she is renowned for her reputation; why, then, would her life be taken here?"
What kind of evil person commits such an evil deed?
Its circumstances are obscure and known only to the gods; at this time, we have not yet discerned its cause, and we too would incur the fault of transgression.

Thereupon, the assembly of officials was overcome with profound sorrow and distress; harboring mutual doubts, they rested their chins upon their hands in dejection. The officials then entered the garden once more to search for him with meticulous scrutiny.
Beholding the scene once more, he saw only the woman prostrate upon the ground and thought:
"Is it not because the power of the karmic retribution from the previous life of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa cannot be severed?"
"Why has this woman’s life come to an end?
At that time, the various police officers deliberated among themselves, saying,
"By whom has this courtesan been killed?"
"We have thoroughly and repeatedly inspected our park from every side, yet we find no other signs of activity; we see only the golden-colored youth.
The officials immediately summoned the youth and questioned him, saying, "By whom was this courtesan killed?"
The youth replied, “Your Excellencies, please examine this clearly: although I witnessed the scene of these events, I truly do not know who killed them.”

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Weijing and others, who have received the purple robes and the title of State Preceptor Guangfan. At that time, the various patrol officials deliberated among themselves, saying:

"As everyone observes, this youth’s demeanor and appearance are refined and well-behaved; it is certain he could not have committed such a grave deed. Furthermore, at present there are no other unusual signs. We have encountered such hardship in our duties; how now shall we proceed with this matter?"
One among them said:

"This matter is truly beyond our capacity for deliberation; the Minister of Justice presides over the law in the kingdom. We should now lead this boy and woman there to investigate and debate the case in detail."
Once the council had reached its decision, they placed the woman upon a bamboo litter and, taking the boy with them, proceeded together to the judicial authorities.
At that time, the minister Vīrabhadra, who was charged with administering the law, was assembled there with the various judges.
Seeing those police officers approaching from afar, he immediately asked them:
"For what purpose have you officials come here?
What business do you have?"
The officials replied:

"This woman was killed in the garden of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha; we do not know who took her life. We have conducted a thorough investigation in three ways, and within that garden we saw only the youth Suvarṇavarṇa and no other signs of the crime.
We immediately questioned the youth, saying: 'Who has caused this woman's death?'"
The youth replied:
"Your Excellencies, please examine this clearly; although I have seen the scene of the incident, I truly do not know who killed him."
"We have now been brought here for supervision; we pray that you will grant us a clear judgment.
At that time, the minister said, "Wait a moment;
I must first conduct a thorough investigation."
Thereafter, he went to the king’s residence to seek a judgment according to the law.
At that time, the Minister of Law went to King Ajātaśatru’s palace and saw the gatekeeper guarding the royal gates; he approached and asked:
“Where does the king reside, and what is he doing?”
The gatekeeper said, "The King has now ascended the hall and summoned the palace ladies; they are currently providing entertainment with the sounds of drums, pipes, and singing.
At that time, the minister sought an official at the palace gate and, entrusting him with the matter, presented it as a memorial to the King:

"Now there is Sūryaprabha, the son of the merchant leader, who has murdered the courtesan Kāśisundarī within his own garden; if we do not now receive the King’s command, none of us ministers shall be able to adjudicate this matter."

At that time, the palace attendant in charge of the ladies hurried to the king’s presence and reported the matter in detail. The king was in the midst of his amusements and had no leisure for careful examination;
he therefore commanded the attendant: "Go and tell the minister Virūḍhaka that he must investigate the matter with great care and according to the facts."
The female messenger received the command and went out to proclaim the King’s decree, ordering the ministers of war and the various judicial officials to investigate the matter thoroughly.
Once the proclamation had been made everywhere, the minister of war returned to the legal office and said to the patrol officers:
"You must go and summon the executioners and have them come here at once."
Having arrived, he said to them:

"This youth has murdered the courtesan Kāśisundarī within his own garden. You should now go and seize him; beat the drum to proclaim this at the crossroads and thoroughfares so that all may hear, then go out through the southern city gate to the cemetery and strike him with an iron fork until his life is extinguished. Afterwards, place him together with the dead woman upon a pyre of wood and set fire to it."

At that time, although the executioners heard this command, they beheld the golden youth, whose physical marks were as magnificent as a mountain of gold; their hearts were pierced with pain, and they said to one another, "How can you say such a person as this may be put to death?"
This youth is rare among men; his deportment is worthy of admiration. Although we are engaged in the work of slaughter, we too possess a heart of compassion; how could we bear to harm such a person?
"Rather than this, let us ourselves end our own lives; we shall never, under any circumstances, dare to carry out the execution here.
At that time, having heard the deliberations of the executioners, the fierce and violent minister spoke again in anger:
"Why do you delay for so long?"
"Why do you not swiftly comply with his command?
At that time, the executioners joined their palms, stepped forward, and all pleaded piteously, saying:
"O Great Minister, O King!"
"Please desist now; although we are among those who deal in slaughter, we are likewise unable to carry out this deed with vigor.
Why is this? This youth possesses such an upright and majestic appearance that he is beloved by all people; how could we bear to cause his death at this time?"
Having heard this, the minister became even more incensed and said to those men:
"If you do not obey the king's command, then today all your wives, children, and kinsmen shall surely die along with you."
When the executioners heard these words, they were all struck with terror and said to one another,
"Why is it that the Chief Minister, who administers the law, now acts contrary to the True Dharma instead of proceeding according to principle?"

"This youth possesses such a magnificent and rare countenance that he is difficult to find among men; yet you insist on abandoning him to bring about his death, and further declare to us that if we do not kill him, our wives, children, and kinsmen shall all die with him."
"Why do we undergo such hardship?
What should we do now? At that time, the executioners, driven by the fear of death, immediately devised a plan:
"This boy is beloved by all; he should be led to a crossroads or a busy thoroughfare where many people gather so that the multitude may witness his condition.

Yet, within the space of a single turn of the foot, that great crowd will surely give rise to feelings of compassion, unable to bear the sight, and will certainly devise means to rescue and protect him."
Thereafter, the various meat-cutters and slaughterers were oppressed in body and mind as if being sliced and carved; they all wept with tears and spoke these words:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"What sinful karma have we committed that we are so tormented and forced to carry out such meaningless and harmful deeds?
At that time, the minister Virūpa, his anger increasing even further, said to the executioners:
"Why do you delay this any longer?"
When the executioners heard these words, they all wept; yet suppressing their grief, they proceeded to approach the youth, seize his garment, and bind his two arms.
Once he had been bound, the fierce and cruel minister thoroughly inspected the matter and immediately removed him from the office of the legal authorities, leading him away to the charnel ground.
At that time, all the people among the spectators were overcome with grief at the thought of parting and wept; they all spoke these words:
"Alas! What peril and distress!"
"This youth is rare among men; his life is now destined for its end.
The executioners took charge of the youth and paraded him through the streets and alleys at a slow pace, hoping he might yet be saved, and then led him further into the marketplace.

At that time, all the men and women, both great and small, dwelling within and without the city of Rājagṛha, as well as the multitudes of people who had come from other regions, gathered together to witness the golden-colored youth with his arms bound.
Having seen this, they were all moved by poignant compassion; their minds became bewildered and agitated, and they spoke together, asking:
"For what reason is this person bound in such a manner?"
At that time, the executioners choked with emotion and wept bitterly as they replied to the crowd:

"Some say this youth has murdered the maiden Kāśisundarī; therefore, he is being held here, intending to cast him away. This is heard by all people everywhere: he shall now go to the cemetery, and before long, he shall pass away."
Having heard this, the multitude were all filled with sorrow and suffering, and with one voice they cried out these words:
"Alas! Alas!"
"How perilous and distressing!

Yet this youth possesses such upright and majestic features that all delight in beholding him; his limbs are perfectly formed and endowed with a golden radiance, pleasing to the eye and gratifying to the mind as all gaze upon him together."

His demeanor is serene and composed, his wisdom is sharp and keen, and he is endowed with a compassionate heart that cherishes all sentient beings; always giving rise to the desire for the Dharma and possessing great majestic virtue—how could such a person as this be put to death?
The noble sages were once manifest and clear; why have they now vanished?
The True Dharma is obscured while non-Dharma blazes forth. The King presides over all as the supreme sovereign; why is it that he thus oppresses and harms people with such injustice?
At that time, the multitude spoke these verses:
“His physical form is humble and reverent, yet most noble; Adorned with the most supreme and excellent marks.
We gaze upon him thus again and again; This exquisite beauty is such as we have never known before.”
We all behold this youth, now held fast by the butcher;
in him, the most extreme sorrow arises within all beings, shattering and destroying both body and mind.
He is able to open the eyes of joy for many people, and is likewise beloved by many.
How could the king’s severe punishments reach this wondrous body?
When the great assembly constantly gazes upon it, their hearts of joy can never be satiated;
how then could they abandon it and entrust it to those who practice the Dharma?
Alas! These ministers and counselors lack compassion;
though they constantly speak of various laws and precepts, they are well able to practice according to what they preach.
Having carefully observed such well-disciplined men, how could they have given rise to such sinful karma?
This is indeed practicing what is contrary to the Dharma; the True Dharma will be obscured or utterly extinguished.
If this power is now exercised, we shall all suffer the pain of separation and dispersal.
When the multitude of people had finished reciting these verses, there were also many women in the city who felt an intense affection for this youth.

Among them, some women, tormented by the suffering of separation, rolled upon the ground; some women beat their knees in grief; and some women’s minds became bewildered and deluded—each one experiencing great anguish just like a mother separated from her own son.

At that time, all the people within and without the city of Rājagṛha, perceiving that this youth was about to lose his life, were all overcome by the agonizing pain of separation; they called out to one another in a chaotic clamor, trembling with fear and panic, their sorrowful suffering beyond remedy.

At that time, there was a young girl in the house of the merchant-suzerain Sūrya; having happened to hear of these matters while out in the marketplace, she immediately wept with grief and quickly returned to her own home, where she went to the mother of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa.
Having arrived, he hurried forward and threw his whole body to the ground. At that time, the mother of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa was bewildered and confused, and she immediately asked:
"What is it that you have done? You should tell me at once."
The young maiden said:
"Venerable mother, you should know that Prince Kanakavarṇa has had his arms bound and is being led away by the executioners. Everyone says:
'He will kill that girl Kāśisundarī in his own garden; before long he will go to the charnel ground, where his life will come to an end.'"
"Thus it was heard and known by all the people at the crossroads and in the streets.

When the boy’s mother heard these words, her grief and suffering became so profound that she fainted and fell to the ground. Water was sprinkled on her face, and after a long while she regained consciousness; rising from the ground, she cried out:
"Alas! How bitter!"
My son! Alas! My son!

Immediately, overcome by the terror and alarm of battle, he lost his composure; clutching his knees in grief, his hair disheveled, he fled from his house and ran to the crossroads and through the alleys. Pressed by the sorrow and suffering of separation from his son, his strength failing and his heart exhausted, he raised his voice in a cry, asking everyone he encountered:
"Where is my son, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa?"
Alas! I do not see my son now.
O virtuous ones, I pray that you grant me protection!
"Please grant us protection!
Let me now behold my son.
Thus she wept piteously, wandering through the streets and alleys and staying wherever she found herself.

At that time, the wife of the merchant leader Sūrya, being tormented by the most extreme grief and distress at not seeing her son, the Golden Boy, wandered about in a state of confusion, crying out in a loud voice; to whomever she encountered, she paid homage and, with palms joined, said:
"Please, save me quickly!"
"May you quickly rescue and protect us!
Until my son reaches the forest, please grant us space within it so that we may see him.
She spoke further, saying:
"You should feel compassion for me so that my son does not come to ruin and I may see him.
Having spoken these piteous words to the people, while she still had not seen her son, the mother cried out once more: "Alas! Alas!"
"Why do I not see my son?

At that moment, he threw his entire body to the ground, writhing and rolling about upon the earth, leaping and bounding like a fish cast out onto dry land. He was restless and distraught, finding no place of rest; his heart was as if being cut to pieces, and his grief increased even further. Like a newborn calf that has lost its mother cow, he was filled with manifold alarm and distress, crying out in desperation:
"Alas! How bitter!"
O my son! Alas!
That which was cherished by your mind!
Alas! O you of excellent patience! Alas!
O you of great filial piety!
How bitter it is!
You who have sought with many prayers for the beloved son you have now obtained!
Alas! Your wondrous form was a sight for people to behold with joy. Alas!
The limbs of the body are perfectly complete. Alas!
This body of radiant golden hue!
Alas! The multitude of people gaze upon him with delight. Alas!
Within the assembly, eyes opened wide with joy. Alas!
Those who are sharp-witted and wise have uttered these vast, fearless, and pleasing words of excellence.
Alas! He who possesses vast compassion, whose Dharma is complete, and who loves sentient beings—alas! Alas!
O most brilliantly radiant family! Alas!
The bright lamp within my own clan!
Alas! That which my heart loves and delights in— alas!
The great treasure within my heart!
Alas! My gatherer of truth!
Alas! My wondrous nectar-eye. Alas!
I am deeply attached to my own continuum! Alas!
You are the great jewel of my clan.
Alas! Alas! Why is it that these officials who oversee the Dharma do not investigate with care, yet leave my son to face imminent death?
At that time, the boy’s mother, joining her palms once more, again addressed all the people with a plea of lamentation; her strength failing and her heart exhausted, she spoke these verses:
“Alas! How bitter!”
I have no one now to whom I may speak;
how am I to conduct myself now?
I am like one in a dream, or as if insane; my heart is oppressed and utterly bewildered.
Deeply oppressed by the sorrow and suffering for my son, with a mind utterly distressed, agitated,
and distraught, I now entreat all people with repeated cries of lamentation and increasing tears.
My mind is neither disciplined nor tranquil, nor is my countenance composed; my heart finds no delight whatsoever.
My son is about to be cast into the charnel ground; may you now grant him protection and deliverance.
If you possess a heart of compassion, you will surely have the power of a good protector;
according to what my mind truly seeks, may I now behold my son.
Now I have no delight in anything at all—neither exquisite unguents such as purple sandalwood, nor various kinds of manifold ornaments; out of compassion for suffering, I renounce them all.
My bracelets and other such finery shall no longer serve to adorn my body.
My beloved child is about to depart; my grief is profound, for I am unable to embrace him or cherish him with my own hands.
I shall no longer circumambulate you three times, nor shall I pay homage at your feet.
I do not yet understand by what cause you have placed my son in the charnel ground.
I observe that the ten directions are all empty and vast; I see only destruction and conflagration.
My own mind is likewise scorched and aflame; My thoughts are deluded and bewildered, leaving me at a loss for what to do.
Quickly placed in the charnel ground, To be executed by those who uphold the law— Alas, never again shall such great suffering be seen!
This is not a crime committed in my present life; It must be the lingering retribution from another birth.
Now my grief and suffering for my son are deep, like a fierce fire consuming light grass.
If my heart is truly sincere, and if this enemy is as harmless as a kinsman,
then when the circumstances regarding my son become true, may he now be delivered from this peril.

At that time, the merchant leader Sūryodgata, having crossed the great ocean and successfully accomplished his profit, returned to the great city of Rājagṛha before long.
As he was entering the city, the merchant leader suddenly beheld an inauspicious omen; immediately, fear arose in his heart, his body trembled violently, and his eyes twitched.
This omen was as follows: a flock of birds gathered before him, crying out with harsh, clamorous voices.
The merchant leader, who was well-versed in interpreting omens, immediately thought to himself:

"The signs I have just observed are extremely inauspicious. It is certain that my son, the golden-hued youth, will encounter some calamity; it must be near at hand, for according to the teachings on portents, there will surely be a separation."
Thereupon the merchant leader spoke in verse:
“As both my eyes twitch together, And the flocks of birds cry out with harsh clamor,
It is certain that at this very moment, The suffering of separation from my son must be near.”

Furthermore, if the limbs of the body tremble and quiver, and if the mind gives rise to feverish distress and terror, it is certain that the father and son shall now part; the evil omens are as before and must be imminent.

After the merchant leader had spoken these verses, while his body and mind were trembling with fear, he contemplated hundreds of thousands of meaningless matters; hesitating and circling about, he did not know where to rest.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"For what reason have I returned to this city?
Later on, when he heard a great multitude raising their voices in wailing, the merchant leader, upon hearing that sound of lamentation, again pondered the matter.
He then went to a crossroads and again saw many people who, like those afflicted by the terror and harassment of a rākṣasa, were each oppressed by the suffering of separation.
Standing before the merchant leader, he saw one person and immediately asked:
"O Benevolent One!..."
"What event has occurred such that the circumstances are as they are?

The man replied, "The merchant-suzerain Sūryodana has a son named the Youth Suvarṇavarṇa, whose physical marks are handsome and who is endowed with every virtue. Yet, that youth killed the maiden Kāśisundarī within his own garden. The king’s officials were unable to investigate the matter and handed him over to the executioners, who intend to cast him out at the crossroads and thoroughfares. This is what everyone hears; before long, the youth will go to the charnel ground, where his life will come to its end."

At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader Sūrya, being overwhelmed by the suffering of separation from his son, immediately fainted and fell to the ground. Water was sprinkled on his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
Supported by others, he slowly rose and wailed most bitterly, his tears flowing like rain. Looking around in all directions, he spoke these words:
"Alas! Where is my son, the golden-colored youth, now?"

Thereupon, the merchant leader hurriedly traversed the alleys and streets in search of her, until he saw his wife in a state of wild confusion with her hair disheveled; she beat her breast and wailed piteously, running to and fro in distress because of the extreme agony of being separated from her son.
Upon seeing this, the merchant leader was overcome with intense grief and distress; choking with sobs and shedding tears, he gradually approached her.

When the wife saw her husband, she wailed even more piteously; as the arrows of sorrow pierced her heart, her tears flowed like rain, and she quickly went before her husband and threw her entire body to the ground.
Thereupon, the merchant leader Sūryodgata took his wife’s hand and wailed aloud; the wife then stepped forward, prostrated herself with devotion, and spoke these words:
“O noble husband!
"Save me! Save me!
I now beg my husband for that beloved son; may my husband look upon me with compassion."
She spoke in verse:
"I pray that my husband now comfort me; I am without fortune and find no joy.
Now that I am parting from my son, I suffer extreme anguish and weep in vain."
When the husband and wife together learned of their son’s birth, they experienced the greatest joy;
why then, now that this beloved child must soon face death, do they cling to him as he undergoes it?
My son was well-disciplined and possessed youthful vigor; he was thoroughly proficient in many types of scriptures.
His physical appearance was so majestic and peerless that there was no one like him. Now this son of great wisdom is about to lose his life;
he cuts off the lineage of my great clan and destroys the very root of my great family.
The great auspicious lamp of light for our clan has been extinguished by such rays;
my son, the jewel within my heart, the one I cherish most deeply in my lineage,
my son— the eye of nectar among the multitude— is now to be executed by those who uphold the law.
Everything was done for the sake of my son; losing him is like the destruction of one's eyes.
My heart-treasure, my son, has likewise perished; why is he now being destroyed?
"You must quickly exert diligent effort and employ extensive skillful means for my son's sake;
if anyone can save my son at this time, I shall now bestow all precious treasures upon them."
I see your son at this moment, his life still remaining before he faces execution;
according to your wishes and reflections, you should now swiftly perform the act of rescue.

At that time, although the merchant leader Sūrya was overcome by the piercing and agonizing grief of separation from his son, he nevertheless exerted himself to steady his body and mind and proceeded to where the crowd of people was gathered. Joining his palms, he addressed them, saying:
"O worthy sirs!..."
Listen all to my words: at this time, when such perilous, evil, and difficult circumstances have arisen, why do you not employ some skillful means to release and rescue them?
If matters in the wilderness were difficult to investigate clearly, you would surely see them now that we are in the royal city;
moreover, since my son’s virtues are so manifest, for what reason have you handed him over to the executioners to be taken away for execution?
Why do you not give rise to even a small measure of compassion and strive diligently to rescue and protect us?
Why does the King not carefully consider his manifold laws?
Why do you not rouse your hearts with vigor and courage to release my son?
Then, one person from among the multitude replied: "O Merchant Lord!

We all know that this boy of yours is endowed with every virtue; yet at this time, you are not the only one suffering hardship alone. All of us, both those within and without, share equally in this grief and sorrow. However, we have not yet seen any means by which the boy might be released; therefore, our hearts are each filled with anxiety, and we all give rise to burning distress."
The merchant leader spoke again:

"O worthy ones! You should further know that this boy is ultimately and purely virtuous; his compassion is profound and he possesses great majestic power. He is fully endowed with the desire for the Dharma and loves sentient beings; how could he ever resolve to engage in such a meaningless and harmful act?"
How much less could he have committed such an evil deed?
I pray that you, virtuous sirs, will now specifically and thoroughly investigate these circumstances.

If, upon careful examination, it is found that this boy’s account is true, then I pray you will release him from this peril. If your assembly can provide detailed testimony regarding this matter, and all the people likewise follow your instruction, then not even the slightest fault can be found.

Furthermore, there is no other compassionate heart to be found; if this is so, you who are well-disposed toward virtue and manifest with compassion should, having aroused a heart of pity, go to the King’s presence and request his command to instruct the ministers and officials before you, so that they may proclaim the matter exactly as you have said, without any deviation, for it is worthy of trust and hearing.

"Virtuous ones, you should know that because I am now enduring the ultimate hardship of separation from my son, I shall bestow upon you all manner of precious treasures as those who can protect me. I pray only that you will extend your great kindness and examine this matter for the sake of this youth with thorough and proper discernment."
At that time, when the multitude of people heard the words of the merchant leader and fully understood his meaning, they said to one another:
"This youth is now endowed with all virtues; he is truly worthy of our deep affection and respect."
Immediately, from among the assembly, they summoned two or three wise men who were clear-sighted regarding correct principles and dispatched them to the king’s presence to report in detail:

“If Your Majesty, for the sake of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, now commands those ministers and aides to investigate the matter thoroughly and repeatedly to ascertain its truth or falsehood, we, the populace, shall offer one hundred thousand pieces of gold to Your Majesty.”
The king followed the petition.
At that time, a wise man went to the Office of Legal Affairs and first instructed them to investigate thoroughly the matter concerning the minister Dāruṇa.
Then, seeing two or three people approaching from afar, the minister Dāruṇa immediately asked:
"You have no business here; for what reason have you come?
They replied, "We reside in the great city of Rājagṛha, where the multitude of people has made this piteous appeal:"
"O Benevolent One!

This youth Suvarṇavarṇa is now of such exquisite and dignified appearance, endowed with every virtue and beloved by many. As he is about to depart, all the people within the city of Rājagṛha are deeply distressed; how much more so for this man who always delights in the True Dharma and the various codes of law, who is perfect in virtuous conduct, and whom the multitude trusts as being entirely free from even the slightest fault."

"O Benevolent One, the King has commanded us: 'Now, for the sake of the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, re-examine and deliberate thoroughly upon the previous matter. We shall present one hundred thousand pieces of gold to the King, and the merchant lord Sūryaprabha himself will also prepare and offer many precious jewels, so that the King’s vast treasury may be further enriched."
When the minister Virūḍhaka heard these words, he replied with indignation:
"The matter has long been settled; why do you all insist on further deliberation and debate?"

Furthermore, why do you say that one hundred thousand pieces of gold should be given to increase the royal treasury? Do I, at this time, take wealth through improper means to augment the king’s storehouses? You truly believe you understand the King’s intent;

yet you, as a multitude, employ clever schemes and stratagems everywhere, desiring to cause the King to act to his own disadvantage. This is not a skillful means; rather, it is you who utter words of derision and slander against the King. If, in other matters, you wish to incite the King to act in such a manner, you will see many people utterly ruined.
At that time, after the minister Virūḍhaka had rebuked those two or three people, he immediately summoned four kinds of wicked men:
namely, those who commit extremely evil deeds, those who lack patience, those who lack compassion, and those who lack pity.
Having summoned them, he said:
"You must now quickly drive those executioners out of the city and, according to my words and the king's decree, put that boy to death."
"You must not hastily release him, nor should you release any other ministers or officials who might speak out against us.
It would be most excellent if you were to follow my instructions;
however, if you disobey my orders and harbor divergent views, I shall bind you all with great enmity."
They replied, "We now obey your command. At that time,
having received the decree, the four executioners each took up sharp swords and proceeded forward as guards.

At that time, the executioners deliberated on a hundred schemes and devised various stratagems; they advanced slowly, seizing the youth, and led him around the four crossroads and through the streets and alleys, desiring that everyone everywhere might hear and know of it, whereupon they spoke these words:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"What stratagem can we now employ so that this youth may escape this peril?
How could we, at this time, commit such a meaningless and harmful act?"
At that time, the four execution officers, each grasping a sharp sword, went before the various butchers and addressed them, saying:

"You should act in accordance with the instructions given by the great minister and perform this task with haste. If you do not quickly depart from the city and execute the boy according to those laws, I shall put an end to your lives this very moment."
Then those four types of extremely wicked executioners, each wielding a sharp sword of fearsome appearance, glared with angry eyes at those various slaughterers.
At that time, fearing for their own lives, they were all struck with terror and said, "Alas!
At this moment, we have no further means to save this youth; we must obey his command and lead him to execution."
Having spoken thus, his eyes filled with sorrow and he shed tears.
At that time, the four supervising officials hurriedly drove the youth Suvarṇavarṇa out of the city.
When the youth departed from the city, hundreds of thousands of people rushed forward to gaze upon him; they wept with grief and, with one voice, all spoke these words:
"Alas! How bitter!"

Alas! The great treasure of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha has been lost; furthermore, the ancestral lineage of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha is utterly severed and destroyed. The bright torch within the clan of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha is about to be extinguished; the supreme crest-jewel of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha’s clan has fallen. The pure eye of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha is extinguished; all the exquisite ornaments of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha are now scattered and dispersed. The heart of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha is so deeply wounded it is as if being torn open; the life-force within the body of the merchant-suzerain Sūryaprabha has perished.
Alas! Alas! Why has this youth been sent outside the city to a wilderness that is remote, desolate, and silent?
Wandering and revolving in distress, with no rescue and no refuge?

Now this youth, within the most excellent city of Rājagṛha, is like the pure moon being swallowed by Rāhu; furthermore, this great city of Rājagṛha is like the sun in the sky vanishing during the day;
the multitude of people dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha have lost the eye of nectar and are bewildered as to their direction.
The multitude of inhabitants dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha, who were bound by deep and continuous affection, have now all been dispersed;
the magnificent adornments of the inhabitants of the great city of Rājagṛha have now fallen into ruin;
the crest-jewels of the inhabitants of the great city of Rājagṛha have fallen away.
The cherished treasures of the people dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha have now all been destroyed;
since the eyes of the inhabitants of the great city of Rājagṛha have been lost, what shall they behold?
“Having now witnessed this event, how could we possibly feel joy?
In our hearts, we truly feel that we have no one left to rely upon.
At that time, after the youth had departed the city, the official in charge of pursuit sent a messenger to inform the minister Vīraka:
"The youth Suvarṇavarṇa has already departed from the great city of Rājagṛha.
Upon hearing this, the minister Pracaṇḍa was filled with joy.
At that time, two or three of those who had arrived earlier, having heard this news, became sorrowful and unhappy; remaining silent and without support, they returned to search within the city.

Those who had previously deliberated together each recounted the aforementioned matters in detail. Having heard this, the multitude was filled with grief and desolation, finding no refuge; they consulted one another, saying:

"You should know that our sovereign, King Ajātaśatru, is an evil king who does not follow the correct principle. Having formerly taken his father's life, he now commits further unrighteous acts, having caused the execution of a man of superior wisdom, virtuous and of handsome appearance, whom all loved and cherished."
Alas! How utterly devoid of compassion is this king! Alas!

If the king does not recognize those with virtue, and if the king and his ministers lack superior knowledge and insight, why does he not command that they be examined and deliberated upon in accordance with the true Dharma and Vinaya?
Why does he easily cast aside such excellent and virtuous people?

Furthermore, is it perhaps because the times are such that the True Dharma is obscured and perverted while non-Dharma increases? In this age of turbidity, people believe the words of the wicked, thereby causing those of virtue and supreme goodness to suffer the pain of separation.
Alas! Alas! How profoundly meaningless this is!
