At that time, having heard these various accounts, the merchant leader Sūrya’s mind was shattered; he was overcome by extreme grief and suffering, fainted and fell to the ground. Water was sprinkled upon his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
Sitting down slowly, he wept and spoke these words:
"Alas! Alas! How bitter!"
"My only son is now about to lose his life.
Having said this, she raised her voice again and wailed, reciting a verse:
"Alas! How bitter!"
My son’s eyes are so bright and joyful; alas!
the great ornament of our clan. Because my merit as your father is so meager, I wail aloud for the sake of harming you.
For your sake, my heart has been scattered; even now it wanders lost in all directions.
Severed from you, the fire of grief blazes forth—how bitter!
It burns my heart and mind.
You are a person of refined virtue and wisdom, one who increases love, joy, and compassion;
yet I am your father, an extremely wicked man, who has brought many calamities upon you at this time.
When your son was first born that day, I attained a joy and bliss beyond compare;
now that I am about to part from you, the fire of grief burns my heart with extreme intensity.
Alas! The king and his ministers lack compassion and discernment; seeing this man who is fully endowed with the Dharma and Vinaya, they are unable to deliberate upon his case with thorough scrutiny.

Alas! You who rule as the sovereign of a great kingdom, you have failed to manifest a heart of compassion; you were unable to investigate with such careful discernment, and thus, because of you, my son has been cast aside.
The most excellent and virtuous person in the world never conceals his thoughts;
known by all as a son of noble character, he now wails aloud because he has been harmed by you.
Where now are all these holy sages of this great city’s moat, scattered as they are?
May you who shine like those of such virtue be released at the moment of execution.
Lord Śakra, the Sovereign of Devas, together with the World Protectors and all other deities of great majesty and power,
may you all deign to open your hearts of compassion even slightly, and now provide excellent protection for my son.
The sages who have attained great power through the observance of precepts, and all other silent sages as well—
bowing down to you so that you may open your heart of compassion, please now provide protection for my son.
At that time, after the merchant lord Sūrya had spoken these verses, wholesome wisdom suddenly arose within him, and he reflected to himself:

"My current lamentation is in vain and of no benefit. I have heard that there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, whose merits are immeasurable, who regards all throughout the world as his own kin, and who responds to thoughts with great compassion."

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, acts as a sovereign for those who have no master; he acts as a protector for those who have no refuge; he acts as a place of refuge for those who have nowhere to turn; and he acts as a destination for those who have no direction.

"Furthermore, when all sentient beings in the world are oppressed by every kind of hardship, suffering, and perilous difficulty, they constantly give rise to extreme fear; yet our Buddha, out of compassion, skillfully delivers them. It is like merchants crossing the sea who encounter a great makara fish and feel intense terror; at that moment of fear, they call upon the Buddha, and the Buddha, responding to their thought, immediately delivers them."

"Furthermore, for example, Aṅgulimāla killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people, intending to kill one more—his own mother—but as she was terrified and her life was about to end, the Buddha used skillful means to deliver her."

Furthermore, there are those bound by the power of enmity from past lives who receive the body of a yakṣa—namely, the yakṣas of the wilderness, the yakṣas of seizure, and so forth—who roam the world for the sake of food and drink, slaughtering countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.

These yakṣas consume human flesh and blood, craving their foul taste; they gnaw, lick, and snatch about, displaying their hideous tongues, with hard, long, and sharp fangs and contorted, ugly faces. As they press close upon people, they are truly terrifying; yet the Buddha skillfully delivers such sentient beings.

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, has skillfully delivered my son from this hardship and suffering; if that Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great compassion and holds all sentient beings with supreme love, may he naturally know my thoughts.
While the merchant lord Sūryodgata was reflecting thus, there was a faithful and virtuous upāsaka by his side, to whom the merchant lord asked:
"Virtuous one!
Where is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to be found now?"
At that time, the upāsaka, having reflected deeply upon the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wept with tears and sobbed with a choked voice. He then spoke a verse, responding to the merchant leader:
“The Great Teacher of this world, Who can grant the supreme bliss to the world, Who treats all beings in the world as one’s own kin— That Buddha, the Great Master, has already entered parinirvāṇa.”
He who was the illuminator for those in darkness has become the illumination itself; he who was the refuge for those without refuge has become the refuge itself.
Now that the light of the Buddha-sun has grown dim, it is beyond the reach of even a lamp burning with exhausted oil.

At that time, when the merchant leader Sūrya heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already entered parinirvāṇa, his grief and suffering redoubled; the arrow of sorrow pierced his heart, and he fell to the ground in a swoon. Water was sprinkled on his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
Supported by others, he gradually rose and, facing the direction where the World-Honored Buddha had entered *nirvāṇa*, wailed aloud and spoke this verse: “Alas!

The Dharma-King, the All-Knowing One, Who could eliminate faults and the multitude of enemies— Now that you have abandoned those who have no refuge, The World-Honored One has passed away; what shall I do?”
Alas! The conduct of the Most Supreme and Victorious One—He who loves all sentient beings as one, who can reunite all who are separated, and who, as the Guide, reveals the path to Nirvana.
Alas! How is it that in this world, the pure eye is shrouded by the veil of ignorance?
If sentient beings are separated from the World-Honored One, they will revolve in the cycle of birth and death without end.
The Buddha has come from the path of quiescent extinction;
most supreme in compassion and great in valor, if this world is now without refuge, who else can be the sovereign to serve as our protector?
All things arise from the True Dharma; from the Dharma are born the sons of the Buddhas.
Now that the sons of the Buddhas have departed from this world, who else remains to serve as our refuge?
Sentient beings have many kinds of true intentions; the Buddha can uproot their suffering and bring them all to fulfillment.
He illuminates the pervasive objects of sentient beings' love, then returns to the void and rests in silent stillness.
All the multitudes are equal; hearing what the Buddha has taught, they give rise to courageous vigor.
Now that the World-Honored Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, who else will proclaim the True Dharma?

Alas! The people and devas of the world are all bereft of light and utterly ruined; it is most difficult for a Holy Honored One to appear in the world, yet the Buddha, the Great Muni, has now passed away.
Having heard that the Buddha, the Holy One, has already entered parinirvāṇa, and that the beloved True Dharma has likewise ceased,
all sentient beings who deeply delight in the Dharma— whom else is there now to perform such virtuous deeds?
The single flavor of compassion is great fearlessness; it is that upon which the Greatly Compassionate One relies.
It can universally accomplish all merits; after its cessation, what further could be attained?
What is called "bringing benefit to the three realms" is the arousal of the mind of great compassion;
this compassion is itself true wisdom, which relies equally upon the practice of equanimity.
Alas! The Buddha’s jewel of great merit, accumulated over tens of millions of eons, perishes as soon as it relies upon this difficult land; all the True Dharma likewise falls into ruin.
The World-Honored One, the Guide, has departed from this world; alas!
Shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, all that was accomplished through diligent effort is now destroyed amidst the perils of this life and this world.
How great! The Most Victorious One is the Buddha-jewel; how is it that at this very time they have all been scattered?
Deeply lamentable is the world, as all things conducive to destruction are now set in motion.
With the Buddha’s passing, the assembly of bhikṣus is likewise empty;
like a herd of cattle that has lost its mother, when wise people behold these circumstances, who would not feel great compassion and distress in their hearts?
Prostrating ourselves fully upon the ground in reverent offering, we pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, which are free from all dust;
now that the radiance of the Buddha-sun has faded into darkness, we have no one left to whom we may turn for refuge.
The great matter of impermanence is most cruel and poisonous;
all sentient beings receive it equally, and now even the Buddha has been assailed by you, leaving me today without protection.
The Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path is like a wondrous medicine; it can cure the root source of the disease of afflictions.
O Great Teacher!
O Great Compassionate One!
O Great King of Physicians!
Even now you have fallen into the category of the impermanent.
Alas! How bitter!

Without compassion and with extreme swiftness, the World-Honored One, our compassionate father, has entered parinirvāṇa; all the worlds are now shrouded in darkness—who shall open the eye of illumination?

Alas! The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; the jewel of my son's heart will not return. Now that my son stands on the verge of execution, I pray that the Buddha will come to rescue him from this calamity.

Bhagavān, universal savior from all suffering and affliction, supreme refuge for all beings—my son is without support and his life is about to perish; I pray that you grant him deliverance this very moment.
If today I have attained a true benefit, as has been taught by the One of Great Majestic Power,
and my loved ones are not scattered or separated from me, then this is indeed the attainment of the supreme word.
After the merchant leader Sūryodgata had spoken these verses with such piteous words, he further addressed the upāsaka, saying:
"Among the Buddha’s great śrāvaka disciples, to whom did the Buddha entrust the teachings before entering parinirvāṇa?"
The upāsaka said:
“O caravan leader!
Listen attentively!”
Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, having entrusted his teachings to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, entered parinirvāṇa;
that Venerable Mahākāśyapa, in accordance with the World-Honored One’s command, having entrusted his teachings to the Venerable Ānanda, subsequently entered nirvāṇa.

At this time, it is the venerable Ānanda, possessed of great majesty, who upholds the teachings of the Dharma. That venerable one possesses a compassionate heart like that of a Buddha; he is able to tame, gather, and transform all sentient beings in every country, city, village, and location throughout all directions. Among sentient beings, if there are those who have not yet planted roots of goodness, he employs skillful means to gather and transform them so that they may plant such roots. For those who have already accumulated all roots of goodness and attained continuity, he causes them to reach maturity.
For those whose roots of goodness are already matured, he enables them to attain liberation.
If there are those afflicted by the disease of entangling afflictions, he preaches the sublime nectar-medicine of the True Dharma for them, causing them to be healed, just like a king of physicians.

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings shrouded by the darkness of all afflictions, he proclaims the True Dharma; with pure radiance, he destroys the gloom of afflictions. Like the Sun God, his speech is radiant, harmonious, and well-ordered; like the Moon God, it is as lovely as the blooming of a kumuda flower.
He constantly instructs and subdues the various minor kings with the True Dharma, like a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
By means of his own wisdom and supreme eloquence, he tames and overcomes the entire host of heterodox outsiders, who are like a herd of deer, just as a lion does.
He points out the laws and guides all beings like a master guide;
he extensively proclaims the True Dharma for sentient beings and increases their spiritual wealth like a merchant leader.
They cause all beings to plant seeds of goodness, providing shelter and causing them to grow, just like a great cloud.
They instruct others on what is beneficial and harmful, just like parents.

They skillfully tame all those sentient beings who are difficult to subdue; they enable those not yet liberated to attain liberation, those not yet at peace to find peace, and those not yet in *nirvāṇa* to abide in *nirvāṇa*. For all those sentient beings oppressed by various dangers, evils, hardships, and sufferings, and struck by great terrors, they cause them to be delivered and freed from them.

"To speak briefly, that noble and holy one possesses great majestic power and is capable of performing all the works of a Buddha; he responds according to his mindfulness, just as he does now for you, providing deliverance in accordance with your thoughts during this time of your son's distress."
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader Sūrya was like one who had been restored to life; rolling about in agitation, he spoke thus:
"O virtuous one!..."
"Where is that Venerable Ānanda now?
The lay follower replied,
"O caravan leader!"
"Venerable Ānanda is currently at the Āmra Grove in the city of Vaiśālī.

Having spoken thus, the merchant-suzerain Sūrya rose immediately, and with respectful devotion, he knelt until his knees touched the ground; facing the city of Vaiśālī, he joined his palms in homage, his eyes brimming with tears, and spoke these words:
"O Venerable One of Great Compassion!"

My son now suffers the pain of separation; oppressed by grief and distress, he has no one to whom he can turn for relief. With my utmost sincerity and a heart of profound sorrow, I now weep and beseech the Venerable Ānanda: may you deign to grant him protection.
Thereupon, the merchant leader spoke these verses:
"This Venerable One is most supreme; He clearly understands the minds and intentions of all sentient beings.
He knows all things according to their nature and as they are wished for; I pray that he will now listen as I speak of this matter."
Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already entered parinirvāṇa; yet the Buddha’s disciples possess great majesty.
The Venerable One is of peerless erudition, able to uphold the Tathāgata’s pure teaching.
He has skillfully comforted my afflicted heart and serves as a refuge for the world.
You who always delight in benefiting sentient beings, I pray that you now examine this matter:
for what reason has my son now been brought to such harm? How could he have come to such a state?
I am now in peril and my son has no refuge; I pray that the Master’s majestic power will provide protection.
If the Holy One does not remain in the world, there will be no one further able to benefit sentient beings.
When those who believe in the good are about to be harmed, who other than the Master could grant them release?
Remaining in this world to benefit all beings, you are well able to uphold the Buddha’s True Dharma;
you should now give rise to a heart of compassion and compassionately accept and protect my son.
I have exhausted all directions and means, yet achieved nothing; now I have no refuge and no savior.
Father and son alike are submerged in the mire of sorrow; O Venerable One, out of compassion, please lift us up.
Now, with deep trepidation, I offer this earnest plea: O Śāriputra, benefactor of the world, what else remains?
The words spoken by the Teacher, Śākyamuni, now appear like light shining in the darkness;
save for you, Venerable One, who performs deeds of benefit, there is no one else capable of providing protection.
I pray that the Venerable One will swiftly descend; may you rouse a heart of compassion to save my son.
For the sake of my son, my mind is gripped by grief like a captive; the harassment of this wicked man is unbearable.
I, along with my wife and children, are utterly without refuge; I pray that the Joyful One bestows joy upon us.

When the merchant leader Sūryodgata had spoken these verses, the Venerable Ānanda’s heart was moved with increased compassion; three times by day and three times by night, he reflected upon this, and using the divine eye attained among the śrāvakas, he surveyed the world: "Which phenomena are increasing?"
What phenomena are diminishing?
What is perilous and evil?
What is difficult and painful?
What constitutes oppression?
What constitutes the presence of such matters as perilous, evil, and arduous oppression?
And what constitutes the minor?
What is increasing? What is expanding?
And which beings within the paths of the miserable realms shall I uplift?
Whom among the gods shall I establish in the happy realms and the path to liberation?
Whom, submerged in the mire of desire, shall I personally rescue and pull out?
"Who among those who have strayed from the noble wealth shall I cause to increase and expand that noble wealth?
Venerable Ānanda constantly observes sentient beings in this manner, no differently than Venerable Śāriputra and the others.

At that moment, the Venerable One, with his purified divine eye, beheld the golden youth, whose roots of merit planted in the past had reached maturity through superior practice, yet who was now entangled and oppressed by perilous, evil, and arduous suffering.

Having seen this, the Venerable One immediately extended his arm, like that of an elephant king, and swiftly vanished from the palace halls where King Ajātaśatru resided; remaining invisible, he merely snapped his fingers in the air to awaken him.
At that time, while the king was immersed in the pleasures of the palace, suddenly a voice resounded from the air, saying:
"Great King!
You have committed an unwholesome act; that youth Suvarṇavarṇa is entirely without fault, yet you yourself were unable to examine the matter with careful scrutiny."
At this moment, you have sent him out from the great city of Rājagṛha to the charnel ground to be cast away and executed; Your Majesty should now quickly put a stop to this matter.
At that time, having heard the words of the Venerable Ānanda from the air, King Ajātaśatru immediately turned around in agitation and fear, and prostrated himself at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda.
He then rose from his throne and raised a great voice, proclaiming to the four quarters, saying:
"Listen well! Go quickly to the charnel ground and announce my words:
'Do not kill that Golden Child; you must release him immediately.'"
"Among you, whoever is able to go and inform him, I shall bring forth that hidden gold treasury and bestow it upon you, and I shall also grant you five large villages."
When the great multitude heard the king’s proclamation that the beloved Golden Boy was to be released,
hundreds of thousands of people rushed out, vying with one another to announce the news.
At that time, the four executioners, together with the butchers, drove the golden-colored boy along until they reached the charnel ground.

At that moment, a female acquaintance and friend of Kāśisundarī, having adorned herself with various exquisite garments of blue, yellow, red, and white, arrived at the charnel ground in a palanquin. Thereupon, that acquaintance gathered firewood in that location, intending to construct a wooden cage for the pyre.
At that time, the executioners said:
"It is not yet appropriate for you to arrange the wooden cages for use; wait a moment, and once we have finished setting up the stakes for the boys, we shall kill them immediately."
"Then, having placed this boy of golden hue together with that girl Kāśisundarī upon the same pyre, set them ablaze.
Having spoken thus, the executioners immediately lifted the spit and set it upon the ground.

At that time, when the youth Suvarṇavarṇa saw that the stake had already been fixed in the ground, he immediately thought of his mother; overcome with intense anguish, his eyes filled with tears as he cried out:
"I am now parting from my mother forever; where is my mother at this moment?"
"In the past, when my mother lost me from her embrace in the middle of the night, even a brief moment of not seeing me caused her extreme suffering.
Furthermore, she thought: 'I have only this one son; now that we are separated, how can she continue to live?'"
"Alas! I truly have no merit to bring about this separation from my mother; both mother and son now endure great suffering.
At that time, the executioners dug into the ground and prepared to set up the stake, consulting one another and saying:
"Among you executioners, who is capable of raising the pike and setting up the Golden Boy?
They each pushed one another aside, saying, "You should set him up!
Then, one man among them said:
"I am now afflicted by a wind-disorder and have a headache; I cannot raise myself up.
Another among them said, "I am now suffering from back pain."
One said, "I now have pain in both my flanks.
The other said:
"I now have a pain in my belly.
Each of those executioners spoke of their own ailments and sought to avoid one another, unable to bear performing such meaningless and harmful tasks.
The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of the Golden-Colored Boy, Scroll Five.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the *śramaṇa* subject Dharmapāla, a Great Master of the Transmission of the Sanskrit Language (*Fan*) and Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Hongluqing*), who was conferred the purple robe.
At that time, having heard the various executioners conversing with one another, the Golden-Colored Youth saw the fork being dug up from the ground and held upright; he then spoke these words:
"Alas! How bitter!"

Now, as I undergo this perilous oppression, I have conceived a profound sense of weary detachment toward the vast faults of birth and death; I joyfully aspire to seek the supreme path of liberation. With no refuge for my body, a sense of treacherous and terrible fear arises within my mind.
In that very instant, he wept aloud again, crying out:
"Alas! Today, having exerted my strength to such an extreme difficulty to obtain this human body, I have been unable to accomplish any great beneficial deed."
Alas! I am once again wandering through the ocean of birth and death;
furthermore, I now abide in the conduct of birth and death.
Furthermore, I have wandered aimlessly and hesitantly amidst the vast wilderness of birth and death and its various perils;
furthermore, I am now returning to the most treacherous and evil places within birth and death;
furthermore, I am now falling back once more into the great abyss of birth and death.
Furthermore, I now cast myself back into the great net of birth and death;
furthermore, I shall be born within those various hells such as Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci;
furthermore, I shall be born among the animal realm, such as elephants, oxen, herds of beasts, winged birds, and various other species.

Furthermore, I shall constantly undergo sufferings such as hunger and thirst there, being born among those classes of hungry ghosts who do not obtain even a small portion of discarded food and drink, nor access to excrement or urine; all such realms are places of suffering and affliction.
In the past, I heard that the appearance of a Buddha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this world is as rare and supreme as the udumbara flower.
That Blessed One knows all laws and teachings, and is able to proclaim and awaken the world; he possesses in a single instant the Dharma that is so difficult to encounter.

Furthermore, I have now obtained this human body, born in a superior realm; my faculties are unimpaired—neither deaf nor mute—and I am neither crippled nor lame, possessing full physical strength. Moreover, I am able to understand the meaning of all phenomena, whether they be well-spoken or ill-spoken.

"Now that I am separated from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, I shall have no protection; furthermore, if I do not escape the eight difficulties, though I have obtained a human body, it will be fruitless and without benefit. What should I do at this time?"
Where is that Blessed One, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, now residing?

I pray only that you, O Greatly Benevolent One, will turn your thoughts toward me; have pity on me who am now without support, without a lord, without rescue, without refuge, without direction, and without illumination—suffering from perilous evils and hardships of extreme oppression.
"The World-Honored One possesses great compassion; may he deign to awaken us and come to our rescue.
Furthermore, he reflected to himself:
"How meager is my merit and how heavy are my karmic offenses, that the World-Honored One should so swiftly enter parinirvāṇa?"
While he was thus reflecting with trepidation, a sense of virtuous wisdom suddenly arose.
He further thought:

"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already entered parinirvāṇa, and the Greatly Virtuous One among the Buddha’s disciples, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa—who was entrusted by the Tathāgata to uphold the teachings—has also entered parinirvāṇa."

I have heard that the Venerable Ānanda currently upholds the Tathāgata’s teachings; he possesses great supernormal power and great majestic virtue, is able to extensively bring benefit to all sentient beings, and bears the burden of sentient beings without ever resting.
Yet that Venerable One possesses great compassion; he should take thought for me as I endure this hardship.
I pray only that the Venerable One, with a compassionate heart like that of the Buddha, will come quickly to rescue and protect me.

Having reflected thus, he immediately wept with tears of sorrow and, further intensifying his profound revulsion for the terrors of saṃsāra, gave rise to a supreme resolve for deliverance. Turning toward the Venerable Ānanda from afar, he lamented with piercing grief, speaking in verse:
“Within the terror of birth and death, I am capable of great fear; I have never known the arising of joy.
Venerable Ānanda, you know all this completely; I pray that you will now listen to these words.”
After the Buddha, the Omniscient One of Great Compassion, had entered parinirvāṇa through his emanations,
he entrusted the gateway of the True Dharma that benefits sentient beings to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa;
that Venerable One then brought about their welfare and, having completed his transformative work, passed into nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, through the gateway of benefiting the world, he entrusted [the teachings] to Ānanda of great majesty;

and to the Venerable Kāśyapa of great renown. From the time after his parinirvāṇa until the present day, the Venerable One has been a single kinsman to the world, extensively performing what is beneficial and bringing joy to sentient beings.
He acts as the sovereign lord over the three realms that have no master; he bestows fearlessness upon those who are terrified;
he places the weary in a place of rest; and he serves as a refuge for those who have no refuge.
The Venerable One is the sole kinsman of the world; he is capable of accomplishing all that the Great Teacher did.
Among the disciples of the Buddha, he is the most honored attendant, and now he skillfully upholds the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Venerable One, now that I am in this land of suffering and hardship, if you do not deign to rescue me, I have no other lord upon whom to rely; I see that I am now utterly destroyed.
All who are born are certain to return to death; the wise should not harbor fear of death.
O Venerable One, you are able, within the wheel of birth and death, to well know the essential paths of liberation.
If one can escape the eight unfavorable conditions, every action will be fruitful and death itself will be sweet;
yet to accomplish such a feat in a single instant is extremely difficult, and for this reason, I am filled with sorrow.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world to teach the Dharma to all is the most supreme and exceedingly difficult to encounter;
O Venerable One, you should now come with mindfulness, just as the Buddhas of the past personally transformed and delivered beings.
The Venerable One’s compassion is most firm and steadfast; He has appeared for the sake of all sentient beings.
Do not forsake me with your great loving-kindness and compassion; I now seek to enter the path of liberation.
The Venerable One possesses the power of great merit, Constantly giving rise to the mind that benefits sentient beings;
Now, amidst my own hardships and afflictions, I pray only that you will observe me with compassion.
I am now in peril and suffering, without protection; may the World-Honored One illuminate me with your divine eye.
O Venerable One, descend swiftly out of your compassion; you should now rescue me from this suffering.

When the youth Suvarṇavarṇa spoke these verses, the Venerable Ānanda, for the sake of bringing about the benefit and happiness of the world at large, gave rise to a compassionate thought. He universally observed the inclinations and desires of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, maintaining an uninterrupted flow of altruistic intent. Then, with his divine eye, he beheld the youth Suvarṇavarṇa in extreme suffering, without any refuge or support.

Having performed this contemplation, he gave rise to a heart of compassion and emitted subtle, wondrous light that pervaded the cities, palaces, and all surrounding regions, so that every realm was completely illuminated.

Immediately, together with his retinue of five hundred great arhats, each exerting their supernormal powers, they simultaneously ascended into the air. Like clouds or a canopy, they remained suspended in mid-air, manifesting all manner of auspicious signs everywhere; a surrounding radiance shone broadly upon all things as they circled toward the Śmaśāna (Cemetery).

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the ruler of the land, was atop a lofty, wide, and exquisitely pure pavilion. He beheld the Venerable Ānanda and the assembly of bhikṣus appearing like the crescent moon; the Venerable One sat cross-legged in their midst, soaring high into the air like a cloud or a canopy, adorned with various wondrous and lovely ornaments, as he gradually approached the place of the charnel ground.
Having seen this, the lord of the land immediately thought to himself:

"The Venerable Ānanda has surely come here for the sake of that Golden-Clad Youth. Now that the Venerable One has arrived, he will certainly manifest rare and auspicious signs and intend to proclaim a never-before-heard Dharma. I ought now to go to him with all haste."

Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru paid his respects and prostrated before the Venerable One and his retinue of Arhats; having descended from the high tower, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of attendants and escorted by them on foot, he proceeded forward toward the Śmaśāna (cemetery).
At that time, the four executioners all gave rise to anger; seizing their swords, they threatened the various butchers and addressed them, saying:
"Why have you delayed this matter for so long?"
"Do not hastily impale the youth Suvarṇavarṇa upon the stake.
Upon hearing these words, all the executioners were struck with terror and immediately set up the stake for the youth Suvarṇavarṇa.
At that time, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa again gave rise to an extreme sense of weary detachment; seeing the faults of saṃsāra and having no place of refuge, he uttered these words:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Alas! If the Venerable Ānanda does not take me into his care now, I shall surely perish.
As the youth spoke these words, the Venerable Ānanda approached from afar, raising his voice to comfort them all.
He then comforted the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, saying to him:
"Son, do not fear!

You are one who is well-disciplined and knows the Dharma and Vinaya; I shall now suppress this unrighteousness for your sake, so that it may not cause harm, just as the venom of a snake or an extremely wicked person does."

Therefore, I now cause you to escape such perilous danger; I now fulfill your wishes for you just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, did. At this time, I shall proclaim what is appropriate according to the knowledge and vision of the Buddha. Furthermore, just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having entrusted the True Dharma to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, acted in accordance with that teaching through his true deeds, so do I now speak to you the Dharma taught by the foremost Śrāvaka of great majestic power.
I shall now fulfill your aspirations;
I shall now bring to an end for you the fear of death and all fears within saṃsāra;
I shall now extract for you the arrows of doubt and conceptual proliferation.
"You have covered your pure eye with the veil of evil views; I shall treat it with the medicine of wisdom to restore its clarity.
Now I shall extinguish the fire of your anger; I shall now cause you to be purified of greed;

I shall now cause you to plant the seeds of virtue extensively; I shall now pull you out from the mud of birth and death; I shall now cause you to cross over the ocean of suffering; I shall now lead you beyond all perilous boundaries; I shall now untie the bonds of affliction for you; and I shall now shatter the gates of hindrances for you."

To speak briefly, I shall now act for you as is appropriate: that which you have accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭi-nayuta* eons—difficult to attain and most supreme—is the exhaustion of all afflictions and the realization of Arhatship. With the fire of wisdom, you have thoroughly burned away the fuel of all afflictions; having attained this superior state, you are free from the disease of doubt. Just as a great tree that has stood for a thousand years is extremely difficult to fell, you have used the vajra of wisdom to sever it at its very roots.
At that time, the Venerable One spoke again in verse:
"Greed, hatred, and pride constantly continue, Flowing endlessly into the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Boarding the vessel of diligence and wisdom, I shall now cause it to dry up for your sake."
Birth is great suffering, and old age is its root; death is the ultimate place of peril.
The sharp, diamond-like blade of supreme wisdom is keen and firm; it shatters all mountains of suffering, crushing them utterly.
Throughout thousands of koṭis of kalpas, you have diligently and painfully accumulated that which was never before attained;
that which is most difficult to obtain has now been made available for you—the attainment of the dharma free from outflows.

At that time, having heard these words from the Venerable Ānanda, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa felt as though he had been restored to life; his body and mind became tranquil and he was filled with great joy. He gazed up into the sky with single-minded concentration, staring fixedly at the Venerable One.
At that time, the four execution officials said to the butchers:
"You should know that these bhikṣus are people of compassionate heart; they have now come through the air and may cause us obstacles and difficulties."
"You all should now quickly place the boy upon the stake; otherwise, will we not be transgressing the King's command, inviting guilt and bringing about what is meaningless and disadvantageous?"

When those executioners heard these words, they were all terrified for their wives, children, and kinsmen that their lives would be taken; immediately, they lifted up the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, intending to place him upon the stake.

Venerable Ānanda swiftly employed his supernormal powers to manifest a pure lunar disc upon that forked branch; its radiance was brilliant and white. Within the disc appeared a wondrous lotus pedestal, vast in extent. Through the empowerment of the Venerable One’s supernormal powers, the golden boy was naturally caused to sit cross-legged upon the lotus pedestal. Having ascended the seat, he surveyed everything in all directions.
At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of nayutas of worthies and sages in the void, who all raised their voices together, saying:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
He spoke these verses:
"How marvelous!
The great power of the True Teaching; the Buddha’s omniscience is truly unprecedented, and now his śrāvaka disciples likewise are able to perform the miraculous feats of a Tathāgata."
At this very time, the Venerable Ānanda’s great power and majesty are clearly manifest;
his deeds are entirely identical to those of the Sugata, and the vast True Dharma is unprecedented.
Although the light of the Buddha-sun has already set, the venerable one’s majestic radiance shines forth once more;
all afflictions and distresses are entirely dispelled—how marvelous!
Auspicious and greatly joyful,
with the great majestic power of the virtue of his own wisdom, His radiance brilliant and his adornment magnificent,
the Venerable One is like the exquisite orb of the moon, Appearing in the midst of space, pure and serene.
The light of the Sugata having already set, Darkness now shrouds all the worlds;
But the Venerable One’s divine radiance shines forth again, And the True Dharma is now most clearly revealed.
Although the most supreme Jewel of the Buddha is now hidden, his inconceivable virtues are entirely complete;
he is the Great Auspiciousness, the crest-jewel of the world, whom the Venerable Ānanda is able to reveal and manifest.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was situated high in the void, like the pure lunar disc in autumn; his radiance was brilliant and white, illuminating all things. Furthermore, he appeared like a canopy of clouds, manifesting auspicious signs that were pervasive and pure. With his own majestic light eclipsing the sun, he stood in the midst of the air surrounded by a retinue of five hundred great Arhats, and spoke these verses for the youth Suvarṇavarṇa:
“The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has appeared in the world; This is indeed the supreme and most rare wonder.
He is the most excellent teacher of gods and humans, Whose five eyes are pure and free from obstruction.”
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught in the past: this sublime Dharma-gate of purity that is free from suffering;
if one can understand the cause of this suffering, all such suffering can be completely severed.
By knowing suffering, one can sever its origin; thus one can transcend the phenomena of suffering.
By practicing the Noble Eightfold Path according to the truth, one proceeds toward Nirvana and attains peace and happiness.
Now, as I speak according to what the Buddha has taught, all phenomena of suffering are entirely extinguished;
right wisdom can shatter the mind of ignorance, and through this cessation, one shall no longer undergo future existence.

When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these verses, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, having heard this Dharma, shattered the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of a self with the vajra of wisdom, and immediately realized the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

At that time, having realized this fruit, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa experienced a supreme sense of well-being, joy, and delight, like a merchant who has gained great profit, like a farmer whose sown seeds have ripened, like a warrior who has achieved victory in battle, or like one who has become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Immediately joining their palms in reverence, they addressed the Venerable Ānanda with verses of praise:

“We take refuge in you, Venerable Ānanda; We take refuge in the most supreme Great Honored One, And we further take refuge in all the sons of the Buddha, Who have raised the great Dharma-banner of the Muni.”
Rare is your compassion, so exceedingly vast; rare is your compassion, most supreme.
Now, as I am tormented by suffering and utterly perilous, may you, O Venerable One, compassionately deliver me.
In this place, the Venerable Ānanda can hear all those sounds;
I am oppressed by suffering and have no one to turn to, yet the Venerable One has rescued me so that I have attained liberation.
Amidst the path of affliction that blazes most fiercely, it is through the power of the Venerable One that I have attained coolness.
The mind of compassion is like the pure lunar disc, from which emerges the pure moon of the Muni.
Whatever I have now attained and whatever I have accomplished was not due to my parents or various kinsmen;
it is because this Venerable Good Friend has appeared that I have obtained such supreme benefit.
The Venerable One well closes off all evil realms, And likewise can open the gate of liberation;
He dries up the entire stream of birth and death, And thoroughly shatters the mountain-like heap of bones.
Birth and death are fundamentally without beginning, middle, or end; The various terrors are accumulated through afflictions.
By means of the gate of the equality of the vajra of wisdom, The Venerable One has skillfully transcended all extremes.
Sunk deeply since beginningless time, with the arrow of sorrow piercing the heart and yet not extracted, I have now encountered the Supreme Great Physician King;
born from the mouth of the Dharma, I am freed from all ailments.

At that time, those noble beings in the sky gazed intently upon the Venerable Ānanda; in an instant, they spontaneously cleared away all earth, stones, sand, and gravel from within and without the Śītavana charnel ground. They sprinkled it everywhere with sandalwood-scented water, burned various famous incenses, erected victory banners and jeweled pavilions, and further scattered garments adorned with pearls and all kinds of lovely, exquisite flowers. Suddenly, that place became pure and magnificently adorned, like the Joyful Garden (Nandana) of the devas.

At that time, the various worthies and sages arranged for the Venerable Ānanda a magnificent display of diverse and exquisite precious jewels in rows, establishing for him a great lion throne made entirely of gold and jewels, along with a jeweled footstool; furthermore, they individually prepared seats adorned with jewels for the assembly of five hundred arhats.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda descended from the air and took his place upon the lion throne; the five hundred great arhats also descended from the air, each ascending to their respective seats.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the lord of the realm, together with his retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of ministers and attendants, having arrived at the assembly, beheld various sublime signs.

He beheld that golden youth, his radiance pure and brilliant within a stainless lunar disc, seated upon a lotus pedestal; like the full moon in an autumn sky when the clouds have dispersed, and like a golden banner, his light was fiercely blazing, auspicious, and extraordinary.

When the king had observed this, he was struck with awe and wonder, giving rise to a most supreme and extraordinary mind. The hairs on his body stood on end and his face beamed with joy; like the surging waves of the ocean, his pure faith deepened further. He immediately prostrated himself fully upon the ground before the Venerable Ānanda, bowing with the utmost reverence. Raising his mouth toward the Venerable’s feet, he extended his homage once more, then knelt with palms joined, gazing up at the Venerable Ānanda with sincere devotion as he spoke these verses:
"I take refuge in the Great Sage, the Most Supreme!
Today you have performed a noble deed, Able to universally deliver those in this assembly, And furthermore, to rescue and uplift us."
If we, this multitude of people here, were not sustained by the Venerable One,
and if his voice had resounded widely throughout this assembly, we would all have been utterly destroyed.
Had it not been for the protection of the Venerable One, all activities for the benefit of sentient beings would have ceased;
we, the great assembly, at this very moment, would all have been scorched and consumed by the raging fire.
How marvelous!
Venerable One of Great Supreme Wisdom, Possessing the most sublime heart of compassion, Your rare and excellent conduct is thus; To manifest and proclaim it is truly extraordinary.
The clouds of spiritual transformations you now manifest, we all behold as something unprecedented;
this supreme, tranquil, and great majestic radiance is no different from the light of the Tathāgata.
All the perils and sufferings of the world have gathered together; O Venerable One, you are our sovereign, our refuge, and our savior.
You are able to bring vast benefit to all sentient beings, just as the Buddha’s compassionate heart universally loves and cherishes them.
The World-Honored One universally beholds all worlds, And we have all attained great joy and bliss;
Now you, O Venerable One, illuminate the world, Upholding the pure teaching of the Muni.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having offered this verse in praise, had his wishes fulfilled to his heart's content and felt great joy in his mind. He rose quickly and went forward to where the iron fork had been previously placed; there he extended both hands to receive the golden-colored boy, feeling the utmost delight as if he had obtained a beloved son.

At that time, the youth descended naturally from his lotus seat. The king’s affection for him deepened further; he hurried forward to embrace him, caressing him again and again, gazing at him with wide eyes until his eyes were filled with joy. He spoke these verses:
"When I first attained the royal throne in the past, My joy at that time was not so profound.
Seeing you now, amidst such pressing hardships, Attain liberation brings me double the joy."
From the circle of his face emerge pure eyes, Like the petals of the utpala flower;
Their radiance blazes, outshining the light of the moon. Now, at this very moment, we have obtained the sight of him;
His physical marks are perfect and his form is supple. He is fully endowed with merit and adorned with all ornaments.
All your limbs are perfectly complete, And you are seen by all, radiant and brilliant.
What kind of merciless and utterly wicked person did you encounter in the past,
That they would take you— a person beloved by the multitude— and cause you to be killed and cast away?
Your conduct is profoundly serene and disciplined; those who hear your words are filled with joy.
Your physical form is so upright and majestic that it is rare even in this world—whom in all the world would not love and revere you?
Why give rise to anger toward one who possesses virtue? How could merit ever tolerate the presence of fault?
With a mind as truly adamantine as theirs, how could one conceive of distinctions therein?
Those whose hearts are made of iron and stone, and those who are utterly devoid of thought—such as these would destroy their own consciousness; they should feel no love for your son.

The firm, great vajra-flame blazes intensely; as if someone were to lift it and place it upon my crown, or as if a sharp sword were to sever my neck and chest—when you see me thus destroyed, you shall be like that as well.
Furthermore, like fierce and evil thunderbolts and hailstones falling from the sky, they strike at my heart.
Now, you who were beloved by all—by whom were you commanded to commit this slaughter? Alas!
Who uttered such fierce and cruel words, causing you to perform such a deed? What most wicked enemy has bound your heart, that you now find no joy in yourself?
Why does the King of Death come to harass you?
For what reason has he conceived such loathing?
Who was it that killed you in the past?
"You should now quickly speak for me.
At that time, having heard these words from King Ajātaśatru, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa immediately gave rise to this thought:
"If I were now to report those past events in detail to the king, would it not be as if I were committing an evil deed against the minister Pracaṇḍa?"
"Why is this? Because the king's nature is violent and impetuous; his wrath will manifest in an instant, and he will take your life right now.
She then reflected further:

"I have merely examined my own past karma; throughout the various births I have experienced in previous lives, I certainly created various unwholesome karmas myself. Now that they have matured, their retribution is manifest before me. Thus I know that the causes of karma from previous lives cannot escape their retribution. Therefore, at this time, I am truly without fault; it is because others wished to kill me that I was cast away."
Having formed this thought, being certain and free from doubt, he immediately went before the king and spoke these verses:
"As I have previously, in former lives, Created for myself unwholesome karma, The fruition of that karma has now ripened; Its retribution shall now manifest."
The unlovely fruits summoned today are all due to causes of unwholesome action committed by oneself;
there is no doubt that one must receive retribution at this time—Your Majesty should investigate this for my sake with care.
Having spoken these verses, the youth approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated himself fully upon the ground to pay homage at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the youth, saying: "Young man!

This girl Kāśisundarī had previously had her limbs covered by snake venom; through the power of your true empowerment, cause her now to rise and move with swift ease and recovery as before, and also cause all the members of this assembly to give rise to pure faith."
At that time, having heard the words of the Venerable One, the youth Suvarṇavarṇa became firm in his deep resolve toward all sentient beings and immediately gave rise to this thought:

"By the power of the true empowerment of my courageous exertion—if the Dharma is true and what I have spoken is true—then regarding this girl Kāśisundarī, I have certainly never given rise to even the slightest affliction, whether it be greed, hatred, delusion, or malice, nor any other distinct mental factors or secondary afflictions; since the Dharma is true and my words are true, may the poison in this woman's body be dissolved and she be restored to her former state."

After the youth had performed this true empowerment through his contemplation, the poison in the body of the maiden Kāśisundarī was dissolved; she immediately regained consciousness, rose up and turned about, and became as healthy and comfortable as before. Looking around in all four directions, she then beheld the entire assembly gathered there.
At that time, the entire great assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of humans and devas spoke with one voice, saying:
"How marvelous! How rare!"

The youth Suvarṇavarṇa’s mind was pure; possessing great spiritual efficacy and great power, he was able to act in this way through the force of his true empowerment, causing the young girl Kāśisundarī to rise up in lightness and ease, and restore her beloved life.

Then that maiden Kāśisundarī looked about her once more with careful attention, surveying the entire assembly; she even saw in the Śmaśāna forest the Venerable Ānanda seated upon a lion throne in the shape of a half-moon together with a great multitude of bhikṣus, amidst a vast and exquisite radiance of various jewels, arranged in successive order; and she also saw King Ajātaśatru, the sovereign of the land, present in the assembly along with hundreds of thousands of ministers, aides, and retinues.
Furthermore, she saw herself previously lying upon a bamboo litter, adorned with blue, yellow, red, and white silken fabrics.
Upon seeing this, the young girl felt doubt and fear in her heart, thinking:
"Is this perhaps what I have seen in a dream?"
"Is your mind deluded and confused?
Or should you know that such a state has been brought about by the retribution of your own karma?
Thereafter, her kinsmen explained the preceding events to her in detail and truthfully, saying to the young girl:
"These various signs and phenomena are all because the Venerable Ānanda has descended here and, through his majestic spiritual power, restored your life.
At that time, having heard these words, the young girl immediately conceived a most supreme, pure, faithful, and marvelous mind toward the Venerable Ānanda. She then reflected to herself:

"Previously, while in the garden, I harbored intentions to cause harm to that fierce and cruel minister; oppressed by the fear of death, my mind was daily confounded. In this state of evil, I felt deep loathing and aversion, realizing that this female body brings about much suffering and affliction."
Alas! Alas!
The name "woman" is more utterly base and lowly than other classes; it is the gathering place of all sufferings. How can I now abandon this female state, which my mind so detests?

Having formed this thought, he quickly rose from the assembly and sought out an exquisite robe. Holding it up, he approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, and offered the robe to him. Generating the most supreme and pure faith, he reflected upon the Venerable Ānanda’s most excellent virtues:
"Previously, by the power of your true empowerment, you have granted me tranquility; your Dharma is true, your words are true.
Among all the disciples of the Tathāgata, you are the foremost in learning—the most eminent among the eminent."
The highest, the highest among the highest; a dragon among śrāvakas, a lion among śrāvakas,
a great seer among śrāvakas, one who is well-tamed among śrāvakas, a *padma* flower among śrāvakas,
a *kumuda* flower among śrāvakas, a white lotus among śrāvakas, and a charioteer among śrāvakas.
The teacher among śrāvakas, the moon among śrāvakas, the sun among śrāvakas, the jewel among śrāvakas, the crest-jewel among śrāvakas;
one who is highly learned in the Dharma, one who upholds the teaching,
an arhat whose taints are exhausted and whose task is accomplished, having laid down the heavy burden and attained...
Having attained their own benefit, with all fetters of existence exhausted and their minds well-liberated, they possess great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue,
as well as great radiance, serving as a great field of merit.
"Venerable One, since you possess such great merit, and since the Dharma is true and your words are true, may I this very day transform my female body into the form of a male."

As these words were spoken, through the power of the Venerable One’s true empowerment, the young girl Kāśisundarī was transformed in that very instant from a female body into a male form. The resulting male body was endowed with perfect physical characteristics; it was upright, exquisite, and a joy for all to behold, and his person was adorned with various fine garments and ornaments.

At that time, various kinds of exquisite and pleasing celestial garments rained down spontaneously from the sky; these garments were so vast they filled the void like a wheel, covering everything everywhere. In an instant, within that Śītavana charnel ground, the wheel of garments eclipsed the sun’s radiance so that it was no longer visible.

At that time, when the great assembly of gods and humans in the gathering saw this event, they were all struck with wonder, realizing that the Venerable Ānanda possessed such great majestic power and merit.
Immediately, there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas in the sky, all of whom spoke these words:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"

This is vast, extraordinary, and truly unprecedented: the Venerable Ānanda, endowed with great majesty and virtue, acting as a most supreme and pure field of merit, has caused that maiden Kāśisundarī, while offering a single garment in the practice of pure giving, to have her female form transformed into a male form through the continuity of her power of aspiration.
"How magnificent are these practices and vows!
How truly sublime they are!
At that time, all the devas and humans conceived pure faith; they immediately rained down various celestial flowers from mid-air and played exquisite, lovely celestial music.

At that time, the man Kāśisundara, through the great majestic power of the Venerable Ānanda, had his own desires fulfilled according to his wishes. Having clearly observed such present karmic retribution, he gave rise to a heart of supreme joy; the hairs on his body stood on end, and he immediately rose and approached the Venerable Ānanda. With both knees touching the ground, he joined his palms in reverence and, with sincere devotion, praised him by speaking these verses:
"I take refuge in the one difficult to encounter and inconceivable, Adorned with pure and wondrous merit.
Today I have no other support; It is because of the Venerable One that I have regained my life."
If I had not now obtained you, protected by your pure eye of wisdom, my remaining life could not have survived;
O Venerable One, you have now restored my life to me.
How marvelous!
The great power and majesty of merit; how marvelous!
Universally bestowing joy upon all sentient beings.
Now, amidst this pressing suffering and hardship regarding form, you have skillfully provided protection for many.
How marvelous!

You are a worthy recipient of offerings, most exceedingly rare and perfectly pure. With a single garment I express my heart of giving; through your majestic power, a small act has been transformed into a great benefit.
Furthermore, even a single garment, though exceedingly small, when offered to the Great Muni, the Honored One, will be fulfilled according to one's own wishes;
this is the fruit manifested through the power of your own virtue.
In my view, this female body has accumulated vast and manifold faults;
through the empowerment of the Venerable One’s majestic power, it shall be transformed into a male body.
As he turns again and again, his features resemble those of a celestial being;
his body is adorned with divine ornaments, and from the sky there falls a rain of exquisite celestial robes, scattering down in profusion to increase his joy.

Such is this sublime field of merit; if a person cannot act in accordance with reality, that person will have meager fruits of fortune and their benefit will be in vain, bound as they are by the enemies of ignorance and other afflictions.
Having spoken these verses in praise, the man clearly observed such manifest karmic retributions and thought to himself: "My physical appearance has now become like this;

furthermore, I have clearly perceived the fruits of both the desirable and the undesirable, with both principle and fact made evident. I shall no longer remain in the householder's life, but must seek to go forth into homelessness."
Having formed this thought, he approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Venerable One!
I now wish to go forth purely within the Dharma of the Venerable One, receive full ordination to assume the form of a bhikṣu, and vow to practice the holy life under the Venerable One."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda immediately instructed him in the method for going forth; having thus become a bhikṣu, he severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, the merchant-suzerain Sūrya and his wife, already tormented by the anguish of separation from the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, were fleeing in a state of frantic alarm through the streets, lanes, and alleys of Rājagṛha. They collapsed upon the ground, rising and falling again and again, halting and lingering in their movements, bewildered and distraught with fear. Raising their hands to strike their own bodies, they cried out in a loud voice:
"Alas! What misery!"
My son! Alas! My son!
Overwhelmed by grief, they wept once more.
At that moment, the merchant leader suddenly heard someone say:
"The Venerable Ānanda has come through the air to the Śītavana cemetery to protect the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, performing many wondrous and extraordinary deeds for his sake."

When the merchant lord Sūryodgata and his wife heard these words, it was as if nectar-water were poured upon their hearts and crowns; they gave rise to a state of supreme joy, like the most excellent delight experienced by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) upon receiving the consecration of his rank.
Immediately, he rose from the ground, rolling over, and hurriedly ran out of the great city of Rājagṛha toward the Śmaśāna (cemetery).

Upon arrival, he saw the Golden Boy, as pure and radiant as the full autumn moon when the clouds have dispersed from the sky and Rāhu has removed his veil; he was sitting calmly near the Venerable Ānanda.

Furthermore, he beheld the Venerable One’s great power and majesty, which produced rare and extraordinary signs and phenomena, such that gods and humans were struck with wonder at his vast and divine transformations.

Upon seeing this, the merchant leader conceived a supreme, pure, and extraordinary sense of faith toward the Venerable Ānanda; prostrating himself fully upon the ground, he paid homage at the Venerable One’s feet.

Having risen, he again knelt with both knees upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and gazed up with sincere devotion. His great joy reached its peak, and tears flowed from his eyes as he praised the Venerable Ānanda with single-minded devotion, speaking these verses:
"How marvelous!..."

Venerable One of great merit and power, whose vast majesty and spiritual authority are most manifest, I now stand amidst peril and dire distress; may you, Venerable One, graciously provide me with protection and refuge.
How marvelous!
How marvelous is the great and supreme virtue of compassion!
How marvelous!
Your wondrous wisdom is perfectly complete;
you, the World-Honored One, possess all-knowledge, most supreme, pure, and luminous.
Just as I am now, for the sake of my son, submerged in the perilous sea of suffering, [I pray you grant me relief].
Venerable One, with great majesty of wisdom, You skillfully rescue me through your expedient means.
If I had not now encountered you, And been sustained by your compassionate heart,
I and my wife and children would long have been cast Into the net of sorrow and suffering, from which there is no escape.
Venerable One, you have now descended here, born of the power of great compassion;
the son has already crossed the ocean of sorrow and likewise emerged from the perilous place of grief.
The rope of sorrow that once bound me has now been released; the wandering flux of sorrowful conduct has now ceased.
The delusions, fears, and terrors of sorrow have now been eliminated; I have now emerged from the cage and shackles of sorrow.
Not mired in the mud of sorrow, Not wounded by the thorns of grief,
Not invaded by the venomous snake of lamentation, Not struck by the arrows of misery,
Not severed by the sword of despair, And not encountering the enmity of sorrow.
The great fish of sorrow and affliction do not devour one another, nor are they scorched by the fires of grief.
Today, O Venerable One, you have performed a noble deed; your wondrous light shines universally upon this great assembly.
The pure eyes of all sentient beings are now fully opened, and the minds of all are filled with joy.
The Venerable One whose name is the Honored Ānanda, Born from joy for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings;
Thus skillfully opening the gate of deliverance, I now have attained great rejoicing.

At that time, after the merchant lord Sūrya had spoken these verses in praise of the Venerable One, he went together with his wife to where the youth Suvarṇavarṇa was. With a mother’s heart, his affection and love for him intensified; he rushed forward to take him in his arms, caressing him again and again, his great joy overflowing until tears fell from his eyes.
The parents simultaneously raised their bowls and gazed intently at the boy with joyful eyes, reciting this verse:
“The auspicious marks of the full autumn moon, The pure radiance of your body shines everywhere;
All our manifold aspirations are now fulfilled— Parents rejoice once more to behold your face.”
With eyes of deep blue and pupils like the luster of red copper, Long, broad, and exquisitely beautiful, most perfectly majestic— This is because the Venerable One has descended;
Father and mother rejoice to behold your face again.
