At that time, the Golden Boy, his mind utterly weary of and detached from the faults of birth and death, immediately informed his parents and proceeded to the place of the Venerable Ānanda. Prostrating at the Venerable’s feet, he spoke these words:
“I now wish to leave the household life in purity within the Dharma of the Venerable, receive full ordination to assume the form of a bhikṣu, and vow to cultivate the holy life under the Venerable.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda immediately instructed him in the dharma for going forth.
Once he had become a bhikṣu, in a mere moment he severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship.

Having realized this fruit, he uses the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) to clearly contemplate the causes of karma from his successive previous existences. He then perceives that his own body is endowed with extremely superior and great power of merit (*puṇya*), and he thinks:

"Although I have now obtained such power of merit, this meritorious life has its limits; the fact that I have received such a retribution as this must surely be due to the various causes of merit I created in the past."
"I should now, for the sake of all sentient beings, open the gateway to merit so that they may develop reverence, and furthermore, manifest the majestic power of my own merit.

Having thought this, he immediately removed the garment he was wearing and offered it as a pure gift. By his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), as soon as one garment was removed, another appeared spontaneously; in this manner, garments were repeatedly removed and reappeared. As they were removed, they were reborn in such great numbers that they formed a heap before the Venerable Ānanda.

The robes he had accumulated were exquisite and priceless; their radiance was as brilliant as the newly risen sun, and like a mass of blazing light from Jāmbūnada gold, the more one gazed at them from every angle, the more beautiful their luster became.
At that time, when the entire assembly in the gathering had seen this event, their hearts were filled with wonder and they all spoke these words:
"How marvelous! How rare!"
How marvelous! How rare!
How marvelous!
Blessings possess supreme power.
How marvelous!
They are able to perform such vast and majestic meritorious deeds.
If the succession of robes shed by this venerable one were to continue without interruption, even those priceless, vast, and exquisite garments would not reach their end.

Then the Venerable Suvarṇavarṇa first offered these robes to his parents; thereafter, he made a pure gift of the robes to the assembly of bhikṣus headed by the Venerable Ānanda, extending even to the entire multitude gathered in the charnel ground. He bestowed two robes upon each person to wear, yet because of the supernatural power of the bhikṣu Suvarṇavarṇa, although they were thus distributed so universally, the heap of robes was not exhausted.

At that time, the Venerable Suvarṇavarṇa, by means of his own supernatural power, leaped into the air and proceeded to the great city of Rājagṛha. Throughout all the streets and alleys, he removed the exquisite golden robes he was wearing and piled them into a vast heap.
Then, throughout the great city of Rājagṛha, he proclaimed in a loud voice:
"All you people, know this! I now remove the robes I am wearing and bestow them universally upon all. You who wish to receive and use them as appropriate, take them as you please."

Upon hearing this, in an instant, a vast assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of people gathered together to behold the sight. Throughout the streets and alleys of Rājagṛha, a magnificent heap of golden robes was piled high, glowing like the light of the rising sun or the radiant luster of Jāmbūnada gold.
The Venerable Suvarṇa stood aloft in the air, his majestic splendor blazing forth like a mountain of gold, auspicious and intensely brilliant.

When the entire great assembly beheld this phenomenon, they were all struck with wonder; their faces were as radiant and serene as the appearance of the ocean waves, and they all thought to themselves:
"How marvelous!
How marvelous!
This matter is truly rare!
What cause and what fruit are cultivated such that the majestic spiritual power and virtuous strength are all so exceptionally sublime?
"If we were able to know the causes being cultivated and act accordingly as they truly are, the majestic power of the fruits we obtain would likewise be so.
These people, following their own inclinations and having conceived doubts, then deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Now, the majestic power and virtuous strength of this Venerable One are so extraordinary; has he long cultivated the practice of ascetic observances?"
"Is it because he possesses the wisdom of the divine eye?
We should now inquire of him.

Having thus deliberated among themselves, the multitude raised their hands, brightened their eyes, and joined their palms; they gazed with sincere devotion toward the sky and, taking refuge and prostrating before the Venerable Golden One, spoke these verses with one voice:
“Venerable One, you who possess such great and supreme merit, Should have attained the wisdom of the divine eye;
Able to bestow such great majestic power, Venerable One, you should now explain this to me.”
If one seeks wealth, happiness, and merit, whether in this world or in another,
what supreme practice must be cultivated to achieve perfection?
Venerable One, you should now explain this to me.
Then that Venerable One, the Great Being, gave rise to a heart of even more exalted compassion;
he uttered words of vast joy, his wondrous voice pervading all directions.
I now proclaim this meaning, clearly revealing and showing it to you all;
spreading it forth extensively according to its proper sequence, listen attentively to what I say.
In this world and in worlds beyond, whatever accomplishments, gateways of manifold merit, wealth, joy, virtues,
and wonders I have attained— all these are obtained through the cultivation of merit.
If you weary of all sufferings and desire to achieve happiness, you should swiftly cultivate the causes of merit; then, blessings and joy will all be gathered unto you.
For all who seek to achieve pleasant fruits, whether in this world or in another, they will certainly obtain them without doubt;
for through the cultivation of merit, there is a fruit.

Householders, lay devotees, and merchant leaders, as well as brahmins and other such classes of people, enjoy vast wealth and pleasures according to their hearts' desire; this is because they cultivated merit, and thus these fruits exist for them.
If one desires among human beings to obtain a retinue such as a wife, concubines, and children,
who are harmonious, complete, and pleasing to the mind, it is because of the cultivation of merit that these fruits arise.

With physical marks of humility and supreme excellence, opening eyes that bring delight for all to behold, he has attained wondrous majesty and splendor among men; such is the fruit born from the cultivation of merit.
If one wishes to achieve success among human beings— possessing a complete retinue that remains unbroken,
and enjoying inexhaustible wealth and resources— it is through the cultivation of merit that such results arise.
Desiring to possess supreme merit and the recollection of past lives, so that those who hear one's words all believe and comply,
and always being held in high esteem by the multitude among humans— these results arise from the cultivation of merit.
If one desires to accomplish vast merit that follows one through every successive birth,
and to experience enjoyments among humans that bring satisfaction to the mind, these results exist because of the cultivation of merit.
If one among humans desires to achieve accomplishment, such that countless treasures are all abundant and overflowing—
remaining firm for a long time without diminishing and being perfectly complete— it is because of the cultivation of merit that such fruits exist.
If one wishes to be born in Uttarakuru, there is no sense of "I" or "mine" for those born there;
their lifespan among humans is fixed, and they possess these fruits by virtue of having cultivated merit.
All fields, seedlings, grains, rice, and so forth, grow extensively and naturally without being sown;
that people enjoy such abundance is the fruit resulting from the cultivation of merit.
The garments from the kalpavṛkṣa trees are exceedingly sublime;
those robes are natural and not man-made, covering the limbs of the body as one desires. This fruit exists because of the cultivation of merit.
Furthermore, desiring rebirth in Uttarakuru, receiving uninterrupted retribution among humans,
and upon death being born in the heavens— these results arise from the cultivation of merit.
The dragon kings receive superior retributions like those of devas; the food they consume has a flavor like *sudhā*.
They enjoy celestial blessings within the earth because of their cultivation of merit; it is due to this merit that such fruits exist for them.
The king’s majestic splendor is supreme and auspicious; his attainments are complete, no different from those of the gods.
Honored by the people as their sovereign, his excellent merit increases; for through the cultivation of merit, such fruits arise.
The Universal Monarchs and minor kings, who become lords of the earth according to their respective merits, possess a majestic splendor equal to that of the celestial lords;
such results arise from the cultivation of merit.
If one desires to exhaust all [desires] among humans without remainder, to achieve all things such as the seven precious jewels,
and to enjoy the inexhaustible wealth of a universal monarch (cakravartin), it is because of the cultivation of merit that such fruits exist.
King Vemacitrin and all the hosts of asura kings enjoy constant pleasures equal to those of Śakra;
this is the fruit resulting from their cultivation of merit.
The most excellent Vaiśravaṇa and the other World-Protecting Four Great Kings increase their various enjoyments and joy; this is the fruit resulting from the cultivation of merit.
The wondrous gardens of joy within the heavens are the supreme enjoyments therein;
constantly sporting with celestial maidens in those parks is the fruit that arises from the cultivation of merit.
All the various celestial kings, including Śakra, Lord of Devas, who possess supreme excellence, enjoy exquisite delights that ever increase;
these are the fruits resulting from the cultivation of merit.
In the heavens, everything is according to one's desire; wealth, joy, and enjoyments are all inexhaustible.
One dwells in wonderfully transformed palaces in sublime comfort; these fruits exist because of the cultivation of merit.

The ten supreme qualities within the heavens—such as lifespan, physical form, power, and so forth—increase in excellence from one heaven to the next; these exist as fruits because of the cultivation of merit.
The various superior things of the desire realm, such as the fullness of wealth and pleasure among the gods,
and the sovereign enjoyment therein— all these fruits exist because of the cultivation of merit.
Whatever sublime desires one may wish for, all enjoyments in the heavens are obtained exactly as intended;
these are acquired without the need for strenuous effort, for they are the fruits of having cultivated merit.

All the Brahmā assemblies and other devas, practitioners who cultivate meditative concentration and dwell in the stages of dhyāna, have attained the gateway to the joy and bliss born of seclusion; because they have cultivated merit, such is their fruit.
The practitioner of concentration attains the bliss born of meditative absorption; when craving is exhausted, that sublime bliss increases further.
Having attained the bliss of tranquility, equanimity and mindfulness are perfected; because of the cultivation of merit, such is its fruit.

All the śrāvaka assemblies of the Buddhas, each possessing the foremost and supreme merit, have fully perfected their vast and majestic spiritual power; these results exist because of the cultivation of merit.
Having diligently practiced for a hundred eons, one attains the fruit of pratyekabuddha enlightenment;
having perfected supreme, wondrous merit and majestic power, such results arise from the cultivation of merit.
Supreme, immeasurable, and beyond comparison, Universally adorned with all virtues,
The Honored One who has realized perfect and complete enlightenment— This exists as the fruit of having cultivated merit.
With beauty in the prime of youth and manifold excellences, adorned with the virtues of a noble lineage,
surrounded by a retinue of courtesans summoned by merit, one experiences pleasure at will without hindrance;
having cultivated supreme merit, one is born in heaven, endowed with the fruits of great fortune such as celestial maidens.
One obtains all that is pleasing, born of merit; all desires are fulfilled.
Through the cultivation of merit, these gains are never interrupted, adorned as they are by pure and supreme wisdom.
Through merit one can give rise to pure faith, Possessing swift eloquence and perfect memory;
Through merit one can proclaim lovely speech, And through merit one attains great renown.
All these, as well as all other Exalted, virtuous, and wondrous qualities, Are born solely from merit.
There are no wondrous joys in this world that can be accomplished without the cause of merit;
therefore, those who constantly seek such sublime happiness should cultivate and accumulate the multitude of merits.
Because I formerly cultivated even a small amount of merit, I was able to encounter Vipaśyin Tathāgata;
through fulfilling my aspirations and inclinations, I have attained ultimate, vast, and supreme accomplishment.
In the past, I was born among the gods of the six heavens of desire, serving as their sovereign lord.
Having passed through many thousands of koṭis of births, I experienced supreme bliss in each of those celestial realms;
there was never any suffering, nor any deficiency. It was likewise so when I was at the pinnacle of excellence among human beings.
Supremely honored as universal monarchs and the like, Possessing all manner of wealth and pleasures in full,
One knows that merit possesses great power; In every place of rebirth throughout those realms,
I have accomplished everything as required, Experiencing sovereign mastery over all blessings and joys.
Physical marks and extensive learning are both fully perfected; From his mouth issues the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus.
His wondrous voice brings joy and delight to all who hear it; The words he utters are cherished by all people.
Because of the power of my past vows, The merit I have now attained is likewise so.
Perfectly endowed with physical marks and meritorious virtues, all who see him give rise to a heart of joy;
his family lineage in this life is exceedingly vast, and his precious wealth, riches, and pleasures are beyond measure.
Clad in robes of Jāmbūnada gold of wondrous hue, they cover his body in adornment that is most lovely to behold.
The various states of my body are vast and all-pervading, Fragrant like the scent of sandalwood;
This sublime fragrance wafts everywhere, universally perfuming all, And those who catch its scent with the wind give rise to love and joy.
Whatever aspirations I may have— For clothing, precious jewels, and other articles of pleasure—
Whenever I give rise to any thought, I immediately accomplish everything.
Within the pure teaching of the Great Śākya Lion, I have now fully completed the dharma of renunciation;
having realized the sublime fruit of Arhatship, I dwell in the cool land of tranquility.
I shall now cross over this present life alone, and shall no longer undergo future existence;
nor shall I return again to this world, for I have already realized the bliss of untainted Nirvana.
Arising from the causes of past karma, the retribution experienced in the present is exceedingly vast;
though the matters I now encounter are such, the ultimate limit of this retribution cannot be seen.

When the Venerable Suvarṇavarṇa had spoken these verses, there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of vast multitudes who, having heard such unprecedented, immeasurable, and inconceivable matters of merit, were all struck with wonder and gave rise to a most supreme sense of marvel.

He then developed sincere respect for the pure teaching of the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher; according to his wishes and to the best of his own ability, he practiced giving, made great vows, and performed various meritorious deeds.

At that time, the Venerable Suvarṇavarṇa, for the sake of the countless multitudes of all classes within the city, opened the gates of merit and inspired in them profound faith and reverence. Having expounded upon various meritorious deeds as was appropriate, he immediately exercised his supernormal powers to return from the air to the Śītavana cemetery. There, he paid homage by touching the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and the other assembly of bhikṣus in succession, and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the lord of the land, heard that the minister Vīrabhadra had previously, within the garden, committed an act of malice against the maiden Kāśisundarī out of hatred and envy; he further learned that the youth Suvarṇavarṇa, who was originally without fault, had been framed for a crime and was to be executed and cast away. Upon hearing this, the king became violently incensed and, looking toward his attendants, commanded them, saying:
"You must know this: this most wicked man has committed such an evil deed; you should seize him and put him to death."

At that time, the minister Virūḍhaka was following the king and was also present in the assembly; having suddenly heard these royal commands, he was struck with the fear of death, his entire body trembled, and his mind and eyes became as bewildered as if consumed by fire. He immediately rose and rushed forward, fleeing in a state of frantic agitation.
At that time, the king’s ministers and hundreds of thousands of people were simultaneously seized by rage; they rushed forward in competition to pursue and seize him.
Once many had captured him, their hatred and anger intensified, and they struck him together until his body was overwhelmed by pain and he could no longer resist.
At that time, the minister Virūḍhaka, distressed and weeping, approached the Venerable Ānanda and said:

"I pray only that the Venerable One will give rise to a heart of rescue and protection to save me from this suffering. Now I am without a lord, without a savior, and without a refuge; despised by all, my life is about to expire."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the assembly, saying:
"Cease for now! You must not commit murder;
I shall inform the Great King, the ruler of the land."
When the multitude of people heard these words of the Venerable Ānanda, they immediately released him and no longer held onto him.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda looked toward King Ajātaśatru; the king, discerning his intention, addressed the Venerable one, saying:

"If this fierce and violent minister can go forth into the pure life within the Dharma of the Venerable One, and even serve as a lay follower for the rest of his life, I shall release him now according to the Venerable One’s instruction."
The Venerable One replied,
"Such was the matter.
When the multitude of people heard these words, they completely ceased all acts of striking and causing suffering.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Venerable Suvarṇavarṇa, saying:
"By the power of your true empowerment, cause all the physical pains of this fierce minister to be completely dispelled, so that he may regain his former ease."

Immediately, the Venerable Suvarṇavarṇa gave rise to a profound and firm resolve for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. He then invoked the power of his true empowerment and spoke these words:

"If this Dharma is true and my speech is true, then although this minister Virūpa has done me no small harm, I have not conceived even the slightest thought of malice toward him. By the truth of this Dharma and the truth of these words, may all the physical pains of this man be instantly relieved and he attain ease."

When these words were spoken, the pains of that fierce and violent minister were dissipated and he regained his former ease; he was immediately able to rise up and conceived deep faith and joy in the Tathāgata’s pure teaching. He approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, and spoke thus:
“I now wish to go forth purely in the Dharma of the Venerable One, receive full ordination to assume the appearance of a bhikṣu, and under the Venerable One, vow to practice the holy life.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda immediately instructed him in the dharma for going forth, until he had become a bhikṣu.
In a mere moment, he severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship.

Having realized this fruit, he immediately leaped up into the air and manifested various miraculous transformations, causing all those in the assembly to feel peace and tranquility in both body and mind.

At that time, the bhikṣu Pracaṇḍa descended from the air and approached the assembly of bhikṣus headed by the Venerable Ānanda; he prostrated at their feet in succession and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, when the entire assembly had witnessed the Venerable Ānanda performing such extensive and wondrous deeds of great supernatural power, they conceived the utmost pure faith and reverence toward him; all were filled with joy and gazed upon him with sincere devotion.
Venerable Ānanda, for the sake of the entire assembly, he preached the Dharma appropriately according to their respective dispositions.

At that time, among the hundreds of thousands of people in the gathering, having heard what was taught, there were differences in the fruits and benefits they attained and the realizations they achieved: some in the assembly realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to some who realized the fruit of *arhat*; some gave rise to the mind of *śrāvaka-bodhi*, up to some who took refuge in the Buddha, those who found joy in the Dharma, and those who revered the Saṅgha. Each received benefit according to their capacity and remained as they were. Furthermore, the merchant leader Sūryodgata and his wife, within this assembly, perceived the Truth and attained awakening.

Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of devas and humans who gave rise to pure and reverent faith; they rained down celestial precious robes and played exquisite celestial music, and also rained down various wondrous flowers of the heavens—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and māndārava flowers—in such vast quantities that they accumulated up to the knees.
Furthermore, various celestial flowers were scattered everywhere, filling the Śmaśāna (cemetery) to its limits, as they gave rise to a heart of reverence and extended their offerings.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Radiant Dharma,
the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing, and others, by imperial decree. At that time,

having witnessed such various and rare miraculous manifestations of the humans and devas in the great assembly, King Ajātaśatru, the sovereign of the land, gave rise to a mind of supreme, pure faith, reverence, and wonder, and spoke these words of praise:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!
Truly, this has never occurred before."
The Venerable Ānanda’s own power of merit is thus preeminent and most manifest; furthermore, he is able to bring forth the great majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata’s supreme and pure teaching.
“Great, indeed! Great, indeed!

The unsurpassed, pure teaching proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, with his most excellent knowledge and vision, having been entrusted to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, that Venerable One has truly fulfilled its purpose.”
"Alas! The holy sun of the Tathāgata has set.
Venerable Ānanda, by the light of your own merit, you shine forth brilliantly, illuminating all directions."
"Alas! The wondrous moon of the Tathāgata has vanished and no longer shines with constant brilliance, as if swallowed by that Rāhu, the King of the Asuras.
Venerable Ānanda, from your own moon of wisdom, you spread light that fills the sky, illuminating everywhere like a grove of kumuda flowers in full, lush bloom."
"Alas! The Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa; the world is scattered and in extreme sorrow and suffering, like a blazing light whose heat and affliction press upon us.
The Venerable One is pure, and his great cloud provides universal shade; the sublime words he utters are like a rain of nectar, sprinkling and moistening the world, causing all to rejoice."
"How magnificent!
The supreme aspiration of the Tathāgata;
Venerable One, you are upright and virtuous, and are able to fulfill it all."
"How magnificent!
The unsurpassed teaching of the Tathāgata;
Venerable Śrutadharin, you are able to reveal it everywhere."
"How great! The unsurpassed teaching of the Tathāgata;
the Venerable One has taken it upon himself and made it manifest in such a way."
"How marvelous!
Venerable One, among the śrāvakas you possess the most supreme renown; your deeds are truly accomplished, endowed with such qualities as have never before existed.

By means of your own sublime virtues and great majestic power, you bring benefit and fulfillment to boundless sentient beings, and extensively expound and elucidate that Dharma of the Great Merit of Omniscience."
"How marvelous!

Venerable sir, you have now been able to manifest the great majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher—power born of great compassion and appearing as the wisdom that brings benefit."

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having thus praised the Venerable Ānanda, gave rise to a heart of supreme faith and reverence. He immediately rose and stepped forward, prostrating his entire body upon the ground to pay homage at the Venerable’s feet. Thereafter, rising again, he knelt with both knees on the ground; the hairs on his body stood erect with joy as he joined his palms in solemn respect and spoke these verses:
"I take refuge in the most excellent among men; I take refuge in the Venerable One, ocean of great learning.
I take refuge in the rare and inconceivable one; I take refuge in the bearer of the Buddha’s teachings."
The great power of our Buddha’s pure teaching—how marvelous!
The Venerable One has correctly revealed it; the Venerable One is rare and inconceivable, skillfully bringing benefit to the world.
All the unsurpassed teachings of the Tathāgatas were entrusted to the Greatly Wise Honored One, Kāśyapa;
Kāśyapa in turn charged them to you, the one who acts according to what is right—this is precisely what you, O Venerable One, have now accomplished.
The Venerable One has brought me great benefit, extraordinary and beyond the reach of thought;
through the gateway of the Buddha’s omniscient merit, he has caused universal awakening and understanding to arise this day.
What are the rare and marvelous deeds of the Tathāgata?
The Venerable One’s benefit for others is likewise so; through the Buddha’s omniscience and great compassion, he is now able to fully explain and clarify them all.
The Venerable One currently dwells in the stage of a śrāvaka; what I have seen is truly rare.
Just as the Buddha has given rise to great compassion, he extensively brings benefit to all sentient beings.
The multitude of people in the kingdom of Magadha—how wonderful!
Today they have gained a sublime benefit; all those sentient beings who were heedless have obtained this advantage because of the Venerable One.
The Tathāgata has entrusted his pure teaching to you, O Venerable One;
within the state that is identical to that of the Tathāgata, today you likewise act as a Great Sugata, performing vast and marvelous deeds.
Because of that noble venerable Ānanda, who extensively manifested rare and great majestic power, I have formed this recollection of the Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One;
with sincere devotion, I take refuge and offer praise.
I take refuge in the World-Honored One, the Great Fearless One; I prostrate to the Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among bipeds.
May the Śrāvakas likewise manifest such majestic power, giving rise to deeds that benefit sentient beings.
All the great powers of the Tathāgatas, He has correctly and skillfully explained so that they are made manifest;
Though the World-Honored One has passed into extinction, he remains as if present; The Venerable One’s skillful transformation is never in vain.
At that time, after King Ajātaśatru had praised the Venerable One with these verses, he asked:
"Venerable One,
what causes did the merchant leader Sūryodgata and his wife cultivate in their past lives?"

The excellence of the retribution they have now manifested is such as this: they were immensely wealthy with abundant treasures while living at home, and within the Buddha-dharma, they attained the vision of the truths and realized enlightenment.
Furthermore, what causes did those two bhikṣus, Kāśisundarī and Caṇḍa, cultivate?

Having been born into a prominent family and possessing vast wealth and accumulated treasures in this world, he left the household life to practice the path within the Buddha-dharma; having severed all afflictions, he realized the fruit of arhatship.
"What were the causal conditions cultivated by that Bhikṣu Suvarṇavarṇa in the past?

How is it that in this life his retribution is so extraordinary: that he was born into a wealthy and eminent family; that he is handsome and beautiful, endowed with perfect physical marks; that a golden light constantly illuminates him, such that all people gaze upon him with eyes of admiration; that a golden, exquisite robe spontaneously covers his body; that his entire person is fragrant like sandalwood; and that from his mouth issues the wondrous fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, which those who smell it as the wind carries it forth develop hearts of love and joy?"

At the time of his birth, golden robes and kumuda flowers rained down spontaneously from the sky; endowed with such unprecedented signs of great majesty and virtue, he subsequently left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
"I only pray that the Venerable One will graciously provide an exposition.
At that time, the Venerable One addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:

"Great King, you should know that all of these have arisen from the cultivation of various roots of merit throughout successive past lives, reaching their culmination as the ripening of results in this present life."
They now experience their retribution.
"Great King!
Listen attentively now!"

In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The city was named Bandhumatī, and that Blessed One dwelt and stayed there.

At that time, there was a merchant leader in the city named Wonderful Ear (*Sudarśana*). He resided within that city as a man of immense wealth; his treasures were so vast and abundant that their quantity equaled the riches of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, and he was the most eminent among all families in the city of Pāṭaliputra, with no one to rival him.

Because that merchant leader was of great wealth and prosperity, he chose a woman from a distinguished family to take as his wife; subsequently, while sporting and enjoying himself with his wife, she became pregnant.

Later, before the son had yet been born, that merchant leader Citraśravaṇa, together with five hundred merchants as his companions, desired to cross the great ocean to increase his profits; meanwhile, the fetus his wife carried continued to grow.

Thereupon, the merchant leader and his caravan departed from their own home to travel to a foreign land; they engaged in business according to their means and gradually accumulated some wealth. However, within that [foreign land], their wealth was either consumed by a great fire, seized by bandits, or stolen and taken away by family members and traveling companions.

Subsequently, his wife gave birth to a boy when her pregnancy had reached its full term; the child’s skin was coarse and black, his appearance was hideous, and he possessed eighteen kinds of loathsome characteristics. His body and mouth were filthy and filled with a foul odor, such that family members and relatives who caught the scent on the wind would turn their faces away and depart.
Furthermore, when the boy was first born, a fire broke out within the house, incinerating all their wealth, treasures, and means of livelihood until nothing remained.

At that time, the merchant’s wife, in a state of panic, took her newborn son in her arms and fled from the house. All the wealth, provisions, and articles of enjoyment within the house were consumed by the blazing fire until nothing was left; only then did the fire spontaneously extinguish itself.

Then the merchant’s wife entered the dilapidated and ruined house, tore off half of her own garment, spread it upon the ground, and laid the boy down there. She then sighed deeply in self-lamentation, rose up, and with tears streaming down, thought of the merchant Sutejas, saying:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Alas! Why has my home now been thus destroyed and scattered?
At that time, all the slaves, servants, kinsmen, and laborers within the merchant leader's house, seeing the fire consume everything and reduce it to ruin, were all struck with terror.
"Is it not the case that we too shall all be destroyed because of these evil conditions?
Having thus deliberated together, they abandoned the merchant leader’s residence and dispersed.
Only a single female servant, who had long cherished filial piety and righteousness, reflected to herself:
"Now, within the home of this merchant leader Sumukha, all wealth and possessions have been consumed by fire and his kin are scattered; he is desolate and without refuge—what indeed remains?

The merchant leader’s wife is alone, without companion or protector. I ought not now to follow the example of others and abandon her to depart; for the time being, I shall simply dwell here in mutual dependence with the merchant leader’s wife."
Again he reflected:
"Since the merchant leader’s wife has had her household wealth and provisions consumed by fire, she cannot even prepare a single day's meal; what is to be done?"
"What shall we do? Having had this thought, the woman's messenger immediately went to the homes of all the kinsmen and relatives of the merchant leader Subhakarṇa.
Having arrived, he said:

"O kinsmen, you should know that the merchant leader’s wife now dwells here in a state of poverty, distress, and urgent peril; you ought to devise skillful means to provide for her upbringing and protection."
Then his kinsmen raised him exactly as he had said; however, before long, instances of harmful and profitless events occurred repeatedly within the household of his relatives.
The relatives deliberated and said:

"Now this son of the merchant lord Subhakarṇa is extremely inauspicious and lacks merit; because of his birth, everything within the merchant lord’s house has been destroyed. If we, his relatives, were now to raise him, our own houses would likewise be destroyed before long, just like this one."
"Why is this? Even those who merely hear the name of this merchant's son give rise to fear; how much more so those who dwell with him?
Then his relatives spoke to her messenger, saying:
"From this day forward, you must no longer enter our house.
At that time, having been insulted and mistreated by those relatives, the female servant reflected to herself:
"Now that this wife of the merchant leader has no refuge whatsoever anywhere, by what means can she possibly survive?"
"Perhaps at this time I should go to another's house to seek labor, and whatever wages I receive, I shall use them to sustain the merchant leader’s wife.
Having had this thought, she immediately went to another's house to perform various tasks, receiving wages according to her labor.
Having obtained it, she took it back to her camp to trade for food, with which she fed herself, her son, and the caravan leader’s wife.
Subsequently, because the child born to her possessed such hideous features, she gave him the name "The Child of Hideous Appearance."

"At that time, the female servant went daily to another's house from behind the scenes, exhausting her meager strength to prepare the midday meal for him. As her labor increased, her wages likewise became generous; through her single-minded diligence, the three lives were preserved. Although matters proceeded thus, it was nonetheless extremely arduous."
Then, the wife of the merchant leader Citraśravaṇa suddenly felt a thought arise:

"In my household, there were formerly many servants, laborers, kinsmen, and relatives, yet they have all departed; now only this female slave remains to support me, and it is by her that my remaining life is sustained. Within my maternal clan, she has been held in affection for a long time; however, as she works alone with great effort for so many days, could she not be weary?"
"Could it be that he has grown weary and abandoned his work?

Furthermore, working with only one person, the wages are so meager that what is earned is insufficient for sustenance. I should now acknowledge my own past karma; since my transgressions have led to this, I shall accept the suffering with equanimity. I shall join her as a servant and labor alongside her."
Having had this thought, he immediately summoned his female servant and went together to another house to calculate the labor and take payment, intending to bring it home for their sustenance.

However, the elder’s wife possessed such delicate and exquisite limbs that she could not endure even the slightest hardship; scorched by the fire of hunger and oppressed by manifold sufferings, she became utterly exhausted and bewildered in an instant. She lay down to rest, weeping and sighing deeply, when she suddenly recalled the merchant lord Sudarśana and spoke with bitter grief:
"Alas! How painful!"
"Why do I now undergo such ruin and hardship?
Is it not because others previously saw me alone as the most eminent in the city, possessing abundant wealth and every requisite?"

Why is it that today my merit and power have been so utterly exhausted, such that within this royal city I am most severely ruined? Day after day I must go to the houses of others to labor for hire to sustain myself, enduring many kinds of suffering and oppression.
At that time, because she was oppressed by such bitter anguish, the merchant’s wife gazed at her handmaid and remained there weeping.
Then, the handmaid’s own grief and suffering increased all the more, and she too shed tears and spoke these words:
"Alas! How painful!"

Alas! The wife of the merchant leader, who formerly lived in wealth and power, wore exquisite garments and various ornaments; her body was adorned with wonderful perfumes and flower garlands, and her mouth constantly held and chewed exquisite incense.

At that time, they swallow their saliva [in contentment], like celestial maidens who constantly sport in the Joyful Garden (Nandana-vana); food, drink, clothing, and all manner of exquisite jewels and ornaments are fully abundant;
and their servants, retinues, kinsmen, and friends—both internal and external—are flourishing, such that whatever is given to them is received in full sufficiency.
Why has she now fallen into such ruin? Her appearance is truly pitiable:

her hair is disheveled and matted, her body is defiled with dust and grime; assailed by manifold sufferings, her entire frame is withered and emaciated. Her tattered garment is worn and filthy, swarming with fleas and lice and suffused with a foul odor. Within this royal city, she is the most lowly and wretched, seeking sustenance by laboring for others as a hired hand—this state of decay is indeed a matter of profound sorrow.
Alas! One's share of merit swiftly turns to ruin. Alas!
That which is accomplished through wealth and nobility does not endure for long. Alas!
How diverse are the various distinctions of karmic retribution!
Then, after the lady’s messenger had thus lamented, she spoke further in verse:
“In the past, your body was clothed in exquisite garments, Adorned with ornaments of many jewels;
Formerly, you possessed the superior beauty of a celestial maiden, Yet now, dwelling in a humble alley, your suffering has increased.”
Why is it that at this time things have come to such an extreme, with all portions of merit utterly destroyed?
Your limbs are emaciated and covered in filth, your body shrouded in a single tattered and worn garment.
In former times, she possessed the countenance of a celestial maiden, and people would open their beautiful eyes to gaze upon her together;
yet now she is no different from an ugly demon, and all who see her give rise to loathing and rejection.
In the past, you possessed abundant wealth and treasures, being the most eminent within the city;
you practiced the impartial distribution of alms to all beggars, yet now you are utterly exhausted, impoverished, and lowly.
In the past, enjoyments increased one's joy, and one’s family was wealthy and abundant;
now that the retribution is manifest, vast suffering and grief constantly pursue one.
Alas! Saṃsāra is worthy of reproach; alas!
Wealth and status are certain to be impermanent. Worldly pleasures pass away before us, and one will surely experience suffering thereafter.

"At that time, the wife of the merchant leader Sumukha, together with her female servant, went daily to other houses to work for wages. Because the power of merit of that boy of ugly appearance had been exhausted and his karma had increased, the wages she received gradually diminished day by day."
Thus it continued until later, from the first rising of the sun until the end of the evening, he labored with redoubled effort yet received no wages.
Furthermore, at the very last, all work everywhere had ceased, and there was no longer any employment available.
Then the merchant’s wife immediately consulted with her female servant, saying:
"At this time, we have no place to hire out our labor; we should go about begging for alms."
Having said this, she immediately took a clay bowl and went out herself to beg for all the food they had.
When the boy Viśākha grew up and was able to walk, his mother told him:
"From this time forward, you should support yourself by begging for food."
Having spoken thus, he also gave him a clay bowl.

The son immediately took the bowl and went about the streets and alleys to beg for food to support himself; because that youth’s body was coarse and dark, his appearance hideous, and he possessed eighteen kinds of loathsome features, people who saw him would cover their faces and depart.
Whenever he went to the door of another's house, because he was so emaciated and filled with a foul odor, those who smelled it on the wind would cover their noses and pass by.
Or they would strike him with sticks, wood, tiles, or stones to drive him away, saying:
"Leave my house at once!"

He was like a wriggling insect, wandering through cities and towns filled everywhere with sand, gravel, and filth; wherever he went, he was beaten and driven away by sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones. He ran about seeking even a single meal but was unable to obtain any, and the earthen vessel he carried was likewise struck and shattered to pieces.
"At that time, the youth, despised and loathed by others, wept in distress and hurried to his mother's side.
When his mother saw him, she leaned over her knee in sorrow and spoke these words: 'Alas!'"
"My son’s peril is extreme; what kind of person is this, devoid of compassion and unafraid of the consequences of their sin, that has struck you to inflict such suffering?"
At that time, the youth, with a sobbing voice and weeping, spoke these verses:
“Going from place to place to the houses of others, I originally lived by begging for alms;
Yet now, instead of receiving sustenance, All who see me come to strike me with sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones.”
Upon hearing this, his mother hurried forward, took the child of hideous appearance into her arms, and weeping with great compassion, spoke these verses:
“Is it not that during your previous lives, You once committed unwholesome deeds?”
Now that you are struck by others, is this not the fault of your own actions in this present life?
Your body is hideous and emaciated; all pleasant things have utterly dispersed.
You are impoverished, distressed, and in extreme peril, with no one to give rise to compassion or pity for you.
Alas! Now that my family is scattered and ruined, my body is wounded and my utensils are broken; since the requisites for begging have failed to be provided, how can I sustain my life through alms?
Parents separated, where can a child find refuge?
The home destroyed, auspicious signs have faded; not a single alms-bowl remains. At this time, who would give to you again?
Relatives, loved ones, and friends, as well as lords and elders, have all departed;
since your alms-bowl no longer remains, who now will give to you?
Who has seen you afflicted by poverty and disease?
Yet within this state, you have been able to give rise to a courageous mind!
Alas! You have been brought to such ruin by the sinful karma of your previous lives.
Alas! You are a gentle and virtuous person; why is there no one to show you compassion?
The hearts of men are as hard as iron and stone, inflicting harm like sharp blades and axes.
Amidst manifold destruction and further poverty and suffering, how could one endure giving rise to a harmful mind?
Seeing this beggar assailed by the pain of hunger, no one dares to give rise to a courageous spirit of compassion;
emaciated by hunger and thirst, his heart utterly exhausted, he is scattered and ruined, possessing not a single thing.
Entangled by the suffering of illness, assailed by the fever of affliction—truly, this is the destruction of destructions.
With faces clouded by poverty, hardship, and sorrow, oppressed by the cries of hunger and thirst;
with parched shoulders and necks, with but a faint trace of strength remaining—who among those who see them would not be moved by compassion?
How could it be right to strike you here, given that in past lives you harbored a mind of pride and arrogance?
Now, entangled by the many sufferings of illness, you are overwhelmed by extreme pain with no one to show compassion;
oppressed by the misery of poverty, hunger, and thirst, what is achieved by wandering about as a beggar?
At times, one may see before oneself but a tiny morsel, the discarded remnants left by crows and dogs. Alas!
My body is utterly devoid of merit; lacking any means or plan, what am I to do?
"Past karma is the cause of this destruction; held by the lord of karma, it is now thus.

When the merchant’s wife had spoken these verses, she remained for a short while to rest before the dilapidated house where she lived, her mind continuously tormented by many forms of distress and sorrow.

Because that ugly-faced boy had previously been beaten until blood flowed and stained his body, she took him into her embrace; with tiles, rubble, and various impurities filling her lap, she stroked the boy’s body with her hand and rose slowly to go into the streets and alleys.

He saw the sons of noble and eminent lineages, or the sons of merchant lords, as well as other wealthy elders and brahmins, wearing exquisite Kāśika garments that were pure white and clean, adorned with various ornaments such as highly valuable and beautiful pearl necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and armlets, and decorated with radiant, exquisite flower garlands and various finery.
Having seen this, he looked back upon his own body, situated in a state of extreme hardship, distress, and peril.
Furthermore, observing the ugly child with a countenance of poverty, exhaustion, and sorrow, he immediately let out a long sigh, his eyes brimming with tears, and spoke these verses:
"In the past, I was wealthy and fully satisfied, Adorned with many jewels like a mountain of treasure; Now I am destitute and utterly wretched, My body covered in dust and filth."
When her family was vast and fully prosperous, she enjoyed the most supreme and wondrous pleasures;
now, mother and child are utterly ruined, having returned to a place of filth and impurity.
She skillfully utters various words of begging, yet in the end, there is no one at all who gives her food.
The great ocean of sorrow and suffering has deep waves; it is oppressive, terrifying, and devoid of benefit.
Its loud roar resounds as peril and pain increase; now one is submerged in its deep current of poverty.
Within its treacherous and evil currents dwell aquatic creatures; the breaking waves are swift and again bring danger.
The most grievous great illness brings profound harm; one sinks together with the deep current of poverty.
The suffering of sickness and the sorrow of grief are like arrows piercing the heart;
the lion’s roar resounds through the wilderness, and while flocks of birds dwell together in anxiety for their eggs, the sorrow and suffering of poverty are likewise so.
In the past, you did not practice giving toward virtuous people, nor did you give rise to a mind of pure faith and charity;
now, lacking merit, mother and child alike view all pleasant things as if they were enemies.
In the past, you never gave to beggars, but instead rejected those of meager merit and lowly station;
now that mother and child are separated, you must share in this hardship, peril, and suffering together.
In the past, the noble ones and sages of this land were neither honored nor treated with contempt;
yet now, when mother and son are torn asunder, they too are subjected to the insults of others.
In the past, I once harassed various sages and worthies, Or else struck down others;
now, in this life, when I am struck by others, I must endure the suffering of staffs, wood, tiles, and stones.
In the past, you did not respect others, or you spoke words of reproach and disparagement;
now that you and your children are torn asunder, wherever you turn, you are met with further revilement and blame.
In previous lives, one never showed respect to others, Or perhaps gave rise to contempt for them;
Thus, in this life, there are many extreme evils and hardships, As the contempt shown to others follows one back in turn.
In previous lives, both mother and son were stingy; seeing beggars, we would not give anything away.
Now that I am impoverished and lack even clothing, others likewise do not bestow any gifts upon me.
In the past, you frequently created obstacles and hindrances for others;
now, your own kin and retinue are all separated from you, increasing your suffering in vain as you weep long and bitterly.
In the past, you delayed and missed the proper time, and you did not offer others beds, couches, and the like;
now, you must sleep upon a ground of thorns, for the retribution is manifest and you shall surely experience it yourself.
In former times, you never bestowed upon virtuous people couches adorned with every kind of marvel;
now, as you sit and rise, the earth itself serves as your bed, thickly strewn with a profusion of thorns.
In the past, you never gave shoes, nor vehicles or various means of comfort;
thus, in this life, you tread upon the earth where every place is filled with many thorns and the like.
Regarding dwellings, lodgings for the night, and utensils, he was never generous in the past due to a stingy mind;
relying on his wealth and nobility to exalt himself, he has now fallen into a heap of filth.
In the past, I saw a person emaciated and withered, who, in a time of scorching thirst, required water to drink;
though I saw him, I was unwilling to give him clear spring water, and thus in this life my face is extremely parched and withered.
In the past, when poor people and kinsmen came to me seeking food out of the suffering of hunger, I failed to give rise to a mind of respectful and pure generosity;
thus, in this life, I am destitute of food and left in utter desolation.
In the past, when I saw others experiencing gain, happiness, or well-being, I forcibly gave rise to many kinds of envy and anger;
now, as a result, I have been reborn among those of lowly status, and others come to me with resentment and wrath.
Relying on noble clans for their rebirth as mother and child, they constantly gave rise to arrogance toward others;
or else they harassed those of virtue, and now they must sweetly endure the most grievous suffering they have invited.
In the beginningless ocean of saṃsāra’s birth and death, amidst all the great terrors of sickness and suffering, you never administered medicine to eliminate them;
now, you have summoned a great illness that constantly oppresses you.
If one fails to provide food, drink, and bathing for parents, elders, practitioners, and even the lowliest of the poor,
one will have no merit in this life and shall encounter the suffering of poverty.
I am now utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst, Lacking food, drink, and clothing entirely;
With my heart oppressed by various illnesses and sufferings, Who now shall provide protection?
We, mother and child, now wish to become slaves; who would grant us permission to serve?
That our two lives might be preserved at this time is something exceedingly difficult to obtain in this world.
Alas! In previous lives I did not cultivate merit; alas!
My poverty and destitution are now such as this. Though this kingdom and city are so abundant and prosperous, there is no one to act as my refuge.

When the merchant leader Subhakarṇa’s wife had spoken these verses, she endured hunger and thirst; with body and mind afflicted by grief, mother and son remained together, dwelling according to their karma.

"In the past, that merchant leader Sudarśana ventured upon the great ocean to trade for wealth; when his ship was wrecked and he was drowning in the water, he clung to a single plank and, relying on a young servant boy, endured many hardships and perils until he was finally able to reach safety."
While traveling along the road begging for alms, he returned toward the city of Pāṭaliputra; upon reaching a certain village, he stayed there for the night.
There was a farmer guarding that village who, seeing this caravan leader—a man with whom he had previously been acquainted—thought to himself:
"For what reason does this caravan leader now appear so emaciated and haggard?"
"Since it is certain that all the gold, jewels, and wealth he acquired have been utterly dissipated, and he now comes here supported only by his servant,
shall I inform him of the circumstances regarding the destruction of the merchant leader’s household?"
"Or perhaps the merchant leader will come to know this for himself later?
Having thought this, he immediately took water and offered it to him to wash his hands, and further presented two mung bean cakes to him to eat.
At that time, the merchant leader Subhakarṇa thought to himself, "I ought not return home empty-handed.
He then took one cake and tucked it away in his bosom; next, he broke another cake and shared it with the boy to eat.
Having finished eating, they gradually proceeded forward the following morning.
The merchant leader, his appearance withered and haggard, his physical strength exhausted and weary, and wearing tattered, soiled garments, eventually reached a city.
At that time, the youth Virūpa was already staying in a dilapidated house; when morning came, he suddenly thought to himself:
"I am now so emaciated by hunger and thirst that although my life still remains, what use is it?"
"I should now go and seek my own death.
Having thought this, he immediately went to his mother's place and, approaching her, said:
"I wish to go now to my grandfather's garden."
The mother said, "As you wish. At that time,

after the merchant leader Subhakarṇa had entered the city and gradually reached his own home, he saw that his residence was collapsed and ruined, his kinsmen were scattered, and it was desolate and without support— a mere mound of earth.
Having seen this, he thought to himself,
"How can my home have come to such a state?
The merchant leader then entered the ruined house and saw his wife inside, dwelling there in silence with a single female servant.
His wife’s appearance was dark, haggard, and emaciated; she covered her body in tattered, filthy garments.
Having seen her, he cried out:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! How could this have come to pass?
Having spoken these words, the merchant leader fainted and fell to the ground; after a long time, a cool breeze touched his body and he regained consciousness.
The wife then hurried forward and wailed aloud, slowly recounting the previous events of her family.

Immediately, the merchant leader sighed deeply and said, "In the past, I did not plant fields of merit, nor did I cultivate the power of various meritorious deeds; now I have invited all manner of ruin. What should I do at this time?"
Where else can one go?
Who might there be to look upon me with compassion?
Who will take pity on this one who is so poor and suffering?
I am now submerged in the great ocean of poverty; who will come to rescue me?
I am now mired in the mud of ruin and dispersal; who will cleanse me?
I am now fleeing into the vast river of sorrow; who will ferry me across?
I have now encountered the profound enmity of poverty and suffering; who can act as my powerful adversary?
I have now deeply planted the roots of all manner of sufferings; who can sever and eliminate them?
I have now firmly established the roots of the tree of poverty; who can dig it up?
I am now being scorched by the blazing flames of the great fire of craving; who shall extinguish it?
I am now being gored by the intoxicated elephant of impurity; who shall subdue it?
I am now being stung by the venomous breath of those poisonous snakes of suffering; who will dispel it for me?
I am now being attacked in battle by the great army of all-encompassing, shattering poverty; who will crush and subdue it for me?
I am now bound by the shackles of poverty, which are as solid as the very nature of all suffering; who will deliver me from this?
I am now deep within the den of poverty; who will draw me out?
I have long remained in this poor man’s dwelling, its doors firmly bolted; who will open and lift them for me?
I am now being relentlessly assailed by that wretched person of poverty; who will drive him away?
I am now submerged within a perilous and evil current; who will rescue and receive me?
I am now pursued by the terrors of poverty and hardship; who will protect and save me?
After the merchant leader Wondrous Ear had uttered these various words of poignant lamentation, he again raised his voice and proclaimed:

"Within the three realms, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is most venerable and supreme; there is not the slightest phenomenon that He does not know or does not see, for He understands all things. Such is the natural law of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
He is endowed with all the primary and secondary marks, his radiance pure and brilliant, like the sun shining everywhere, or like a mani-jewel of pristine purity.

Polished and flawless, he possesses all supreme virtues; he is like a blooming lotus, like the newly risen sun, or like the pure and supple bow of Śakra. The light of his topknot-ornament and the mark of the halo blazes fiercely, like a fierce fire into which clarified butter is poured, causing its flames to increase even more intensely.

Furthermore, the clouds of light are endowed with all colors, like the multitude of colors gathered upon the body of a peacock; the Buddha’s light shines universally, destroying all darkness, for birth, old age, sickness, and death constitute the cage of the three realms of existence.

The power of the Buddha’s wisdom is fully capable of opening and resolving all things; the Buddha has already accumulated countless hundreds of thousands of meritorious virtues and powers, thereby perfecting his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*).
The Buddha’s radiance is pure white, like that of a white elephant, white flowers, or white garments; it is as clear and lovely as snow or a lotus root.
The Buddha’s radiance shone brilliantly like Jāmbūnada gold; when it first emerged, its fiery light was clearly manifest, resembling a mountain peak—vast, blazing, and incomparably sublime.

“Among the various marks of the Buddha, the hairs on his body are lustrous and each curls to the right; the halo radiates with sovereign brilliance; the white tuft between his eyebrows manifests a most wondrous sign; and the circle of his face is pure like a lotus first opening.”

Furthermore, in the past, throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddha extensively gave away his head, eyes, hands, feet, and other superior parts of his body, as well as his flesh and blood, wife and children, servants, elephants, horses, carriages, exquisite garments, bedding and seating, gold, silver, and precious jewels—indeed, he renounced everything he possessed, even including his royal throne and kingdom, thereby increasing his vast and supreme practices for unsurpassed *bodhi*. Through this power of non-obstruction, he utterly defeated the armies of Māra.

Pure and immaculate like the orb of the autumn moon, with a garland of a thousand rays of light shining all around, it appeared loftily prominent like the king of mountains. The pure moonlight shone as clouds dispersed in the sky; its pristine white form was like ivory, and it was also like the ocean of milk or white flowers in bloom. The Buddha’s body was radiant, pure, and magnificent, adorned with the marks and signs like a mountain of gold, resembling a peacock peak or a mountain of lapis lazuli, with its halo shining upward.
“The Buddha, with the fire of realized wisdom, has incinerated all evils until they are like ashes. Various celestial kings constantly come to pay him homage;

these celestial kings each wear jeweled crowns of *maṇi* gems and are adorned with exquisite pure gold. They prostrate before the World-Honored One’s pure lotus feet, which possess all the most excellent marks: the ten toenails are the color of red copper, thin, lustrous, and lovely; the tips of the toenails resemble the crescent moon. These lotus feet are pure and stainless, endowed with every adornment, as they tread upon the branches of the tree of sentient beings' craving.”

Furthermore, with the light of wisdom, he shatters all the darkness of ignorance and delusion; he regards the entire world as his sole kinsman and friend, loving sentient beings with impartial compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*). Abiding in the inconceivable realm of great wisdom, he subdues all poisons such as those of dragons and serpents. Having extensively accumulated hundreds of thousands of supreme meritorious deeds and difficult practices for immeasurable eons, he uses the sword of wisdom to sever the roots of all the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings that have existed since beginningless time.

“‘The Brahma King, Śakra, the World-Protectors of the ten directions, and all the great assemblies together praise the supreme merits of the Buddha and his True Dharma. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, give rise to great compassion, universally gathering the world with a single protective mindfulness that is without duality; they preach the Dharma with impartiality through non-dual speech, abiding in śamatha and vipaśyanā. They skillfully expound the three methods of discipline, have already crossed the four torrents, and possess the four bases of spiritual power; through the four means of attraction, they practice in accordance with reality throughout the long night.’”

They bring sentient beings to maturity, sever the five lower fetters, transcend the five destinies, and are endowed with six qualities. They fulfill the six *pāramitās*, open the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, demonstrate the eightfold noble path, and skillfully cultivate the nine successive meditative attainments. Possessing the ten powers in their entirety, their fame is heard everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and they have attained a thousand kinds of supreme mastery.

“During the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night, he constantly surveys the world with the pure radiance of the Buddha-eye: ‘Which phenomena are increasing? Which are decreasing?’”
What phenomena are subject to diminution?
What phenomena are characterized by hardship?
What phenomena are perilous?
What phenomena are oppressive?
What phenomena possess hardship, danger, and oppression?
What phenomena are minor?
Which phenomena gradually increase?
Which phenomena become vast?
Who is submerged in the great ocean of birth and death?
I shall deliver them.
What are those karmas and afflictions by which they are devoured by the great rākṣasas?
I shall rescue them.
What is that time when they are wounded and stung by the venom of the serpent of poverty?
I shall act as their healer.
What is that time when the fire of anger burns their hearts with extreme intensity?
At that time, I drenched their hearts and crowns with the rain of the nectar of Dharma.
What was it that had been shrouded by the darkness of delusion, so deeply obscured and oppressed?
I illuminated them with pure radiance and established them upon the supreme, highest peak of samādhi.
Who are those long afflicted by the suffering of extremely grave illnesses?
I shall skillfully treat them with the medicine of the Eightfold Noble Path, causing them all to attain the ultimate end of suffering.
Who are those long dwelling in the chamber of poverty, its doors firmly barred?
I shall open and raise it for you.
What is that darkness of ignorance which obscures and veils the pure eye?
I shall skillfully illuminate it with the medicine of wisdom.
"What are those most cruel shackles that bind his body?
I shall deliver him from them.
At that time, the merchant leader spoke again in verse:

"The great ocean is the abode of fish and dragons; though the tides of the sea may occasionally miss their appointed time, the Tathāgata’s transformation of sentient beings according to their needs is timely, certain, and never fails."

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin universally surveyed this world and saw that the merchant leader Subhadra was impoverished and suffering, mired in the mud of hardship, peril, sorrow, and fear.
Having observed this, he immediately gave rise to a heart of great compassion, donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Bandhumatī to beg for food in sequence.

At that time, the elders, householders, brahmins, merchant leaders, common people, and countless hundreds of thousands of beings within the city, seeing Vipaśyin—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—entering the city to beg for food, all brought forth exquisite and pure food and drink, desiring to offer it to him; thus, the bowl of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, was filled to the brim.
At that time, out of compassion for the merchant leader Sukarṇa, the World-Honored One went to the center of a four-way intersection and stood there.

The Buddha’s body was radiant, fully endowed with all the marks of excellence; it was as pure and lovely as the newly risen sun, as magnificent as clouds abiding in the sky, as beautiful as the autumn moon, like a kalpavṛkṣa tree, and like a tree of exquisite coral jewels—splendid and delightful to behold.
Furthermore, it is like a golden pillar or a golden tree, lofty, prominent, and blazing with brilliance; like a mass of various jewels, it is a high-accumulated mountain of treasure.

Its sovereign orderliness is like that of a king of geese sporting in a golden lotus pond; its upright gait is like that of Airāvaṇa, the elephant king of the gods, amidst a lotus pool; and like a lion king endowed with great majesty, it is wonderfully adorned and pervades the ten directions as a great gathering of auspiciousness.

The soles of the Tathāgata’s feet bear the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, which is pure, sublime, soft, and exquisite. Upon the soles of his two feet, there are auspicious whorls and virtuous lines, and he possesses the *miṇa* mark, which is wonderfully adorned. His ten toenails are the color of red copper; their radiance is lovely like the newly risen moon, narrow and long, with a single, pure luster. His toes are as soft as *tūla* cotton, and his insteps are full, well-formed, and beautifully positioned—pure, brilliant, and incomparably sublime.
The radiance of the Buddha’s body shone universally throughout the ten directions, and that light also illuminated the dilapidated house of the merchant leader Sudarśana.

At that time, the light emitted by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin was blazing and pure, like the first flames emerging from refined gold, and like various kinds of pure, wondrous flowers, in full bloom, flourishing, vast, and magnificently adorned.
At that time, within the ruined house of the merchant leader, a brilliant light shone forth, illuminating both the interior and exterior with penetrating radiance.

Having beheld this light, the merchant leader was struck with profound wonder and alarm; he rose up suddenly and saw Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his golden light dazzling and adorned with all manner of colors.
Having seen this, he immediately conceived a most extraordinary and pure faith, and thought to himself:
"I am now impoverished and have not a single thing to offer to the World-Honored One."
Turning back to look at himself, he saw the single mung-bean cake he had previously left behind.

Taking it, he said to his wife, "I previously brought home this single mung-bean cake; I now wish to offer it to Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. May the Buddha, out of compassion, accept this offering from one so poor and lowly, which shall become a supreme gift. Although the object is meager, my mind is utterly pure. By planting this small seed of pure generosity today, I pray that the Buddha will accept this gift of mine, so that I may be delivered from poverty and suffering."
The wife replied to her husband, saying:
"Excellent! O Benevolent One!"
"This is most excellent; by means of these roots of goodness, it shall become the cause for liberation from birth and death.
