At that time, the merchant leader Subhakarṇa had this thought:

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Fan Translation, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by imperial decree. "Then, the merchant leader Subhakarṇa immediately had this thought:"
"In this city, I was once wealthy and prosperous, but now I am impoverished. With such meager goods, how can I practice giving?

Although things are thus, there are many ministers, officials, commoners, brahmins, elders, householders, and guild-leaders in this city, as well as a great multitude of people, all of whom would see me offering these few items to the World-Honored One. I should now seek out a leaf to wrap them in, so that others do not see."
Having had this thought, he immediately entered his own dilapidated house and searched everywhere for the leaves, but in the end, he could not find any.
At that time, the merchant leader reproached himself within:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"I am now utterly devoid of merit," he lamented with deep sorrow and sighs.

Immediately, he emerged from his house and gave rise to vast, pure faith; he took a single cake and offered it into the pure alms bowl of the World-Honored One, Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having made the offering, he reverently prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and made this aspiration:
“World-Honored One!

By virtue of these roots of goodness from my slight gift of the Dharma through pure faith, may I, after passing this life, never again suffer such poverty for even a single day in the future; instead, may I attain great wealth and prosperity, with all my enjoyments fulfilled according to my heart’s desire.”

As the merchant lord Sukarṇa made this vow and paid homage to the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, through the Buddha’s supernormal power, his superior retribution was manifested: immediately, his emaciated and feeble appearance vanished, and he regained his former full, exquisite, and radiant physical form. Sustained by the excellence of the merchant lord Sukarṇa’s vow, he dwelt in contentment.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin departed from the city of Pūrṇamadra and returned once more to the wilderness where the Buddha used to dwell.
At that time, among the elders in the city who were former acquaintances of the merchant leader Sunetra, there was one man who addressed the assembly, saying:

"All of you should now see that this merchant leader Sunetra has fallen into such ruin, poverty, and hardship; you must not abandon him. He is capable of rescuing many individuals, whereas one person alone cannot provide for many."
"Virtuous ones, you should all equally share what you have given; let whatever has been offered be placed together in one spot.

Having spoken these words, the elders immediately each contributed countless pearls, exquisite jewels, earrings, bracelets, and various other kinds of wonderful garments—hundreds of thousands of varieties—to assist in the offering. In an instant, gold, silver, precious gems, and all manner of ornaments were piled up to a great height.
At that time, having witnessed the extraordinary nature of the offerings made by the assembly, the merchant leader Sutejas said to his wife:
"Behold how these seeds of pure giving can produce the sprouts of virtue."

His wife was immediately filled with great joy; she reverently prostrated herself toward Vipaśyin Buddha from afar and at once brought the offered robes, ornaments, and other articles into her own home.

At that time, the youth Virūpa went first to his grandfather’s garden; oppressed by the suffering of hunger and thirst, his ugliness became even more extreme. With a heart filled with intense sorrow and loathing, he reflected to himself:
"How is it that my present life is the result of such sinful karma? Devoid of merit and so hideous, I am beset by such torment; what benefit is there in remaining alive?"
"I should now seek my own death.

Having thought this, he went at once to a very high branch of a *pāṭali* tree, climbed up by grasping it, but the branch broke and he fell down with his body; his limbs were mangled, and he suffered extreme agony.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know all things, see all things, and understand all things without exception.

At that time, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, with his pure Buddha-eye which surpasses the fleshly eye, saw this boy of ugly appearance undergoing such suffering. Immediately, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion and, employing his supernormal powers, went to that garden. There, he illuminated and touched the boy’s body with the light of loving-kindness accumulated over a hundred kalpas.

When the youth was touched by the light’s radiance, all the pains in his limbs were completely dispelled; hunger and thirst were stilled, and he quickly attained physical ease. Immediately, throughout his entire body, he beheld Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—adorned with the thirty-two marks, supremely pure and difficult to obtain, accumulated over hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, and brilliantly illuminating all directions with their subtle and wondrous majesty.

"At that time, the youth, beholding the Buddha’s pure marks and signs and their extraordinary excellence, gave rise to pure faith and joy. He removed a piece of yellow cloth from his own body, measuring about one cubit, and offered it to Vipaśyin Tathāgata. Generating a most supreme and pure mind, he placed it upon the Buddha and also offered a single *karaṇḍaka* flower."

Through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, the dimensions of the robes became commensurate with the Buddha’s body, and the flowers remained like a parasol, as large as a chariot wheel, hovering above the Buddha.

When the youth Viśākha saw these signs, his mind was further inspired with an even more exalted and vast pure faith. He immediately paid homage at the Buddha’s feet with deep reverence and made a great vow, speaking in verse:
“The youth Viśākha gives according to his ability To the Tathāgata, the supreme among two-legged beings.
I pray that from now on, throughout this life and beyond, In the future, I shall obtain a wondrous and beautiful form.”
His body is adorned with exquisite golden garments, Resplendent and magnificent with the brilliance of golden light;
From his mouth issues the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, And his body is suffused with the wondrous scent of sandalwood.
His body is like gold, his skin and form sublime; All who behold him give rise to joy and delight.
All attachments and defilements are completely eliminated; all teachings and meanings are thoroughly understood.
The words and meanings that accord with reality are fully assembled, and all that is non-beneficial is distanced.
This is the supreme object of all contemplation, wherein all marks of adornment are perfectly complete.
May I attain Buddhahood and achieve universal fulfillment, Lovingly cherishing all sentient beings with a compassionate heart;
Possessing the great auspiciousness of pure myriad virtues, And being fully endowed with all manner of sublime treasures.

"When the youth Viśuddhavigraha spoke these verses and made this great vow, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, a manifest sign of his superior retribution appeared: immediately, the youth’s extremely hideous appearance vanished and was no longer seen; it was transformed into a most exquisite and dignified countenance, and his body became like the color of gold. Spontaneously and suddenly, lovely, fine, and beautiful golden garments came from the sky and clothed the youth's body, and there were also ornaments such as bracelets, armlets, and necklaces."

Furthermore, the sons of the gods rained down from the sky a multitude of exquisite celestial flowers—namely, *kalanika* flowers, *utpala* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *mandārava* flowers, and so forth—as well as celestial fragrances, such as sandalwood incense, aloeswood incense, *kunkuma* incense, *tamālapatra* incense, and powdered incense.
Furthermore, a great voice resounded from the sky, saying:
"How marvelous!
One who has planted the seeds of pure giving and lovely merit before the Buddha, the Tathāgata, shall now see the most excellent sprouts and stalks emerge."
At that time, fragrant flowers rained down from the sky in such vast and immeasurable quantities that they accumulated up to the knees.
Then, Vipaśyin Tathāgata emerged from the garden and returned to the wilderness where the Buddha used to dwell.
In his own home, the merchant leader Sukarṇa suddenly said to his wife, "Where is my son now?
His wife replied to her husband:
"A while ago, a youth came to me and said,
'I wish to go to my grandfather's garden,' yet he has not returned to this day."
"You should go quickly to the garden to search for him; perhaps that boy has taken his own life.
The husband spoke again:
"For what reason would my son have brought this upon himself?"
The wife replied again:
"Because my son is both ugly and impoverished, and being driven by hunger and thirst, matters have come to this.
The merchant leader immediately went quickly to the garden to search for his son.

Having arrived, he saw a young boy of exquisite and upright features, his body like the color of gold; the garment he wore was likewise golden, and he was adorned with various ornaments, so lovely that all who beheld him regarded him as a celestial youth of supreme radiance.
Having seen this, he was struck with wonder and immediately said:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"Only one endowed with merit can give birth to such a son.
Having said this, he immediately addressed the boy, saying:
"Whose son are you?"
The youth replied,
"I am the son of the merchant lord Sukarṇa. Thereupon,
the merchant lord immediately reflected deeply within himself:
"Is this youth not playing with me?
Having thought this, he again gave rise to doubt in his mind; observing him closely, he spoke once more:
"O youth!..."
"You should speak according to the truth: whose son are you?
The boy spoke again, "Why do you now seek to investigate me in this manner, O Noble One?"
Speaking truthfully, he said, "I am the son of the merchant leader, Sunetra.
The merchant leader then said,
"How marvelous!"
"Young man!
Why do you persist in such playful mockery? How could it have reached this point?
The merchant leader then carefully examined the matter; having understood it as it truly was, he spoke again:
"O youth! Why is this so?

My son was originally of an ugly and repulsive appearance, yet you now possess a form that is exceptionally wonderful, exquisite, and dignified. By what means have you transformed from an ugly state into one of such dignified appearance?"
At that time, the youth opened his eyes with a joyful expression and spoke these verses for the merchant leader:
"In the past, I was tormented by the fire of poverty, Its blazing flames consuming and oppressing my heart.
I threw myself from a tree, grasping its highest branch; As the branch gave way and I fell to the ground, I sought to end my life."
As a branch falls and wounds the body, suffering assails it; prostrate upon the ground, only a faint breath remains.
At that moment, one is bewildered and unconscious, unaware of anything as life is about to depart in an instant.
At that time, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, having observed this, immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion;
out of that compassion, the Great Holy Honored One descended into the garden to deliver me.
The Buddha’s body radiates light of true golden hue, adorned with the thirty-two marks;
as brilliant as freshly smelted molten gold, it shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
When his light touches my limbs, at the moment of contact, they immediately become cool and refreshing.
From this, all harmony and joy arise, as incomparable nectar flows through me.
The accumulation of many sufferings— hunger, thirst, and afflictions— and all unwholesome states that dwelt within my body,
are all extinguished in an instant when touched by the light of the Buddha’s compassion.
I beheld the Great Sage, the Honored One, a supreme and auspicious mass of wondrous light;
through this, I gave rise to a courageous mind, and having seen him, I was then able to uplift myself.
The World-Honored One is the supreme and greatest auspiciousness, Lofty and prominent like a mountain of jewels;
Furthermore, like a flash of lightning pervading the ten directions, Having seen him in the past, pure faith was born within me.

Thereupon, his heart gave rise to great joy; he removed the small piece of cloth he was wearing and, holding it out, offered it to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, giving birth to the most supreme and pure faith.
I also took a single kalandika flower and offered it to the Buddha;
through the Buddha’s spiritual power, it remained suspended in mid-air, covering him everywhere like a parasol.
At that time, having seen him, my heart was filled with joy;
I reverently prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with a truly pure mind, made this great vow before the Buddha:
"By the cause of this gift to the Buddha, may I, after passing from this life, reach my future births."
Having cast off the mark of ugliness, he obtained a wondrous countenance; ultimately, he shall transcend the ocean of birth and death.
Having spoken these words, a golden robe descended from the heavens; his physical form was adorned and likewise golden.
From his body issued the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and from his mouth wafted the rich scent of *candana*.
By the power of this supreme and most excellent vow, may all that I have undertaken be fully accomplished;
adorned with these many kinds of wondrous marks, may all the characteristics produced be pleasing to the mind.
Great rains of priceless, exquisite garments, golden in color and soft to the touch—
these robes emerge from my body simultaneously, appearing in a single instant.
At that time, there were also hosts of devas who rained down throughout the sky exquisite celestial flowers and various pure,
wondrous incenses, such as sandalwood, aloeswood, and the like.

From the sky there arose the cry, "How truly marvelous! Furthermore, the exquisite music of the devas was played, And all together they proclaimed, "We take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One," Such sounds resounded, pervading everywhere.
All that has been done by me now is supreme and wholesome; therefore, I have attained such sublime marks.
All who see me feel joy in their hearts, for my complexion is like the light of gold, pure and beyond compare.

When the merchant leader Subhadra heard these verses, he immediately leaped for joy, his hair standing on end with rapture. In an instant, pure faith arose within him; joining his palms, he paid reverent homage from afar toward Vipaśyin Tathāgata. Having gazed intently upon the boy Sudarśana, he spoke these words: "O boy!..."
"It would now be fitting for you to return to our original home together with my father.
Then, the youth Sunetra conceived a sense of reverence toward his father; he immediately stepped forward, prostrated himself in salutation, and addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, noble father!"
Having spoken thus, they immediately returned together to their own home.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surveyed the lower realm and became fully aware of these events. He then thought:
"This merchant leader, Subhūṣaṇakarṇa, is able to perform excellent Buddha-work in the presence of the Buddha; how could he possibly continue to dwell in a dilapidated house?"
Having reflected thus, he immediately addressed the devaputra Viśvakarman, saying:
"You should now go to the ruined house of the merchant leader Sutejas and transform it into a magnificent, pure dwelling, consisting of eight tiers made of the four precious substances."

At that time, having received his instructions, the devaputra Viśvakarman arrived in an instant at the house of the merchant leader in the city of Pāṇḍumāla. He transformed the residence, making it pure and adorned with the four jewels; its eight pillars, beams, and rafters were tiered in successive heights, exquisite and beautiful, complete with doors, windows, balconies, casements, and walls. At the gate stood a pavilion adorned with ivory, like an *āmra* fruit.

It was draped with jeweled cords interlaced with hanging pearl flower-garlands; banners and streamers were erected all around, exquisitely beautiful, pure white and immaculate like moonlight or a mass of snow. Intermingled with various silks and countless ornaments of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, sapphire, emerald, and other such wondrous jewels, it served as a magnificent adornment. At each of the four gates, a golden vase was placed.
It was completely filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities, and moreover, it was replete with countless hundreds of thousands of exquisite and rare jewels.

When the merchant leader Sukarṇa returned to his own home, he beheld this magnificent dwelling adorned with such precious treasures; having seen it, he was struck with wonder and his heart was filled with joy.
At that moment, his wife’s heart leaped with joy; she took a golden pitcher filled with water and offered it to her husband for him to wash, saying:
"Virtuous one, by the power of your merit you have summoned such a sublime occurrence as this. From where has this most excellent house, adorned with jewels, been established?"

The merchant leader Subhadra was further filled with exultation and supreme joy; he conceived a vast and pure faith in the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, and his body hair stood on end. With palms joined, he bowed reverently from afar toward the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin and spoke these words:
"The Buddha is an inconceivable great wish-fulfilling jewel, capable of serving as the unsurpassed and most excellent field of merit."
Having spoken these words, his face and countenance became as radiant as a lotus; leaping for joy, he spoke this verse:
"Through the merit thus accomplished, a great field of blessings, Free from all faults and defects, I have planted a seed of giving, however minute;
Yet it now summons a supreme retribution so vast."
In the past, I followed my whims and practiced minor acts of giving; I never possessed the resources or conditions for the most supreme generosity.
Now, adorned with these wondrous jewels, from where has this pure residence come?
In my house of old, sorrow and suffering increased; there was nothing remaining but the walls.
Now why is it so bright and vast, like clouds parting, pure and white as the autumn moon?
In the past, my house was everywhere dilapidated and hollow; insects and mice came and went, and burrows were many.
Now it is adorned with the most supreme jewels; the windows and doors are brilliantly illuminated and entirely pure.
In the past, my house was filled with filth, With the foul sounds of foxes howling and dogs barking;
Now this dwelling is wondrously adorned, And these various jewels fill it to overflowing—from where have they come?
In the past, my house was filled with snakes and insects, and I possessed nothing but tattered, worn-out rags;
now I have exquisite garments, and jeweled fly-whisks hanging with pearls that are truly lovely.
In the past, when the house fire consumed the bones of the deceased, dogs came to gnaw upon them, increasing the foulness;
now there are abundant and wondrous fragrant flowers—whence has this exquisite adornment come?
In former times, I was impoverished and deeply afflicted by suffering, with tears flowing like rain upon my face each day;
now, this precious ground is pure and free of dust, everywhere sprinkled with the wondrous scented water of sandalwood.
Formerly consumed by a great conflagration, with crows perching upon its gates and filth flowing abroad;
now it is adorned with exquisite strings of pearls—whence comes this radiance of golden jewels?
Formerly dwelling in a dilapidated hut with its double doors ruined, the interior was vast and open, unobstructed on all sides.
Now the doors are adorned with exquisite crystal; from where has this lofty, broad, and wondrous beauty come?
In the past, I long dwelt in a dilapidated house, Tilted, precarious, and wretched, which all people loathed;
Now my halls and chambers are wonderfully and magnificently completed, With pillars made entirely of mani-jewels and various precious gems.
In the past, oppressed by the suffering of poverty, my mournful cries resounded throughout the four quarters;
now, drums and flutes vibrate with a grand sound, and the exquisite resonance of the *konghou* lute is once more pure and beautiful.
In the past, my house was filled with many impurities and evils, and it was completely packed with withered bones remaining from cremations.
Now, many kinds of exquisite jewels and treasures, gathered as a mass of gems, fill its interior with adornment.
Those ivory ornaments from the past have fallen, scattered, and burned away until nothing remains;
yet now it is adorned again with exquisite *indranīla* gems, and its perimeter is entirely formed of crystal palaces.
All the exquisite seats were once consumed by fire, Leaving nothing to rely upon save the bare ground before one's eyes;
Yet now, with various kinds of wonderful adornments, The seats are arranged in order and fully prepared.
In former times, the ground was used as a seat, filled with all manner of impurities;
now, upon a soft and exquisite silken mat, he dwells in the Auspicious Seat in perfect bliss.
In the past, upon ground overgrown with weeds and thorns, I spread grass to make a bed for my rest;
yet now, with soft *tūla* cotton used as bedding, my heart is filled with profound joy.
In the past, many diverse things were burned and destroyed, and foul odors filled the house extensively;
now it is perfumed by various exquisite fragrances, pervading the entire room in a lovely, billowing mist.
In former times, both within and without were scorched by flames; truly, it was a destruction amidst destruction.
Now, various kinds of wondrous pearls and treasures stand in solemn array, inspiring profound delight.
Formerly dwelling in a dilapidated hut, sparse and leaking, where crows came and left much filth;
now, within this vast and wondrous mansion, pearl necklaces hang down, increasing its splendor and beauty.
In former times, deeply oppressed by poverty and suffering, they reached out their hands with many cries of terror;
now they have erected jeweled banners and streamers, pure, adorned, and most sublime.
I prostrate to the Tathāgata, the Great Holy Honored One; as the Teacher who is the Field of Merit, I take refuge in you.
Now, arising with compassion, come into this place and rescue me from the ocean of poverty.
I take refuge in the Most Honored One in the World, Vipaśyin, whose name is All-Knowing.
Now, arising with a heart of compassion, come here, And cause me to successfully accomplish my purpose.
Just as the vast and supreme palace in the heavens, adorned with inconceivable merit,
Now arise a heart of compassion and come within this place, Causing my own dwelling to become equal to that excellence.
I now take refuge in the Teacher of the Three Realms, Exalted and prominent like Mount Kailāsa;
My dwelling here is likewise so, Resembling the bright and pure moon of autumn.
I recall that in the past, within this great city, I suffered the extreme miseries of poverty;
through the Buddha’s heart of compassion, he came here, and I obtained vast wealth and became most preeminent.
The seeds I have now planted are but small, yet they swiftly bring forth fruits of benefit both vast and deep;
since the Buddha is the most supreme and honored one in the world, who would not extend offerings to him?
After the merchant leader Subhūṣaṇakarṇa had spoken these verses, his pure faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, increased further, and he thought to himself:

"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has come down to this place and enabled me to obtain many most excellent things. It is now fitting that I invite the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with the assembly of śrāvakas, to first extend a modest offering at my own residence."

Having formed this thought, the merchant leader immediately conceived a vast sense of reverence for Vipaśyin Tathāgata and his assembly of śrāvakas. He invited them to his home and prepared pure, exquisite food and drink of a hundred flavors, making offerings with devotion for seven days. When the meal was finished, he prostrated at their feet and spoke thus:
"For as long as I live, I shall provide and offer all necessary articles of enjoyment."

"When the Buddha came to accept the merchant leader’s offering, there was a man guarding a field in another house who had come to the master’s home at dawn to receive food and was returning on his way. Along the road, he heard that the World-Honored Buddha possessed the virtue of a Great Sage, and that this merchant leader, Miao-er, had offered a single bean cake to the Buddha and immediately obtained an auspicious and supreme sign."
Having heard this, he immediately asked a lay follower nearby:
"Virtuous one!
What noble virtues and supernatural powers does that Buddha, the World-Honored One, possess?"
Then that upāsaka said:
"Son, you should know now that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses towering merit—immeasurable, vast, and most supreme. How could I possibly describe it?"
Nevertheless, I shall now speak to you in brief; you should listen well.
That Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, was endowed with the marks of the supreme Great Man;
his pure and majestic physical radiance shone brilliantly, like a mountain of gold or the sun and moon.
His radiance cannot be equaled; he is a hero, one endowed with excellent precepts, one with sublime physical marks,
one of virtuous speech, one of tranquil mind, one of exquisite adornment, one with a beautiful countenance, one of skillful action,
one who well understands the Dharma, one of excellent patience, and one of excellent eloquence.
He is one who is well-disciplined, well-able to transform others, knowledgeable in the codes of conduct, virtuous and compliant, capable of recognizing kindness,
possessing keen vision, with senses stilled, having severed all craving, having extinguished all ill-will,
having shattered the darkness of ignorance, opening the way to liberation, and establishing the True Dharma.
He who halts those on wrong paths, he who reveals the true path, he who manifests reality, he who severs doubt, he who quiets afflictions,
he who destroys all Māras, he who rescues the world, the true Great Dharma King, the true Mahāsattva,
the great Honored One of the world, the banner of great wisdom, the great hero of sharp faculties.

He is the treasury of great merit, the source of the Great Dharma, the Great Sage and Teacher, the bearer of the Great Dharma, the one who hears and upholds the Great Dharma, and the supreme field of merit for great giving. He is reverently honored by Brahmā and Śakra;
he excels the mundane world in benefiting sentient beings, being the most supreme of all, with all outflows extinguished and stilled.
The limit of suffering is clearly and extensively understood by this great Arhat;
he possesses mastery and fearlessness regarding all dharmas and is preeminent in answering questions within all philosophical discourses.

"Untainted by any faults, he develops all sublime meanings; though fully endowed with physical forms, ethical conduct, meditative concentration, diligence, and wisdom, he remains without attachment. He teaches the Dharma without impediment, is liberated from all suffering and affliction, and is free from all conceptual proliferation. For the sake of others, he reveals the dharmas of benefit and harm, bestowing great compassion and skillful means universally upon sentient beings. Possessing pure and superior resolve, he uses the unsurpassed Dharma to instruct and subdue them."

“He is a great king of physicians who skillfully cures all ailments; he possesses spontaneous wisdom and is preeminent throughout the three realms. His physical form is dignified and solemn, endowed with immeasurable majestic radiance. With few desires and contentment, he knows the proper time and the meaning of things. Fully possessed of right knowledge, he subdues the enemies of the afflictions, extinguishes the fires of the three poisons, and remains unmoved by the eight worldly dharmas.”
The sentient beings of the world are in extreme suffering and distress, mired in the great mire-pit of ignorance.

Having observed them all, the Buddha, by means of his power of wisdom, delivers them accordingly. The Buddha gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings; through his own physical form, majestic power, and noble wisdom, he performs the supreme deeds to cause them to transcend [suffering], as the Buddha is the liberator from all sufferings for the sake of the world.

They skillfully provide consolation to all who are terrified; they skillfully rescue all who are submerged in the mire of birth and death; they skillfully bestow coolness upon all whose minds are scorched by the heat of affliction; and for the sake of all indolent sentient beings, they universally inspire and develop the practice of diligent application.

"In the past, throughout countless hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, the Buddha extensively practiced various forms of giving—offering food, clothing, bedding and seating, elephants, horses, carriages, wives and children, servants, as well as his own head, eyes, blood, and flesh, even cutting off his limbs—treating the worthy and the foolish with equality and remaining free from all marks of existence."

"The Buddha gives rise to various skillful means toward all sentient beings, contemplating their benefit at all times as he universally surveys the world. Seeing that all sentient beings suffer from old age, illness, and death—deluded, agitated, submerged, and without refuge—the Buddha, having universally observed them with a heart of compassion whether they are present before him or not, comforts them all."

“As the Buddhas have taught: ‘If one lacks the various merits such as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, then even if one passes through countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of births, one will ultimately never attain the fruit of unsurpassed, quiescent, great bodhi.’”

Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has diligently cultivated all practices; he is the most supreme and honored among all sentient beings, possessing great renown and practicing the Dharma of peace and security. His consciousnesses are perfectly luminous, and his vigor is vast; the vows he has made are ultimately never in vain. He has shattered the darkness of ignorance and abandoned all faults, possessing manifold virtues and a tranquil mind. Having disciplined the three karmas, he is unstained by the objects of the sense faculties and has attained mastery, free from further existence.

Possessing immeasurable light of majestic virtue, a great treasury of wisdom adorned with all ornaments, and features as pure as the full moon, he is reverently honored, faithfully followed, prostrated to, and praised by the kings of devas, nāgas, and asuras, and by all the hosts of celestial beings.
One whose merit and wisdom are perfected, the Great Sage among sages, appearing like the first radiance of emerging golden light;

sovereign within the Dharma and supreme among all dharmas; having crossed over himself and delivered others to the further shore; the foremost of all, revered by the multitude; like a great dragon king, liberated and fearless, the God among gods.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses great merit that is most supreme and immeasurable; how could it be praised with but a few words?"
The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of the Golden-Colored Boy, Scroll Ten;
The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of the Golden-Colored Boy, Scroll Eleven;
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Grandee.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla and others, Great Masters of the Transmission of the Dharma (Chuanfan), Purple-Robed Recipients of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hongluqing): At that time, the upāsaka again spoke a verse:
“With physical marks gentle and full of myriad virtues, Perfectly accomplished and exquisitely adorned throughout.”
Apart from the Tathāgata, the Great Awakened Honored One, there is no other peerless, supreme being.
The Buddha’s holy speech has no equal; the Buddha’s sharp and keen wisdom is likewise without equal;
the Buddha’s holy understanding is again beyond compare; the Buddha, the Great Muni, is without parallel.
The Buddha’s great vessel of the Dharma is without equal; The Buddha’s supreme and wondrous bliss is likewise without equal;
The Buddha’s skillful taming and gentleness have no peer; The Buddha’s ultimate sublimity and excellence are beyond comparison.
The Buddha is the Great Teacher, without equal; The Buddha is the Father of the World, likewise without equal;
The Buddha is the Good Friend, again without peer; The Buddha is the Beloved Relative, beyond compare.
Without self, without fear, and without the unsubdued;
unstained and far removed from clamor, having already transcended the perils of the three realms of existence, free from enmity and affliction, ever pure.

With pure, well-disciplined, and sublime marks, Possessing the power of mindfulness and great mastery, He universally opens the gate of benefit for all sentient beings; The Buddha is the most supreme and peerless.
In brief, this is the collection of all true virtues, The most excellent teaching according to the Dharma;
The Buddha is the unsurpassed Honored One of the three realms— You should believe in and accept these merits.

At that time, having heard those words of the upāsaka regarding the supreme virtues of the Tathāgata, the field-guardian gave rise to pure faith, and his hair stood on end with joy. He then spoke these words:

“When that merchant leader Sumukha offered a single bean-cake to Vipaśyin Tathāgata, he planted the most supreme and pure field of merit. In that very instant, the merchant leader was freed from all poverty and suffering. Relying upon the Buddha’s spiritual power, and sustained by the power of his vow to practice giving with a pure mind using even the slightest material object, he obtained this wish-fulfilling jewel through this superior cause.”

Now, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin has not been encountered for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, being exceedingly difficult to meet; yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, cultivated and perfected supreme, vast, and most excellent meritorious deeds for the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings. Moved by compassion, he extensively employs skillful means to rescue and deliver sentient beings who have been bitten by the venomous snakes of birth-and-death and afflictions and have fallen into extreme suffering, regarding them with loving-kindness and care as if they were his own kinsmen and friends.

As for me now, my household possesses no wealth; though I have long labored with effort, I have never accumulated even the slightest store. Nevertheless, with a pure heart, I shall take the food obtained from tending my own field and, though it be extremely meager, offer it to you as a gift.
"Furthermore, you should make this vow: 'May all sentient beings universally attain the fulfillment of their most supreme aspirations.
As that field-guardian uttered these words, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin immediately manifested his presence before him through his supernormal powers."

At that time, the field-guard saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose majestic virtue was extraordinary and whom he had never beheld before; his physical marks were upright and serene like a mountain of gold, and his radiance shone so brightly that it eclipsed the sun and moon.

Having seen this, he immediately gave rise to the most supreme and vast faith and devotion; with a pure mind, he took all the food he possessed and offered it into the pure alms-bowl of the World-Honored One, Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having made this offering, he further gave rise to supreme pure faith; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he made a great vow and spoke these verses:

“By the merit obtained through this gift to the Buddha, I pray that after this life has passed, I shall give rise to the most sublime heart of compassion And universally bring benefit to all sentient beings.”
Just as the Buddha has realized the unsurpassed path, And just as the Buddha’s marks and signs are perfectly fulfilled,
So shall I become a Buddha, likewise, Universally attaining all peerless dharmas.
Just as the Buddha has proclaimed the True Dharma, And just as the Buddha has accomplished all-knowledge,
May I likewise attain the fruit, Possessing all-knowledge and skillfully teaching the Dharma.
Just as the Buddha, having subdued the armies of Māra, Skillfully turned the pure Great Wheel of Dharma,
So shall I likewise attain the fruit of his deeds, Subduing the armies of Māra and proclaiming the True Dharma.
Within the great ocean of birth and death, the Buddha has himself crossed over and delivered others, bringing all to liberation;
I too shall deliver all sentient beings, leading them to liberation so that we may together return to the Unsurpassed Way.
At that time, Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, immediately uttered a profound and vast sound like the roar of clouds, and bestowed this prophecy upon the field-guardian, saying:
“O son of good family!

In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Sarvārthasiddha; you will become a teacher of the three realms, endowed with great majestic virtue, and by means of supreme power, you will subdue the armies of Māra and perform the Buddha-work as practiced by all Buddhas.
At that time, after the Tathāgata Vipaśyin had bestowed the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the field-guardian, he returned to his original place.

When all the people of the city of Potalaka heard of this matter, even the king, having heard it, recalled the power of the field-guardian’s roots of goodness. The king then prepared his carriage and went to the field-guardian’s dwelling; with a mind of profound faith and respect, he adorned a precious elephant and placed a seat upon it, commanding the man to mount the elephant and accompanying him back to the royal palace to bestow half of the kingdom upon him.
Then the field-guardian immediately addressed the king, saying:
"As Your Majesty has commanded, it is not what this servant desires; according to my own aspiration and joy, I wish to seek renunciation and purely cultivate the holy life."
The king immediately granted his wish, and the king returned to his palace.

At that time, the field-guard went forth as a monk under the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha; he practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) until the end of his days, and after his death, he was reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).

Finally, because that youth Su-lakṣaṇa was endowed with supreme virtues, the multitude collectively enthroned him according to royal protocol; he presided over the throne for sixty thousand years, governing through the True Dharma, and after passing away, was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed King Ajātaśatru,
saying: "Great King,
what do you think?"
Who else could that King Suvarṇalakṣaṇa have been in the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha? It was none other than this Bhikṣu Suvarṇavarṇa.

In the past, when he saw the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, because he was poor, he removed a single small piece of clothing from his own body and offered it to the Buddha. Having made the offering, he immediately made a vast vow. Due to this wholesome karma, he experienced supreme and wondrous bliss among gods and humans; wherever he was born, his body was golden in color, and a golden garment would naturally cover him. At the time of his birth, the heavens rained down various exquisite celestial flowers. Even until now, he possesses great merit and virtue; whenever a fine garment is shed from his body, another grows forth in its place, and he is endowed with all the marks of excellence.
The merchant leader Surasena at that time was none other than the merchant leader Divākara of today;
the wife of the merchant leader Surasena at that time was none other than the wife of the merchant leader Divākara of today;
and the female messenger at that time was none other than the young girl Kāśisundarī of today.
"The house servant at that time was none other than the minister Virūḍhaka here and now.
At that moment, King Ajātaśatru again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying,
"What karma did this Bhikṣu Suvarṇavarṇa create?"
In the past, he was without fault; yet people falsely constructed defiled conditions for him, placing him upon an iron fork to end his life.
Furthermore, by what cause did he immediately leave the household life and realize the fruit of Arhatship?
The Venerable One replied:
"Great King!

In a past age, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

At that time, there was a certain kingdom where, outside the city walls, stood a monastery where a community of monks resided. Among them, one bhikṣu was skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, the brahmins and elders of the city all came to listen to the Dharma, and offerings and provisions gathered from all quarters.

"Subsequently, there was another bhikṣu named Ajita who came to reside in this monastery; he was exceptionally brilliant and skilled in preaching the Dharma, possessing unimpeded eloquence, with speech that was elegant and a voice that was clear and beautiful."

At that time, the entire multitude came to the place where the bhikṣu Ajita was, to listen to his preaching of the Dharma; what he expounded was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, profound in its words and meaning, and characterized by the pure, singular, and pristine conduct of Brahma-faring.

At that time, when the people from the four quarters heard of this, they were filled with faith and admiration; they provided all necessities, including food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness. Consequently, the offerings and gains previously received by the bhikṣu who preached the Dharma were completely cut off.
At that time, the bhikṣu who was preaching the Dharma thought to himself:
"Now that the bhikṣu Viśeṣa resides here with me, my gains and offerings will surely be interrupted."
Furthermore, because these gains have been cut off, will not those who are learned and wise, as well as the faithful lay devotees, cease to show me respect?
Thus, he gives rise to fear.
Having reflected thus, he immediately devised a deceptive scheme to obstruct the matter.
He went to summon a young Brahmin girl and had her return, fabricating grounds for defilement to slander that Bhikṣu, the Unconquerable One.
At that time, the young girl acted according to her instructions.

Later, on a certain day, while that preaching bhikṣu was gathered with the other bhikṣus at the entrance of the monastery cell, conversing as usual, the girl suddenly approached and said to the assembly:
"Among you who have left the household life, could there be anyone who does not practice the holy life?"
"Why is this so? That Bhikṣu Viśeṣa has just now pressured me with defiled intent; among those who practice the holy life (brahmacārin), this is not proper.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they covered their ears and said to the young girl:
"Do not speak thus!
Do not let others hear such evil words.
Yet the Dharma-preaching Bhikṣu uttered unwholesome speech to slander that Bhikṣu Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:
"An unwholesome deed was committed exactly as it was.
Eventually, this report reached the ear of the bhikṣu Anabhibhū.
Upon hearing it, he spoke these words:
"Why has that bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma spoken such words to me?
Having said this, he immediately went to where that bhikṣu was.
Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
"I have not offended you, Venerable One; why do you utter such evil words to revile and disparage me so persistently?
At that time, the bhikṣu who was preaching the Dharma became even more incensed and spoke further harsh words of reproach and disparagement, saying:
"You possess this transgression; in the future, you shall surely suffer the agony of the iron fork."
When the bhikṣu Ajita heard this, he thought to himself:
"Such conduct destroys the dharma of spiritual practice.
Having realized this, he immediately gathered up his robes and bowl, left the monastery, and went to rest beneath a tree as he pleased.
At that time, when the fourfold assembly saw this, they all rushed after him together, exhorting and entreatying him to turn back, but he ultimately did not comply with their request.
Then the bhikṣu who was preaching the Dharma reflected to himself:

"What I have done now is truly unwholesome; for the sake of gain and offerings, I have generated karma leading to the evil realms. Having considered this thoroughly, his heart was filled with extreme remorse, and he thought, "I should go to him and seek absolution for my transgression."

Having thought this, he immediately and swiftly left the monastery to seek out the Venerable Bhikṣu Ajita. Deeply reproaching himself, his eyes overflowed with tears, like a young child weeping piteously without ceasing.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of brahmins, householders, and other assemblies all witnessed this event; having arrived, they immediately approached the bhikṣu Ajita, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him thus:
"Venerable One!..."

I now repent of my transgressions and pray that the Venerable One will grant me forgiveness. Like a young child, like a foolish person, I lacked clarity; for the sake of gain and offerings, I committed unwholesome deeds and uttered unwholesome words based on false causes. To slander and revile the Venerable One was a most grievous offense!
"This is a profound transgression!
Venerable sir, out of compassion, I pray that you will grant me your forbearance.
The Bhikṣu Anabhibhū replied:
“Venerable Sir!

I have already accepted [the teachings]. Now, merely because my mind is weary of clamor and bustle, I dwell beneath a tree in the full lotus posture, sitting in meditation with body upright and mindfulness established, practicing the conduct of tranquility.”

Having spoken these words, the bhikṣu Anabhibhū gave rise to the most supreme sense of weary detachment. He reflected in stillness that the world is truly worthy of awe and dread: conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) flow on and perish without ceasing; the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) circulate and transmigrate through the stream of birth and death; and even the offerings and praises of Śakra and the various devas are not ultimate.

Having formed this thought, his two wings immediately rose and soared like those of a king of geese; held high in the sky, they were pure and brilliant white. The entire assembly beheld them and gave rise to a mind of supreme, pure faith, as he then manifested various miraculous transformations in mid-air.
When the bhikṣu who was preaching the Dharma saw this, he immediately said: "Alas!
How could I have now reviled and disparaged this Great Sage and Holy One?"
Having spoken these words, he fell to the ground, unconscious and prostrate.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candracchattra, knowing this matter, gave rise to a heart of compassion for this bhikṣu, thinking: "May he not lose his life by vomiting blood. He immediately exercised his supernormal powers and appeared before him.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, extended his hand—its webbed fingers and palm adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings—and touched the crown of that bhikṣu’s head to comfort him well.
As soon as the Buddha’s hand touched him, the bhikṣu regained his original state of mind and attained ease; he immediately rose and, before the Buddha, performed a sincere confession.
At that time, the Tathāgata Moon of Wondrous Virtue spoke these verses for the sake of the great assembly:
"When a person dwells in the world, If they utter evil words from their mouth,
It is like a sharp blade or axe That cuts and severs their own body."
One should praise, yet one gives rise to slander; one should slander, yet one gives rise to praise.
Evil speech is born from the mouth, yet that which issues forth goes unnoticed.
When an evil mind first arises, it is small, like losing wealth at a game of dice.
In this world, great evil arises, namely, the slandering of arhats.
When the mind gives rise to the cause of slander, sentient beings fall into the evil realms;
when the mind gives rise to the cause of purity, sentient beings proceed to the happy realms.

“At that time, the Tathāgata Wonderful Moon extensively proclaimed the sublime Dharma for the fourfold assembly; having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, he returned to his original place.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:
“Great King!
What do you think?
Was that bhikṣu who preached the Dharma at that time someone else?
He was none other than this very bhikṣu Suvarṇavarṇa.

In the past, he gave rise to false accusations against the bhikṣu Anabhibhū, slandering and reviling an arhat who had attained the fruits of the path. Due to the retribution of this karma, for five hundred lifetimes he fell into the great hells; having exhausted the suffering and retribution in each individual hell, he fell for another five hundred lifetimes into the realm of hungry ghosts, and for another five hundred lifetimes into the realm of animals. After those respective retributions were exhausted, he was born among humans for five hundred lifetimes, yet in every single lifetime he continued to suffer for his original transgressions.

Because he falsely constructed defiled conditions for others, he was impaled upon an iron fork and underwent great suffering; this continued until now, when his retribution for evil karma was exhausted, and finally, that fierce and tyrannical minister unjustly seized him on false charges of a crime and placed him upon an iron fork, whereupon I used my supernatural power to rescue him and bring about his liberation.
“Great King!

Because of this karmic offense, this person has invited the fruit of suffering. However, having previously gone forth with pure faith and practiced the holy life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Sun-Moon through his roots of goodness, by virtue of that wholesome karma he has now gone forth purely within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.”
"Therefore, Great King!

It would be better for the beings of this world to suffer their own misfortune than to harbor a mind of slander toward others; one should fear ill repute for oneself rather than causing others to incur a bad reputation; and if one experiences happiness oneself, one should immediately share that joy with others."

When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this Dharma, countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings attained great benefit: some realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*, some the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and some the fruit of *arhat*; some resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, some resolved their minds upon the enlightenment of a *śrāvaka*, and some resolved their minds toward refuge and received the lay precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*).
Furthermore, within the assembly, there were those who simply came to know that the Buddha is trustworthy, the Dharma is worthy of refuge, and the Saṅgha is worthy of veneration.
At that time, the merchant leader Sūryodgata knelt on his right knee within the assembly, joined his palms in reverent salutation, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable One!..."

In the past, I made this vow: "I wish to invite the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus to my own home, providing them with food and drink as a modest offering, and presenting each bhikṣu with a superior, exquisite robe worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold."
Alas, how meager is our merit!
Now that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, I now most sincerely invite the Venerable Ones and the assembly of bhikṣus to accept my offerings at my home.
The Venerable One replied:
"Excellent, O caravan leader!"
In accordance with your wish, I shall, together with all the śrāvaka disciples of all the Śākyamuni Tathāgatas throughout Jambudvīpa, assemble and attend your invitation.

At that time, the merchant leader Sūrya, his wishes fulfilled, was filled with great joy. He immediately purified the interior and exterior of the city, removing all earth, stones, sand, and gravel. He erected banners and streamers, sprinkled sandalwood-scented water everywhere, hung flower garlands and various precious ornaments, burned many famous incenses, and scattered exquisite flowers. Having thus arranged these extraordinary and magnificent decorations, he prepared for the occasion.

Having prepared various kinds of pure, supreme, fragrant, and delicious food and drink, he arranged exquisite mats and seats by the time of dawn and interspersed them with pure, wonderful water jars of incense. When the hour for the meal approached, he sent a messenger to inform the Venerable Ānanda:
"The meal is ready; we pray that the Venerable One will deign to come."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, by means of his supernormal power, leaped into the air and emitted golden light that illuminated this Jambudvīpa everywhere. In the sky, *gaṇḍī* drums spontaneously resounded with a great roar, and they proclaimed these words:
"All the Blessed One’s śrāvaka assemblies who have attained supernatural powers, each by their own supernormal power, shall come to attend this invitation."
"May all the assembly of ordinary worldlings also come to attend, relying upon the supernatural power of the Venerable Ānanda.
At that time, having heard these words issued from the dry rattle drum, the entire assembly of śrāvakas each departed from their respective dwelling places—
namely, from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Great Snow Mountains, and the great wilderness.
Mountains, Mount Māla, Mount Khadiraka, Mount Gandhamādana, Mount Sumeru, Mount Yugandhara,
Mount Īṣādhara, and Mount Nimindhara; together with their gardens, groves, trees, villages, cities, rivers, and lakes,
as well as the great oceans, the abodes of rishis, and even the empty dwellings abandoned by the wayside.
In the Śmaśāna and other such places, the great assembly of bhikṣus arose from samādhi; in an instant,
they each leaped into the air like *aśoka* flowers, and multicolored clouds of blue, yellow, red,
and white completely covered them as they descended slowly from the sky into the great city of Rājagṛha, filling both its interior and exterior in a single moment.
The number of three koṭis consists of three categories:
first, the assembly of those whose outflows are exhausted;
second, the assembly of those still in training.
Third is the assembly of ordinary persons who are virtuous.
At that time, once the Venerable Ānanda and the great multitude had arrived at the assembly, they sat down in order according to their rank—superior, middling, and inferior.

At that time, the merchant leader Divākara, having observed that the assembly was seated and settled, personally offered the most excellent and pure food and drink with his own hands. When the Venerable Ānanda and the great assembly had finished their meal and each had washed their alms bowls, the merchant leader immediately wished to offer a set of three exquisite robes, worth hundreds of thousands, to the Venerable and the rest of the assembly; as he did so, he looked up at them with a mind of pure faith.
At that time, the bhikṣu Suvarṇavarṇa, understanding his father’s intention, spoke these words:
“I shall now assist my father in the practice of giving.

Having said this, in the space of a single kṣaṇa, he stripped from his own body the three golden robes he was wearing and offered them one after another to those three koṭis of venerable ones. As soon as he removed each robe, another would instantly reappear, never being exhausted.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of devas in the air all raised their voices together, saying:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"It is truly rare and marvelous!
From the sky, various celestial music resounded once more, and a rain of manifold heavenly flowers fell.

At that time, the entire assembly gathered from all directions—the sovereign King Ajātaśatru, his court ladies, retinue, ministers, officials, and commoners—raised their joyful eyes, witnessed this event, and all exclaimed in unison:
“Excellent! Excellent!
This is truly most rare.”
Furthermore, he praised these words three times:
"How marvelous!
The ripening of the fruits of merit planted is truly sublime."
How marvelous!
All merits possess great power.
How marvelous!
Generosity is a profound and firm field of merit.

Therefore, one should know that if one plants the seeds of giving, the superior retribution will not be in vain. When those possessed of wisdom examine such matters of karmic fruit and retribution, who would not plant in the pure field of generosity?
When he had spoken thus, hundreds of thousands of people joined their palms in homage at his feet and cried out with one voice, "Namo Buddhāya!

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda extensively expounded the Dharma of the purity of giving to the great assembly. Then the merchant-suzerain Sūryodgata rose from his seat, knelt on his right knee toward the Venerable Ānanda, joined his palms in homage, and three times made this declaration:
“Venerable Sir!

That I have now beheld such a sublime sign is not something that could be brought about by my father, nor my mother, nor a king, nor a deva, nor my kinsmen or friends, nor by any śramaṇas or brahmins.”

"Only may the Venerable One, with his compassionate heart, skillfully rescue me. Just as in the past my tears of affectionate love flowed like an ocean, the Venerable One’s supernatural power has dried up the source of that craving."
Having spoken these words, he recited a verse:
"The Venerable One has already transcended birth, old age, and death; He is venerated by all among gods and humans.
A holy lord such as this is difficult to behold even in a thousand lifetimes; To see him now brings the benefit of a truly non-empty, supreme fruit."
Then the Venerable Ānanda extensively expounded the Dharma for the entire assembly gathered there, providing instruction, benefit, and joy as was appropriate.

Having performed this work of a Buddha, countless hundreds of thousands of devas and humans in the assembly, as well as the entire multitude from the city of Rājagṛha, all gave rise to pure hearts, took refuge, and prostrated, saying:
"We have each now obtained excellent benefit."
Having spoken thus, he immediately rose from his seat and departed from the assembly.
